Where does the Amen so resound, like heavenly thunder, that the empty temples of the idols are shaken? Not that the Romans have another faith than this which all the churches of Christ have, but that devotion is greater in them, and simplicity in believing. Again, they are accused of facility and of pride. Of facility, as there: "I beseech you, brothers, that you watch those who cause dissensions and offenses, contrary to the doctrine which you have learned; and turn aside from them; for such men do not serve Christ the Lord, but their own belly; and by sweet words and blessings they seduce the hearts of the innocent. For your obedience is spread abroad to every place. I rejoice therefore in you, and I wish you to be wise in good and simple in evil" (Rom. 16:17 ff.). And of pride: "Be not high-minded, but fear" (Rom. 11:20, 25). And: "I do not wish you to be ignorant, brothers, of this mystery, that you may not be wise in yourselves". And in what follows: "For I say, through the grace that has been given to me, to all who are among you: not to be wise beyond what one ought to be wise, but to be wise unto sobriety" (Rom. 12:3). And more openly: "To rejoice with those who rejoice; to weep with those who weep. Being of the same mind toward one another. Not minding high things, but consenting to the humble. Do not be prudent in your own sight" (Rom. 12:15-16). He also marks the Corinthians, because their women are with uncovered head and the men let their hair grow (1 Cor. 11), and they eat indifferently in temples (1 Cor. 8:10), and, puffed up with secular wisdom, they deny the resurrection of the flesh. That these things in part remain to this day, no one who has seen Achaia can doubt (1 Cor. 4). The Macedonians are praised for love, and for hospitality and the reception of the brothers. Hence it is written to them: "But concerning the love of the brotherhood we have no need to write to you. For you yourselves have learned from God to love one another. And indeed you do it toward all the brothers in all Macedonia" (1 Thess. 4:9). But they are rebuked because they go idly round the houses, and, looking for another's food, while they desire to please each one and run about hither and thither, they report what is done at each person's house. For it follows: "But we beseech you, brothers, that you abound more, and take pains to be quiet, and that you do your own business, and work with your hands, as we commanded you, so that you may walk honestly toward those who are outside, and may desire nothing of anyone" (1 Thess. 4:10-11). And lest anyone think this was urged more from the duty of a teacher than because of a fault of the people, in the second letter to the same he presses and repeats it, saying: "For even when we were with you, we declared this to you, that if anyone will not work, neither let him eat. For we have heard that some among you walk restlessly, doing no work, but acting as busybodies. Now those who are such we charge and beseech in the Lord Jesus Christ, that, working in silence, they eat their own bread" (2 Thess. 3:10 ff.). It would be long if I wished to note, from the Apostle and from all the Scriptures, either the virtues or the vices of the individual nations, since we have come down to these very things we have said from the fact that the Galatians were pronounced foolish and senseless. Whoever has seen Ancyra, the metropolitan city of Galatia, knows with me by how many schisms it is torn even now, by how many varieties of doctrines it is defiled. I pass over the Cataphrygians, Ophites, Borborites and Manichaeans; for these are by now familiar names of human calamity. Who has ever heard, in any part of the Roman world, of the Passalorynchites and Ascodrobi and Artotyrites, and the rest, monsters rather than names? Traces of the ancient folly remain to this day. One thing we add, and so pay what was promised at the beginning: that the Galatians, apart from the Greek speech which the whole East speaks, have their own language, almost the same as the Treveri, and it does not matter if they have corrupted some things in it, since the Africans too have in some part changed the language of the Phoenicians, and Latinity itself changes daily both by regions and by time. But now let us return to our purpose.
Homily on Galatians 3

As ye do not attend, says he, to long discourses, nor are willing to contemplate the magnitude of this Economy, I am desirous, (seeing your extreme ignorance,) to convince you by concise arguments and a summary method of proof. Before, he had convinced them by what he said to Peter; now, he encounters them entirely with arguments, drawn not from what had occurred elsewhere, but from what had happened among themselves. And his persuasives and proofs are adduced, not merely from what was given them in common with others, but from what was especially conferred on themselves. Therefore he says, "This only would I learn from you, Received ye the Spirit by the works of the Law, or by the hearing of faith." Ye have received, he says, the Holy Spirit, ye have done many mighty works, ye have effected miracles in raising the dead, in cleansing lepers, in prophesying, in speaking with tongues,-did the Law confer this great power upon you? was it not rather Faith, seeing that, before, ye could do no such things? Is it not then the height of madness for these who have received such benefits from Faith, to abandon it, and desert back to the Law which can offer you nothing of the same kind?
Commentary on Galatians

This only I wish to learn from you: did you receive the spirit by works of the Law, or by the hearing of faith?

There are indeed, he says, many things that could compel you by questioning to admit that the Gospel is to be preferred to the Law; but since you are senseless and can by no means hear them, I speak with you in plain language and ask about what is ready to hand: the Holy Spirit whom you received, did the works of the Law, the observance of the sabbath, the superstition of circumcision and of new moons give him to you, or the hearing of faith, through which you believed, coming from the Gentiles? But if it cannot be denied that the Holy Spirit, and the powers which at the beginning of faith followed the Spirit once received, were given not by works of the Law but by faith in Christ, it is manifest that you, having begun from better things, are collapsing into worse. Let us consider carefully, however, that he did not say: I wish to learn from you whether you received the Spirit by works; but added: by works of the Law. For he knew that Cornelius the centurion too had received the Spirit by works (Acts 10), but not by works of the Law, which he did not know. But if it is said on the contrary, "Then the Spirit can be received even without the hearing of faith," we shall answer that he did indeed receive the Spirit, but by the hearing of faith and by the natural law, which speaks in our hearts that every good thing is to be done and evil things avoided; by which, as we have related before, Abraham, Moses and the other saints were also justified; and which the observance of works and the righteousness of the Law can afterwards increase: not, however, of the carnal law, which has passed away, but of the spiritual, because the Law is spiritual. Nor indeed, because we prefer faith, do we destroy the works of the Law (Rom. 3), nor do we say, as certain people do: "Let us do evil things until good things come" (whose condemnation is just); but we set grace before slavery. And we say that what the Jews do out of fear, we do out of love: that they are slaves, we sons; that they are compelled to the good, we take up the good of our own accord. Therefore from faith in Christ there is not born a license to sin; rather, from the love of faith the will to do good works is increased, since we do good things not because we dread the judge, but because we know that they please him in whom we believe. Someone may ask: if faith is not except by hearing, how can those who were born deaf become Christians? For anyone can understand God the Father from the greatness and beauty of creatures, and the Creator is consequently recognized from the things created; but the birth, the cross, the death and the resurrection of Christ cannot be known except by hearing. Either, then, the deaf are not Christians; or, if the deaf are Christians, what is said elsewhere by the apostle is false: "So faith is by hearing, and hearing through the word of God". To this, one who is content with a simple answer says that he did not say generally, "The faith of all is by hearing," but "faith is by hearing," which can be taken both in part and in whole: that is, the faith of those who hear, who believe, is by hearing. But one who tries to satisfy this scruple will first attempt to assert that the deaf can learn the Gospel by nods too, and by daily intercourse, and, so to speak, by the speaking gesture of the whole body; and then also this, that the word of God, to whom nothing is deaf, speaks rather to those ears of which he himself says in the Gospel: "He who has ears to hear, let him hear" (Luke 8:8). And in the Apocalypse: "He who has an ear, let him hear what the spirit says to the churches" (Rev. 2:11). And Isaiah: "The Lord added to me an ear" (Isa. 50:4-5). This is the other man, to whom God speaks in secret, who cries in the heart of the believer: "Abba, Father" (Rom. 8:15); and (as we have often explained) just as the body has all its members and senses, so the soul too has all the senses and members, and among the rest ears as well; and whoever has these will not greatly need these ears of the body for coming to know the Gospel of Christ. At the same time, observe this too, that here the Spirit, without any addition, is understood as the Holy Spirit, whom we obtain by the gift of God, and not as the spirit of man, of which it is written elsewhere: "The incorruptible Spirit is in all things" (Wisd. 12:1). And: "The Spirit himself bears witness to our spirit" (Rom. 8:16). And in another place: "No one knows the things that are in a man except the spirit of the man that is in him" (1 Cor. 2:11). And in Daniel: "Bless the Lord, you spirits and souls of the righteous" (Dan. 3:86).
The Stromata Book 3

Does not the Saviour who heals the soul also heal the body of its passions? But if the flesh were hostile to the soul, he would not have raised an obstacle to the soul by strengthening with good health the hostile flesh. "This I say, brethren, that flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God nor corruption incorruption." For sin being corruption cannot have fellowship with incorruption which is righteousness. "Are you so foolish?" he says; "having begun in the Spirit are you now to be made perfect by the flesh."
Homily on Galatians 3

Here again he seasonably interposes a rebuke; time, he says, should have brought improvement; but, so far from advancing, ye have even retrograded. Those who start from small beginnings make progress to higher things; ye, who began with the high, have relapsed to the low. Even had your outset been carnal, your advance should have been spiritual, but now, after starting from things spiritual, ye have ended your journey in that which is carnal; for to work miracles is spiritual, but to be circumcised is carnal. And after miracles ye have passed to circumcision, after having apprehended the truth ye have fallen back to types, after gazing on the sun ye seek a candle, after having strong meat ye run for milk. He says, "made perfect," which means not "initiated" merely, but "sacrificed," signifying that their teachers took and slew them like animals, while they resigned themselves to suffer what those teachers pleased. As if some captain, or distinguished man, after a thousand victories and trophies, were to subject himself to infamy as a deserter, and offer his body to be branded at the will of others.
Commentary on Galatians

Are you so foolish that, though you began with the Spirit, you are now made perfect in the flesh?

If the Galatians had received the Holy Spirit, how were they foolish? But this is at once resolved: they had indeed begun with the Spirit, but when they were being made perfect in the flesh, the Spirit was taken away from them. Hence they suffered so many things in vain, as many as they suffered. That this might not befall him after his sin, David prays, saying: "Take not your holy Spirit from me" (Ps. 50:13). Notice carefully that he who follows the Scriptures according to the letter is said to be made perfect in the flesh. Wherefore that which is written to the Corinthians: "Living in the flesh, we do not wage war according to the flesh" (2 Cor. 10:3), can better be understood thus, that those are said to wage war in the flesh who expound the Old Testament in a lowly manner. But those who follow the spiritual understanding may indeed be in the flesh, because they have the same letter as the Jews, yet they do not wage war according to the flesh, since they pass over from the flesh to the spirit. When you see one who first believes from among the Gentiles, and puts his hand to the plough of Christ, and, with some prudent teacher going before him, so advances along the road of the Law to the Gospel that he understands all those things which are written there, about the sabbath, about unleavened bread, about circumcision, about victims, in a manner worthy of God; and then, after the reading of the Gospel, is persuaded by some Jew, or by an associate of the Jews, to abandon the shadows and the clouds of allegory and to interpret the Scriptures just as they are written: of him you can say: Are you so foolish that, though you began with the spirit, you are now made perfect in the flesh?
Homily on Galatians 3

This remark is far more piercing than the former, for the remembrance of their miracles would not be so powerful as the exhibition of their contests and endurance of sufferings for Christ's sake. All that you have endured, says he, these men would strip you of, and would rob you of your crown. Then, lest he should dismay and unnerve, he proceeds not to a formal judgment, but subjoins, "if it be indeed in vain;" if you have but a mind to shake off drowsiness and recover yourselves, he says, it is not in vain. Where then be those who would cut off repentance? Here were men who had received the Spirit, worked miracles, become confessors, encountered a thousand perils and persecutions for Christ's sake, and after so many achievements had fallen from grace; nevertheless he says, if ye have the purpose, ye may recover yourselves.
Commentary on Galatians

Have you suffered so much without cause, if indeed it is without cause?

Let us consider the unhappy Jews, with how great superstition and labor of observance they live among the other nations, saying, touch not, taste not, handle not; and we shall prove that what is said is true: Have you suffered so much without cause; but the sentence is not at once tempered toward them, and it becomes doubtful, if indeed it is without cause, because it is said of those who are able to return from the Law to the Gospel. But it can better be understood thus: that the Galatians, when they first believed in the Crucified, suffered many reproaches both from the Jews and from the Gentiles, and endured no small persecutions. These they are charged with having suffered in vain, if they withdraw from the grace of Christ, for the sake of which they suffered so much. At the same time there is also this hope: that whoever has labored for the faith of Christ and has afterward fallen into sin, just as he is said to have suffered his former things without cause while he sins, so in turn he does not lose them, if he returns to his original faith and to his former zeal. Otherwise: If, he says, you think that circumcision ought to be followed after grace, then all that you have suffered while living until the present time without circumcision has been brought to nothing. And indeed you seem to me not to have endured these things in vain, for I know that the Law has no force after the Gospel. Or certainly thus: It would have been no light loss if, by following circumcision, you had lost only your former labor of faith; but now the penalty of transgression is also joined to this harm, so that you have both suffered the past things without cause and will be tormented in the future. Some understand it in a more forced way, thus: Consider the former freedom of grace and the burdens of the present observance in the Law, and you will see how many things you have done with fruitless zeal; although the fruit of this error is not to be wholly despaired of, since you were led to this very thing by zeal for God. For pardon can be granted to the ignorant, if, turned to better things, you show that it was your knowledge that wavered in you, not your zeal.
Against Heresies Book IV

But that our faith was also prefigured in Abraham, and that he was the patriarch of our faith, and, as it were, the prophet of it, the apostle has very fully taught, when he says in the Epistle to the Galatians: "He therefore that ministereth to you the Spirit, and worketh miracles among you, [doeth he it] by the works of the law, or by the hearing of faith? Even as Abraham believed God, and it was accounted unto him for righteousness. Know ye therefore, that they which are of faith, the same are the children of Abraham. But the Scripture, foreseeing that God would justify the heathen through faith, announced beforehand unto Abraham, that in him all nations should be blessed. So then they which be of faith shall be blessed with faithful Abraham." For which [reasons the apostle] declared that this man was not only the prophet of faith, but also the father of those who from among the Gentiles believe in Jesus Christ, because his faith and ours are one and the same: for he believed in things future, as if they were already accomplished, because of the promise of God; and in like manner do we also, because of the promise of God, behold through faith that inheritance [laid up for us] in the [future] kingdom.
Homily on Galatians 3

Have ye been vouchsafed, he says, so great a gift, and achieved such wonders, because ye observed the Law, or because ye adhered to Faith? plainly on account of Faith. Seeing that they played this argument to and fro, that apart from the Law, Faith had no force, he proves the contrary, viz., that if the Commandments be added, Faith no longer avails; for Faith then has efficacy when things from the Law are not added to it. "Ye who would be justified by the Law, ye are fallen away from grace:" This he says later, when his language has grown bolder, employing the vantage-ground by that time gained; meanwhile while gaining it, he argues from their past experience. For it was when ye obeyed Faith, he says, not the Law, that ye received the Spirit and wrought miracles.

And here, as the Law was the subject of discussion, he moots another special point of controversy, and very opportunely and with much cogency introduces a notice of Abraham.
Commentary on Galatians

He therefore who gives you the Spirit and works miracles among you, does he do it by the works of the Law, or by the hearing of faith?

Gives (tribuit), that is, ministers (administrat), is to be read in the present tense, so as to show that the Holy Spirit is ministered to the worthy always, every hour and moment; and that the more anyone has advanced in the work and love of God, the more he has in himself the powers of the Holy Spirit, which the hearing of faith, and not the works of the Law, brings to completion. Not that the works of the Law are to be despised, and simple faith sought without them; but that the works themselves are to be adorned by faith in Christ. For shrewd is that saying of a wise man: "Not that the faithful man lives by righteousness, but that the righteous man lives by faith." At the same time it is shown that the Galatians, having received the Holy Spirit after they believed, had gifts of powers, that is, prophecy, kinds of tongues, healings of diseases, and the rest that are enumerated to the Corinthians among the spiritual gifts (1 Cor. 12). And yet after such great things (because perhaps they did not have the grace of discerning spirits) they were ensnared by false teachers. It must also be observed that miracles are said to be worked among those who do not hold the truth of the Gospel: as among those who, not following the Lord, were doing signs in his name, John especially complaining: "Master, we saw someone casting out demons in your name, and we forbade him, because he does not follow with us" (Mark 9:37). This is against the heretics, who think the proof of their faith lies in whether they have done some sign. Though they have eaten and drunk in the name of the Lord (for they too have a sacrilegious altar), and boast that they have done many signs by invoking the Savior, on the day of judgment they will deserve to hear: "I do not know you; depart from me, you who work iniquity" (Matt. 7:23).
Against Heresies Book V

If, then, God promised him the inheritance of the land, yet he did not receive it during all the time of his sojourn there, it must be, that together with his seed, that is, those who fear God and believe in Him, he shall receive it at the resurrection of the just. For his seed is the Church, which receives the adoption to God through the Lord, as John the Baptist said: "For God is able from the stones to raise up children to Abraham." Thus also the apostle says in the Epistle to the Galatians: "But ye, brethren, as Isaac was, are the children of the promise." And again, in the same Epistle, he plainly declares that they who have believed in Christ do receive Christ, the promise to Abraham thus saying, "The promises were spoken to Abraham, and to his seed. Now He does not say, And of seeds, as if [He spake] of many, but as of one, And to thy seed, which is Christ." And again, confirming his former words, he says, "Even as Abraham believed God, and it was accounted to him for righteousness. Know ye therefore, that they which are of faith are the children of Abraham. But the Scripture, fore-seeing that God would justify the heathen through faith, declared to Abraham beforehand, That in thee shall all nations be blessed. So then they which are of faith shall be blessed with faithful Abraham." Thus, then, they who are of faith shall be blessed with faithful Abraham, and these are the children of Abraham. Now God made promise of the earth to Abraham and his seed; yet neither Abraham nor his seed, that is, those who are justified by faith, do now receive any inheritance in it; but they shall receive it at the resurrection of the just. For God is true and faithful; and on this account He said, "Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth."
Against Marcion Book V

But how are we children of faith? and of whose faith, if not Abraham's? For since "Abraham believed God, and it was accounted to him for righteousness; " since, also, he deserved for that reason to be called "the father of many nations," whilst we, who are even more like him in believing in God, are thereby justified as Abraham was, and thereby also obtain life-since the just lives by his faith,-it therefore happens that, as he in the previous passage called us "sons of Abraham," since he is in faith our (common) father, so here also he named us "children of faith," for it was owing to his faith that it was promised that Abraham should be the father of (many) nations.
Of Patience

Accordingly it is patience which is both subsequent and antecedent to faith. In short, Abraham believed God, and was accredited by Him with righteousness; but it was patience which proved his faith, when he was bidden to immolate his son, with a view to (I would not say the temptation, but) the typical attestation of his faith.
Epistle LXII

Also in the priest Melchizedek we see prefigured the sacrament of the sacrifice of the Lord, according to what divine Scripture testifies, and says, "And Melchizedek, king of Salem, brought forth bread and wine." Now he was a priest of the most high God, and blessed Abraham. And that Melchizedek bore a type of Christ, the Holy Spirit declares in the Psalms, saying from the person of the Father to the Son: "Before the morning star I begat Thee; Thou art a priest for ever, after the order of Melchizedek; " which order is assuredly this coming from that sacrifice and thence descending; that Melchizedek was a priest of the most high God; that he offered wine and bread; that he blessed Abraham. For who is more a priest of the most high God than our Lord Jesus Christ, who offered a sacrifice to God the Father, and offered that very same thing which Melchizedek had offered, that is, bread and wine, to wit, His body and blood? And with respect to Abraham, that blessing going before belonged to our people. For if Abraham believed in God, and it was accounted unto him for righteousness, assuredly whosoever believes in God and lives in faith is found righteous, and already is blessed in faithful Abraham, and is set forth as justified; as the blessed Apostle Paul proves, when he says, "Abraham believed God, and it was accounted to him for righteousness. Ye know, then, that they which are of faith, these are the children of Abraham. But the Scripture, foreseeing that God would justify the Gentiles through faith, pronounced before to Abraham that all nations should be blessed in him; therefore they who are of faith are blessed with faithful Abraham." Whence in the Gospel we find that "children of Abraham are raised from stones, that is, are gathered from the Gentiles." And when the Lord praised Zacchaeus, He answered and said "This day is salvation come to this house, forasmuch as he also is a son of Abraham." In Genesis, therefore, that the benediction, in respect of Abraham by Melchizedek the priest, might be duly celebrated, the figure of Christ's sacrifice precedes, namely, as ordained in bread and wine; which thing the Lord, completing and fulfilling, offered bread and the cup mixed with wine, and so He who is the fulness of truth fulfilled the truth of the image prefigured.
Homily on Galatians 3

Even the miracles done by themselves, he says, declare the power of Faith, but I shall attempt if you will suffer me to draw my proofs from ancient narratives also. Then, as they made great account of the Patriarch, he brings his example forward, and shows that he too was justified by Faith. And if he who was before grace, was justified by Faith, although plentiful in works, much more we. For what loss was it to him, not being under the Law? None, for his faith sufficed unto righteousness. The Law did not then exist, he says, neither does it now exist, any more than then. In disproving the need of the Law, he introduces one who was justified before the Law, lest an objection should also be made to him; for as then it was not yet given, so now, having been given, it was abrogated. And as they made much of their descent from Abraham, and feared lest, abandoning the Law, they should be considered strangers to his kin; Paul removes this fear by turning their argument against themselves, and proves that faith is especially concerned in connecting them with Abraham. He draws out this argument more at length in the Epistle to the Romans; however he urges it also here in, the words...
Commentary on Galatians

Even as Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness.

From this place up to the one where it is written: "Those who are of faith shall be blessed with faithful Abraham", Marcion erased the text from his own Apostle. But what did it profit him to have removed this, when the rest that he left is opposed to his madness? Now Abraham believed God when he went out from his homeland into a land he did not know (Gen. 12 ff.); when he trusted that Sarah, ninety years old and barren, would give birth; and when, having heard God's promise that in Isaac his seed would be called, he offered that very Isaac as a victim, and yet did not doubt the Lord's promise. Rightly is faith reckoned as righteousness to such a man, who, having gone beyond the works of the Law, won the favor of God not by fear but by love.
Against Marcion Book V

For ye are all the children of faith," it becomes dear that what the heretic's industry erased was the mention of Abraham's name; for by faith the apostle declares us to be "children of Abraham," and after mentioning him he expressly called us "children of faith" also. But how are we children of faith? and of whose faith, if not Abraham's? For since "Abraham believed God, and it was accounted to him for righteousness; " since, also, he deserved for that reason to be called "the father of many nations," whilst we, who are even more like him in believing in God, are thereby justified as Abraham was, and thereby also obtain life-since the just lives by his faith,-it therefore happens that, as he in the previous passage called us "sons of Abraham," since he is in faith our (common) father, so here also he named us "children of faith," for it was owing to his faith that it was promised that Abraham should be the father of (many) nations.
On Monogamy

For if "faith" is the source whence we are reckoned to Abraham as his "sons" (as the apostle teaches, saying to the Galatians, "You know, consequently, that (they) who are of faith, these are sons of Abraham"), when did Abraham "believe God and it was accounted to him for righteousness?" I suppose when still in monogamy, since (he was) not yet in circumcision. But if afterwards he changed to either (opposite)—to digamy through cohabitation with his handmaid, and to circumcision through the seal of the testament—you cannot acknowledge him as your father except at that time when he "believed God," if it is true that it is according to faith that you are his son, not according to flesh. ... In like manner, too, if you have involved yourself in digamy, you are not the son of that Abraham whose "faith" preceded in monogamy. For albeit it is subsequently that he is called "a father of many nations," still it is of those (nations) who, as the fruit of the "faith" which precedes digamy, had to be accounted "sons of Abraham."
Homily on Galatians 3
Which he proves by ancient testimony thus:
Commentary on Galatians

You know, therefore, that those who are of faith, these are the sons of Abraham.

He argues this more fully in the Epistle to the Romans: that faith was reckoned to Abraham for righteousness, not in circumcision but in uncircumcision (Rom. 4). And, observing it carefully, he teaches that those are sons of Abraham, whoever have believed with the same mind with which Abraham believed while uncircumcised, he who rejoiced to see the day of the Lord, and saw it, and was glad (John 8). Hence it is also said to the unbelieving Jews: "If you were sons of Abraham, you would do the works of Abraham" (ibid. 39). But what other works (at that time, when these things were being said) did the Lord seek from them, except belief in the Son of God, whom the Father had sent, and who says: "He who believes in me, does not believe in me, but in him who sent me" (John 12:44)? Hence also in another place, to those who were applauding themselves on the antiquity and nobility of their race, the answer is given: "And do not say, We have Abraham as our father. For God is able from these stones to raise up sons to Abraham" (Matt. 3:9). No one doubts that the stones there signify the hard hearts of the Gentiles, which were afterwards softened and received the seal of faith. Count up, diligent reader, the virtues of Abraham by which he pleased God before circumcision, and whomever you find in like work, say that they are sons of Abraham, who was justified in uncircumcision and who received circumcision not on account of the merit of works, but as a sign of his earlier faith. For since Christ was to spring from his seed (in whom the blessing of all the nations had been promised, and many ages were to pass between Abraham and Christ), God, providing that the offspring of beloved Abraham should not be mingled with the other nations and his family little by little become uncertain, marked the Israelite flock with a kind of brand of circumcision, so that, living among the Egyptians, among the Assyrians, Babylonians and Chaldeans, they might be distinguished by this seal. Accordingly, for forty years in the desert no one was circumcised: for they were living alone, without any admixture of another nation; as soon as the people had crossed the bank of the Jordan and the Jewish swarm had poured itself into the land of Palestine, circumcision, now necessary, provided against the confusion that would come from mingling with the nations. But that the people is written to have been circumcised a second time by Joshua (Jesu) their leader (Josh. 5) signifies both that circumcision, which had been reasonably practiced in Egypt, ceased in the desert, and that believers were to be cleansed by the Lord Jesus Christ with a spiritual circumcision.
On the Flesh of Christ

And if of Abraham, how much more, to be sure, of David, as a more recent progenitor! For, unfolding the promised blessing upon all nations in the person of Abraham, "And in thy seed shall all nations of the earth be blessed," he adds, "He saith not, And to seeds, as of many; but as of one, And to thy seed, which is Christ." When we read and believe these things, what sort of flesh ought we, and can we, acknowledge in Christ? Surely none other than Abraham's, since Christ is "the seed of Abraham; "none other than Jesse's, since Christ is the blossom of "the stem of Jesse; "none other than David's, since Christ is "the fruit of David's loins; "none other than Mary's, since Christ came from Mary's womb; and, higher still, none other than Adam's, since Christ is "the second Adam.
Homily on Galatians 3

If then those were Abraham's sons, not, who were related to him by blood, but who follow his faith, for this is the meaning of the words, "In thee all the nations," it is plain that the heathen are brought into kindred with him.

Hereby too is proved another important point. It perplexed them that the Law was the older, and Faith afterwards. Now he removes this notion by showing that Faith was anterior to the Law; as is evident from Abraham's case, who was justified before the giving of the Law. He shows too that late events fell out according to prophecy; "The Scripture," says he, "foreseeing that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, preached the Gospel beforehand unto Abraham." Attend to this point. He Himself who gave the Law, had decreed, before He gave it, that the heathen should be justified by Faith. And he says not "revealed," but, "preached the Gospel," to signify that the patriarch was in joy at this method of justification, and in great desire for its accomplishment.
Commentary on Galatians

But the Scripture, foreseeing that God justifies the Gentiles by faith, announced beforehand to Abraham that all the Gentiles shall be blessed in you. Therefore those who are of faith shall be blessed with faithful Abraham.

Not that Scripture itself, that is, the ink and the parchment, which are without sense, can foreknow future things; but that the Holy Spirit, and the sense which lies hidden in the letter, foretold things that were to come many ages later. Moreover, the example that has been taken from Genesis is contained thus in its own book: "And in your seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed" (Gen. 26:4). Interpreting this of Christ, the Apostle says: "It is not written 'of seeds,' as in many, but as in one, 'and your seed,' which is Christ". And this we ought to observe in almost all the testimonies that have been taken from the old books into the New Testament: that the evangelists or apostles trusted to memory, and, setting out only the sense, often changed the order, and sometimes either took words away or added them. But no one doubts that it was not in Isaac and Jacob, or in the twelve patriarchs, and the others who descend from the stock of Abraham, that all the nations were blessed, but in Christ Jesus, through whom all the Gentiles praise God, and a new name is blessed upon the earth. It can also be understood that the Apostle took the example of the seed from another place of Genesis, where it is written: "Now there led out of doors" (no doubt, Abraham) "God, and said to him: Look into heaven and number the stars, if you shall be able to number them. And he said to him: So shall your seed be; and Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him for righteousness" (Gen. 15:5, 6).
Homily on Galatians 3

Further, they were possessed with another apprehension; it was written, "Cursed is every one that continueth not in all things that are written in the book of the Law, to do them." And this he removes, with great skill and prudence, turning their argument against themselves, and showing that those who relinquish the Law are not only not cursed, but blessed; and they who keep it, not only not blessed but cursed. They said that he who kept not the Law was cursed, but he proves that he who kept it was cursed, and he who kept it not, blessed. Again, they said that he who adhered to Faith alone was cursed, but he shows that he who adhered to Faith alone, is blessed. And how does he prove all this? for it is no common thing which we have promised; wherefore it is necessary to give close attention to what follows. He had already shown this, by referring to the words spoken to the Patriarch, "In thee shall all nations be blessed," at a time, that is, when Faith existed, not the Law...
Commentary on Galatians

Whoever therefore believe shall be blessed with faithful Abraham, who, because of his outstanding faith in God, is related to have been the first to believe in him; just as Enosh, because of his preeminent hope in God, one that stood out among the rest, is written to have hoped to call upon the Lord God (Gen. 4:26). Not that Abel also, of whom the Lord says: "The voice of your brother's blood cries to me" (ibid. 4:10), and the others after him, did not hope to call upon God; but that each one is named from that quality which he possesses most of all.
Homily on Galatians 3

Further, they were possessed with another apprehension; it was written, "Cursed is every one that continueth not in all things that are written in the book of the Law, to do them." (Deut. xxvii: 26) And this he removes, with great skill and prudence, turning their argument against themselves, and showing that those who relinquish the Law are not only not cursed, but blessed; and they who keep it, not only not blessed but cursed. They said that he who kept not the Law was cursed, but he proves that he who kept it was cursed, and he who kept it not, blessed. Again, they said that he who adhered to Faith alone was cursed, but he shows that he who adhered to Faith alone, is blessed. And how does he prove all this? for it is no common thing which we have promised; wherefore it is necessary to give close attention to what follows. He had already shown this, by referring to the words spoken to the Patriarch, "In thee shall all nations be blessed," (Gen. xii: 4) at a time, that is, when Faith existed, not the Law; so he adds by way of conclusion,

"So then they which be of faith are blessed with the faithful Abraham."

Then, that they might not turn round, and object that, true it was Abraham was justified by Faith, for the Law was not then given, but what instance would be found of Faith justifying after the delivery of the Law? he addresses himself to this, and proves more than they required: namely, not only that Faith was justifying, but that the Law brought its adherents under a curse. To be sure of this, listen to the very words of the Apostle.

"For as many as are of the works of the Law are under a curse."

This is what he lays down, before proving it; and what is the proof? it is from the Law itself...
Homily on Galatians 3

For all have sinned, and are under the curse. However he does not say this yet, lest he should seem to lay it down of himself, but here again establishes his point by a text which concisely states both points; that no man has fulfilled the Law, (wherefore they are under the curse,) and, that Faith justifies. What then is the text? It is in the book of the prophet Habakkuk, "The just shall live by faith," (Hab. ii: 4) which not only establishes the righteousness that is of Faith, but also that there is no salvation through the Law. As no one, he says, kept the Law, but all were under the curse, on account of transgression, an easy way was provided, that from Faith, which is in itself a strong proof that no man can be justified by the Law. For the prophet says not, "The just shall live by the Law," but, "by faith."
Commentary on Galatians

For whoever are of the works of the Law are under the curse. For it is written: Cursed is everyone who does not continue in all the things that are written in the book of the Law, that he may do them.

I have this custom: whenever something is taken by the apostles from the Old Instrument, I go back to the original books and examine carefully how it is written in its own place. And so I found this very passage set down in Deuteronomy by the Seventy translators thus: "Cursed is every man who does not continue in all the words of this Law, that he may do them: and all the people shall say, So be it" (Deut. 27:26). In Aquila, however, thus: "Cursed is he who does not establish the words of this Law, that he may do them: and all the people shall say, Truly". Symmachus: "Cursed is he who does not make firm the words of that Law, that he may do them, and all the people shall say, Amen". Theodotion, moreover, translated it thus: "Cursed is he who does not raise up the words of this Law, to do them, and all the people shall say, Amen". From this we understand that the Apostle, as in other places, set down the sense of the testimony rather than the words; and we hold it uncertain whether the Seventy Translators added "every man" (omnis homo) and "in all" (in omnibus), or whether it was so in the old Hebrew and was afterwards deleted by the Jews. Now what spurs me to this suspicion is this: the word "every" (omnis) and "in all" (in omnibus), as though necessary to his sense for proving that whoever are of the works of the Law are under the curse, the Apostle, a man of Hebrew learning and most learned in the Law, would never have brought forward unless it were found in the Hebrew volumes. For this reason, reading through the Hebrew volumes of the Samaritans, I found that CHOL, which means "every" or "all", is written there and agrees with the Seventy translators. In vain, therefore, did the Jews remove it, so as not to seem to be under the curse if they could not fulfill all the things that are written, since the more ancient letters of another nation too testify that it was set down. Now that no one can fulfill the Law and do all the things that are commanded, the Apostle testifies elsewhere as well, saying: "For what was impossible to the Law, in that it was weak through the flesh, God, sending his Son in the likeness of the flesh of sin, from sin condemned sin in the flesh" (Rom. 8). If this is true, it can be objected to us: Then are Moses too, and Isaiah, and the other prophets, who were under the works of the Law, under the curse? He will not fear to grant this who has read the Apostle saying: "Because Christ redeemed us from the curse of the Law, being made a curse for us"; and to answer that each one of the saints was in his own time made a curse for the people. Nor, in granting this to righteous men as well, will he at once seem to detract from the Savior, as though he had nothing special and excellent in being made a curse for us, since the others too were made a curse for others. For none of them, although he himself was made a curse, freed anyone from the curse, save only the Lord Jesus Christ, who with his precious blood redeemed from the curse of the Law both all of us and them too, I mean Moses and Aaron and all the prophets and patriarchs. And do not think that this is said from my own sense; Scripture is witness: that "Christ by the grace of God", or, as is read in some copies, "without God, died for all" (2 Cor. 5). But if for all, then also for Moses and for all the prophets, none of whom was able to blot out the old handwriting that was written against us and fix it to the cross (Col. 2): "All have sinned, and lack the glory [that is, grace] of God" (Rom. 3:23). QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 74: WHY ISAIAH SAYS CHRIST COMMITTED NO SIN YET PAUL SAYS HE WAS MADE SIN

WHAT DOES IT MEAN THAT THE PROPHET ISAIAH SAYS OF CHRIST, “HE COMMITTED NO SIN,” WHILE THE APOSTLE, ON THE CONTRARY, SAYS, “HIM WHO KNEW NO SIN, HE MADE SIN FOR US” (Isa. 53:9; 2 Cor. 5:21)? — As far as the sense is concerned, the questions are different, but the words are similar: in one respect they are alike, in another they differ. “He made” and “did not make” are opposed; “knew not” and “did not commit” are similar. The prophet spoke in the person of Christ, because “He committed no sin, neither was deceit found in His mouth”; but the Apostle speaks of the person of God the Father, who made Him, that is, Christ, who knew no sin, “sin for us.” This must be understood in two ways. First, He made Him sin by willing that He be incarnate, so that He whom fate did not touch should take a body from sinful flesh; by this He is said to have been “made sin.” Then, by offering Him for sins, He made Him sin. For in the Law the victim offered for sins was called “sin.” Therefore Christ did not commit sin, as the prophet says; but by the Father He Himself was made sin, as has been shown. And what is it to offer Christ for us, if not to grant power to those who wished to kill Him? This was allowed because it would be for our benefit that He should be the cause of descending to the lower regions, to damage hell of souls. For it is an excessive and unheard-of sin to have killed Him who not only had not sinned in any way, but had also granted life to many. By this sin the Devil was made guilty and lost the boldness to contradict. A similar passage is read in the Epistle to the Galatians: among other things, “He was made a curse for us” (Gal. 3:13). By whom was He made, if not by the Father? For by God’s judgment the cross of Christ is a curse upon the Jews: the death of the Savior cries out their sin. Therefore He allowed Himself to be crucified, so that His passion might profit us, that as we go forth with His sign, we may not be held by the second death. For death fears even His servants, by whom it has been conquered.
QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 40: WHY ISAIAH SAYS CHRIST COMMITTED NO SIN YET PAUL SAYS HE WAS MADE SIN

WHAT DOES IT MEAN THAT THE PROPHET ISAIAH SAYS OF CHRIST, “HE COMMITTED NO SIN,” WHILE THE APOSTLE, ON THE CONTRARY, SAYS, “HIM WHO KNEW NO SIN, HE MADE SIN FOR US” (Isa. 53:9; 2 Cor. 5:21)? — With regard to the point at issue, not only do the words differ, but the persons are different. “He made” and “did not make” are opposed. But since what is said to have been made is not understood as having been made by Him who is declared not to have made it, it cannot be called a contradiction. For the statement of the prophet refers to the person of Christ, but that of the Apostle to the person of the Father. For God the Father reconciled the world to Himself through Christ; and therefore it came about that He, that is, Christ, was made sin. For this is what “He made Him sin” means: He gave Him into the virginal womb, that He might be born as man, made sin in respect of the flesh, because flesh is the flesh of sin, namely that one whom fate and condition did not touch, to bring forth as man. Therefore He was born for this, that He might be offered as a victim for sinners. He is said to have been made sin because, according to the Law, the victim offered for sins was called “sin.” There is a similar passage of the Apostle to the Galatians speaking of the Savior: “Made a curse for us”; (Gal. 3:13) the sense is the same: “He was made sin or a curse for us for our sake by God the Father, who allowed Him to be killed by the Jews, so that, because of their unbelief, they might be disinherited in our favor, with others brought in to take their place; as the Savior says, ‘The kingdom of God shall be taken from you and given to a nation that produces its fruits’” (Matt. 21:43). For everything that God allows is said to be done by Him: because if He did not allow it, it would not happen. Therefore the Lord says to Pilate, “You would have no power over me unless it had been given you from above” (Jn. 19:11). Therefore He is said to “give” power, not by infusing it, but by permitting it, so that when a wicked mind receives power according to its will, it becomes guilty: as the Jews who, in killing the Savior, made Him their curse by God’s judgment. For the cross of the Savior is a curse upon the Jews. It is not like the victim that was offered for sins, which cleansed the one who offered it; but rather, the offered Savior becomes stain and sin for those who offer Him: while justification comes to those who dissent, so that the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles in Christ Jesus. For the offering of the Jews benefited the Gentiles who did not fall away from faith in Jesus Christ.

In reality, the people were subject to another curse, which says, "Cursed is every one that continueth not in the things that are written in the book of the Law." To this curse, I say, people were subject, for no man had continued in, or was a keeper of, the whole Law; but Christ exchanged this curse for the other, "Cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree." As then both he who hanged on a tree, and he who transgresses the Law, is cursed, and as it was necessary for him who is about to relieve from a curse himself to be free from it, but to receive another instead of it, therefore Christ took upon Him such another, and thereby relieved us from the curse. It was like an innocent man's undertaking to die for another sentenced to death, and so rescuing him from punishment. For Christ took upon Him not the curse of transgression, but the other curse, in order to remove that of others. For, "He had done no violence neither was any deceit in His mouth." And as by dying He rescued from death those who were dying, so by taking upon Himself the curse, He delivered them from it.
