Christ redeemed us from the curse of the Law, made a curse for us.

In this place Marcion creeps in concerning the power of the Creator, whom he defames as bloodthirsty, cruel and an avenger, asserting that we have been redeemed by Christ, who is the Son of another, good God. If he understood how buying and redeeming differ (for he who buys, buys what belongs to another; but he who redeems buys, in the proper sense, that which was his own and had ceased to be his own), he would never twist the simple words of the Scriptures into a calumny in support of his doctrine. Christ therefore redeemed us from the curse of the Law, which was established for those who sin, whom he himself rebukes through the prophet, saying: "Behold, you have been sold for your sins, and in your iniquities I have put away your mother" (Isa. 50:1). And the Apostle repeats this very thing, saying: "But I am carnal, sold under sin" (Rom. 7:14). The curses of the Law too, which are written in Leviticus and Deuteronomy, are not fulfilled with God as their author; rather, by a prophetic spirit, the things that are to come upon those who were going to sin are announced to them. But if he should wish to hem us in with the testimony of the Apostle, who says: "Whoever are of the works of the Law are under a curse: for it is written: Cursed is everyone who does not remain in all things that are written in the book of the Law, to do them" (Deut. 27:26), and to assert that all who were under the Law were cursed, let us ask him whether those who are under the Gospel of Christ and do not do its precepts are cursed or not. If he says they are cursed, he will have in the Gospel what we have in the Law. If he denies that they are cursed, then the precepts of the Gospel have been laid down in vain, and those who have fulfilled them will be without reward. Both points, therefore, are resolved in this way: just as Christ Jesus freed us from the curse of the Law, made a curse for us, so also from the curse of the Gospel, which has been established over those who have not done its precepts, he has rescued us, himself made a curse for us, knowing how not to remit even the smallest portion of a talent, and to exact the last farthing (Matt. 5, and Mark 12).
Commentary on Galatians

Because it is written: Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree: that the blessing of Abraham might come among the Gentiles in Christ Jesus, that we might receive the promise of the spirit through faith.

Before we discuss the sense and the words of the Apostle, it seems right to go over briefly the testimony of Deuteronomy, from which the Apostle also took these words (Deut. 21:22, 23), and to compare it with the other editions. The Seventy translators, then, rendered this passage thus: "But if there be in anyone a sin and a judgment of death, and he has died, and you hang him on a tree, his body shall not sleep upon the tree, but burying you shall bury him on that day; because cursed by God is everyone who hangs on a tree: and you shall not defile your land, which the Lord your God will give you for an inheritance". Aquila: "And when there is in a man a sin unto a judgment of death, and he has been slain, and you hang him upon a tree, his carcass shall not remain upon the tree, but burying you shall bury him on that day, because he who is hanged is the curse of God: and you shall not defile your ground, which the Lord your God will give you as an inheritance". Symmachus: "But if there be in a man a sin bringing a judgment of death, and he has been slain, and you hang him upon a tree: his corpse shall not stay the night upon the tree, but with burial you shall bury him on that same day, because he was hanged on account of blasphemy of God: and you shall not defile your land, which the Lord your God will give you for an inheritance". Theodotion: "And because there will be in a man a sin unto a judgment of death, and he will die, and you will hang him on a tree, his carcass shall not sleep upon the tree, because with burial you shall bury him on that same day, because the one hanged is the curse of God: and you shall not defile your adama, which the Lord your God shall have given you as an inheritance". Now ADAMA (אדמה) is the word in the Hebrew language for "earth" or "ground". But in the place where Aquila and Theodotion translated alike, saying: "because the one hanged is the curse of God", the Hebrew has it thus: CHI CALALATH ELOIM THALUI. These words Ebion, that heresiarch, half-Christian and half-Jew, interpreted thus: ὅτι ὕβρις Θεοῦ ὁ κρεμάμενος, that is, "because the one hanged is an insult to God". I remember that in the Dispute of Jason and Papiscus, which is written in the Greek language, I found it thus: λοιδορία Θεοῦ ὁ κρεμάμενος, that is, "a curse of God is he who is hung up". The Hebrew who instructed me in some measure in the Scriptures used to tell me that it can also be read thus: "because God was hanged shamefully". We have gathered these things together for this reason: because it is a most notorious question, and the Jews are accustomed to throw it at us as a disgrace that our Savior and Lord was under the curse of God. First, then, we must observe that not whoever has hung on a tree is cursed before God, but he who has sinned, and on account of a crime has been sentenced to death and raised up on a cross: he is cursed not because he was crucified, but because he fell into such guilt that he deserved to be crucified. Next we must set against them this point: that further on the cause of the gallows is set out more fully, Scripture relating that he was crucified on account of a curse and blasphemy of God. Symmachus translated this more plainly, saying: "because he was hanged on account of blasphemy of God". Lastly, let us ask them whether, if Ananias and Azarias and Misael, refusing to worship the idol of Nebuchadnezzar, had been hanged on a tree (Dan. 3), and Eleazar too, a man of ninety under Antiochus king of Syria, and the glorious mother with her seven sons (2 Macc. 7), they would have reckoned them cursed, or most worthy of every blessing? Surely, if Haman had not himself mounted, as he deserved, the cross that he had prepared for Mordecai (Esther 7), I think Mordecai would have ascended it not as one cursed, but as a holy man. By these and other similar examples it is proved that he is cursed who has committed a crime worthy of the gallows, not he who has been crucified through the iniquity of judges and the power of enemies, or the clamor of the mob, or envy of his virtues, or the anger of a king. Naboth too was once condemned to death by the whole city of Jezreel at the letters of Jezebel (1 Kings 21); but his blood, as a type of Christ, is avenged many ages later, the Lord saying to Hosea: "Call his name Jezreel, for yet a little while, and I will avenge the blood of Jezreel upon the house of Jehu." (Hos. 1:4). So much against the Jews. But to bring the discussion back to ourselves, I cannot know why the Apostle, in what is written: "Cursed by God is everyone who hangs on a tree" (Deut. 21:23), has either taken something away or added something. For if he was once following the authority of the Seventy translators, he ought, as it was published by them, to have added the name of God as well. But if, as a Hebrew of the Hebrews, he thought that what he had read in his own language was most true, he ought not to have taken up either "everyone" or "on a tree", which are not found in the Hebrew. From this it seems to me either that the ancient books of the Hebrews had it otherwise than they have it now; or that the Apostle (as I have already said before) set down the sense of the Scriptures, not the words; or, what is rather to be supposed, that after the passion of Christ the name of God was added by someone, both in the Hebrew codices and in ours, so as to brand with infamy us who believe in a Christ cursed by God. With a bold foot, therefore, I advance to this contest, to appeal to the books: that in no place is it written that anyone is cursed by God, and wherever a curse is set down, the name of God is never added. "Cursed are you by all the beasts" (Gen. 3:14), is said to the serpent. And to Adam: "Cursed is the ground in your works" (ibid., 17). And to Cain: "Cursed are you upon the earth" (Gen. 4:11). And elsewhere: "Cursed be Canaan the boy, he shall be a servant to his brothers" (Gen. 9:25). And also in another place: "Cursed be their fury, because it is bold, and their anger, because it is harsh" (Gen. 49:7). It would be long if I were to list all the curses that are written in Leviticus, and in Deuteronomy, and in Joshua son of Nun; and yet in none of them is the name of God added: so much so that even Satan himself, when he was promising concerning Job that, if he were pressed by great distresses, he would blaspheme, expressed this by the better word, saying: "If he does not bless you to your face" (Job 1:11). And in the books of Kingdoms Naboth is reported to have been stoned for this reason: "because he blessed God and the king" (1 Kings 21). But no one ought to be troubled that Christ was made a curse for us, since God also, who is said to have made him a curse, himself (although Christ knew no sin) made him sin for us; and the Savior emptied himself from the fullness of the Father, taking the form of a slave (Phil. 2): Life died, and the wisdom of God was called foolishness, so that what was foolish of God might become wiser than men (1 Cor. 1). And in the sixty-eighth psalm he speaks of himself: "O God, you know my foolishness, and my offenses are not hidden from you" (Ps. 68:7). The Lord's insult, therefore, is our glory. He died, that we might live. He went down to the underworld, that we might ascend to heaven. He was made foolishness, that we might be made wisdom. He emptied himself of the fullness and the form of God, taking the form of a slave, that the fullness of divinity might dwell in us, and that from slaves we might become the Lord's. He hung on a tree, that, hung upon a tree, he might blot out the sin which we had committed by the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. His cross turned bitter waters into a sweet taste, and, cast into the streams of the Jordan, it raised the axe that had been lost and sunk into the depths (2 Kings 6).
Against Heresies Book IV

For thus it had behoved the sons of Abraham [to be], whom God has raised up to him from the stones, and caused to take a place beside him who was made the chief and the forerunner of our faith (who did also receive the covenant of circumcision, after that justification by faith which had pertained to him, when he was yet in uncircumcision, so that in him both covenants might be prefigured, that he might be the father of all who follow the Word of God, and who sustain a life of pilgrimage in this world, that is, of those who from among the circumcision and of those from among the uncircumcision are faithful, even as also "Christ is the chief corner-stone" sustaining all things); and He gathered into the one faith of Abraham those who, from either covenant, are eligible for God's building. But this faith which is in uncircumcision, as connecting the end with the beginning, has been made [both] the first and the last. For, as I have shown, it existed in Abraham antecedently to circumcision, as it also did in the rest of the righteous who pleased God: and in these last times, it again sprang up among mankind through the coming of the Lord. But circumcision and the law of works occupied the intervening period.
Homily on Galatians 3

How on the Gentiles? It is said, "In thy seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed:" that is to say, in Christ. If this were said of the Jews, how would it be reasonable that they who were themselves subject to the curse, on account of transgression, should become the authors of a blessing to others? an accursed person cannot impart to others that blessing of which he is himself deprived. Plainly then it all refers to Christ who was the Seed of Abraham, and through whom the Gentiles are blessed. And thus the promise of the Spirit is added, as Paul himself declares, "that we might receive the promise of the Spirit through faith." As the grace of the Spirit could not possibly descend on the graceless and offending, they are first blessed the curse having been removed; then being justified by faith, they draw unto themselves the grace of the Spirit. Thus the Cross removed the curse, Faith brought in righteousness, righteousness drew on the grace of the Spirit.
Commentary on Galatians

Finally, he was made a curse, made, I say, not born: so that the blessings which had been promised to Abraham might, through him as author and forerunner, be transferred to the Gentiles, and the promise of the spirit might be fulfilled in us through faith in him: which we ought to take in two ways, either of the spiritual gifts of the virtues, or of the spiritual understanding of the Scriptures (1 Cor. 9).
Against Marcion Book V
"But," says he, "I speak after the manner of men: when we were children, we were placed in bondage under the elements of the world." This, however, was not said "after the manner of men.
Against Marcion Book V

For (with respect to the latter clause of this passage), what child (in the sense, that is, in which the Gentiles are children) is not in bondage to the elements of the world, which he looks up to in the light of a god? With regard, however, to the former clause, there was a figure (as the apostle wrote it); because after he had said, "I speak after the manner of men," he adds), "Though it be but a man's covenant, no man disannulleth, or addeth thereto." For by the figure of the permanency of a human covenant he was defending the divine testament.
Homily on Galatians 3

"To speak after the manner of men" means to use human examples. Having founded his argument on the Scriptures, on the miracles wrought among themselves, on the sufferings of Christ, and on the Patriarch, he proceeds to common usages; and this he does invariably, in order to sweeten his discourse, and render it more acceptable and intelligible to the duller sort. Thus he argues with the Corinthians, "Who feedeth a flock, and eateth not of the milk of the flock? Who planteth a vineyard, and eateth not the fruit thereof?" and again with the Hebrews, "For a testament is of force where there hath been death; for doth it ever avail while he that made it liveth?" One may find him dwelling with pleasure on such arguments. In the Old Testament God does the same thing in many instances, as, "Can a woman forget her sucking child?" and again, "Shall the clay say to him that fashioneth it, What makest thou?" and in Hosea, He represents a husband set at nought by his wife. This use of human examples frequently occurs in types also, as when the prophet takes the girdle, and goes down to the potter's house. The meaning of the present example is, that Faith is more ancient than the Law, which is later and only temporary, and delivered in order to pave the way for Faith. Hence he says, "Brethren, I speak after the manner of men;" above he had called them "foolish," now he calls them "brethren," at once chiding and encouraging them. "Though it be but a man's covenant, yet when it hath been confirmed." If a man, says he, makes a covenant, does any one dare to come afterwards and overturn it, or subjoin aught to it? for this is the meaning of "or addeth thereto." Much less then when God makes a covenant; and with whom did God make a covenant?
Commentary on Galatians

Some think that he said Brothers, I speak according to man because he was about to discuss a man's testament, the death of the testator, and other examples drawn from human likeness; but it seems to me that it was set before partly, indeed, on account of what they suppose, but chiefly on account of what follows, that is: He does not say, "and to seeds," as of many, but as of one, "and to your seed," who is Christ. Ranging through all the Scriptures in mind and memory, I have never found "seeds" written in the plural number, but, whether in a good sense or in a bad, always in the singular number. So too with what he adds: But this I say: the testament confirmed by God; if anyone carefully compares the Hebrew volumes and the other editions with the translation of the Seventy translators, he will find that where testament is written, it does not sound "testament" (testamentum) but "pact" (pactum), which in the Hebrew tongue is called BERITH (ברית). From this it is plain that the Apostle did what he promised, and did not use hidden meanings with the Galatians, but everyday and cheap ones, such as could (had he not set before them I speak according to man) displease the prudent.
Commentary on Galatians

Brothers, I speak according to man: yet a man's testament, once confirmed, no one despises or adds to: to Abraham were the promises spoken, and to his seed. He does not say, "and to seeds," as of many, but as of one, "and to your seed," who is Christ. But this I say: the testament confirmed by God, the Law, which was made after four hundred and thirty years, does not make void so as to annul the promise; for if the inheritance is from the Law, it is no longer from promise. But God gave it to Abraham through promise.

The Apostle, who became all things to all men that he might gain all, a debtor to Greeks and Barbarians, to the wise and the unwise, became foolish to the Galatians too, whom a little before he had called foolish. For he did not use with them the arguments he used with the Romans, but simpler ones, such as the foolish could understand, and almost from the street corner. And lest he seem to have done this from lack of skill and not by art, he first placates the prudent reader, and tempers what he is about to say with a preface set before it: Brothers, I speak according to man. For what I am about to say, I do not say according to God; I do not say it according to hidden wisdom and to those who can feed on solid food, but according to those who, because of the tenderness of their stomach, are nourished on a milky dew and are by no means able to hear things that are great (1 Cor. 5). Hence also to the Corinthians, among whom fornication was reported, and such fornication as is not even among the Gentiles, he says: "I say, and not the Lord" (1 Cor. 7:12). And to the same in the second letter: "What I speak, I do not speak according to the Lord, but as it were in foolishness" (2 Cor. 11:17).
Against Heresies Book V

If, then, God promised him the inheritance of the land, yet he did not receive it during all the time of his sojourn there, it must be, that together with his seed, that is, those who fear God and believe in Him, he shall receive it at the resurrection of the just. For his seed is the Church, which receives the adoption to God through the Lord, as John the Baptist said: "For God is able from the stones to raise up children to Abraham." Thus also the apostle says in the Epistle to the Galatians: "But ye, brethren, as Isaac was, are the children of the promise." And again, in the same Epistle, he plainly declares that they who have believed in Christ do receive Christ, the promise to Abraham thus saying, "The promises were spoken to Abraham, and to his seed. Now He does not say, And of seeds, as if [He spake] of many, but as of one, And to thy seed, which is Christ." And again, confirming his former words, he says, "Even as Abraham believed God, and it was accounted to him for righteousness. Know ye therefore, that they which are of faith are the children of Abraham. But the Scripture, fore-seeing that God would justify the heathen through faith, declared to Abraham beforehand, That in thee shall all nations be blessed. So then they which are of faith shall be blessed with faithful Abraham." Thus, then, they who are of faith shall be blessed with faithful Abraham, and these are the children of Abraham. Now God made promise of the earth to Abraham and his seed; yet neither Abraham nor his seed, that is, those who are justified by faith, do now receive any inheritance in it; but they shall receive it at the resurrection of the just. For God is true and faithful; and on this account He said, "Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth."
An Answer to the Jews

For this fact-that Gentiles are admissible to God's Law-is enough to prevent Israel from priding himself on the notion that "the Gentiles are accounted as a little drop of a bucket," or else as "dust out of a threshing-floor: " although we have God Himself as an adequate engager and faithful promiser, in that He promised to Abraham that "in his seed should be blest all nations of the earth; " and that out of the womb of Rebecca "two peoples and two nations were about to proceed," -of course those of the Jews, that is, of Israel; and of the Gentiles, that is ours.
Against Marcion Book V

"To Abraham were the promises made, and to his seed. He said not `to seeds, 'as of many; but as of one, `to thy seed, 'which is Christ." Fie on Marcion's sponge! But indeed it is superfluous to dwell on what he has erased, when he may be more effectually confuted from that which he has retained.
Of Patience

So faith, illumined by patience, when it was becoming propagated among the nations through" Abraham's seed, which is Christ," and was superinducing grace over the law, made patience her pre-eminent coadjutrix for amplifying and fulfilling the law, because that alone had been lacking unto the doctrine of righteousness.
Homily on Galatians 3

Thus God made a covenant with Abraham, promising that in his seed the blessing should come upon the heathen; and this blessing the Law cannot turn aside. As this example was not in all respects appropriate to the matter in hand, he introduces it thus, "I speak after the manner of men," that nothing might be deduced from it derogatory to the majesty of God. But let us go to the bottom of this illustration. It was promised Abraham that by his seed the heathen should be blessed; and his seed according to the flesh is Christ; four hundred and thirty years after came the Law; now, if the Law bestows the blessings even life and righteousness, that promise is annulled. And so while no one annuls a man's covenant, the covenant of God after four hundred and thirty years is annulled; for if not that covenant but another instead of it bestows what is promised, then is it set aside, which is most unreasonable.
QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 10: ON THE FOURTH AND FIFTH GENERATION COMING OUT OF EGYPT

GOD HAVING FORETOLD TO ABRAHAM THAT THE CHILDREN OF ISRAEL WOULD BE FREED FROM THE DOMINION OF THE EGYPTIANS. THE FOURTH GENERATION, WHY DOES THE LAW SAY, "THE CHILDREN OF ISRAEL SHALL COME FORTH OUT OF THE LAND OF EGYPT INTO THE FIFTH GENERATION?" — As far as the words are concerned, it seems to be a contradiction; but if the sense is examined, it will be found not to differ. For the Law speaks in such a way that those who are diligent and attentive may understand, so that the basis of the truth reveals itself not to the careless but to the earnest. Indeed, God said “fourth generation,” (Gen. 15:16) and Moses wrote “fifth generation.” (Exod. 13:18) Though Moses recorded both, and it is impossible that he should be mistaken, in whom such great power has worked; therefore the meaning must be investigated, since Scripture never speaks anything uselessly or without forethought. Therefore there are two aspects which each mentions. God indicated four generations that were born in Egypt; Moses, however, adding to these one from which these originated when they entered Egypt, says, “In the fifth generation the sons of Israel went out.” For he includes together the generation that entered Egypt and the four that were born there. From Abraham up to the departure of the sons of Israel from Egypt there are eight generations. For they lived two hundred and fifteen years in Canaan from the time the promise was made to Abraham, and two hundred and fifteen in Egypt. These are the years encompassed by the Apostle to the Galatians when he says, “The Law was given four hundred and thirty years later” (Gal. 3:17). Therefore these four generations were born in Canaan: one in Isaac, another in Jacob, a third in Levi, a fourth in Gershon, and Kohath, and Merari. But when the sons of Israel entered Egypt, Kohath begot Amram: this is the first generation produced in Egypt. Amram then begot Aaron and Moses and Miriam, which is the second generation produced in Egypt. And Aaron begot Eleazar and his brothers, which is the third generation. Then Eleazar begot Phinehas, the fourth generation. These are the four generations brought forth in Egypt. Therefore the Lord says to Abraham, “Your seed will be a stranger, and they will oppress them with slavery; but I will deliver them, and in the fourth generation they will come out from there.” (Gen. 15:13) See whether it is not clear that God signified nothing other than what took place in Egypt. Moses, however, in order also to include that generation which entered Egypt together with Jacob their father, from which these four take their origin, said, “In the fifth generation the sons of Israel went out from the land of Egypt.”
Commentary on Galatians

But the simple sense woven in this place has this force: the Apostle teaches that the promises made earlier to Abraham cannot be destroyed through the Law, which was given afterward, nor can later things prejudice earlier ones, since the promises were given to Abraham four hundred and thirty years before, that all the nations would be blessed in him; whereas the observance of the Law, that whoever had done it should live in it, was given to Moses on Mount Sinai four hundred and thirty years later. On the contrary, it could be said here: What need was there, then, for the Law to be given so long a time after the promise, since, once the Law was given, a suspicion that the pledge had been destroyed could arise, and since, while the promise remained, a Law that would profit nothing was given? Foreseeing this question, the Apostle himself puts it to himself in what follows and unravels it, saying:
Commentary on Galatians

In this place the years must be reckoned from the time when the Lord spoke to Abraham, saying: "And in your seed shall all the nations be blessed" (Gen. 22:18), down to Moses the lawgiver: whether they are four hundred and thirty, or how in Genesis the Lord promises Abraham himself that after four hundred years his sons would go out from the land of slavery. For it is no small matter, and though it has been sought by many, I do not know whether it has been found by anyone. That too which is read in the same book about Tamar and her two little ones (Gen. 38), namely that the first, who is called Zerah, put out his hand, and the midwife tied a scarlet thread on it, and then, as he drew his hand back inside, the later one, who is called Perez, stretched out his hand, fits the present place: that Israel showed its hand in the work of the Law, and drew it back defiled with the blood of the prophets and of the Savior himself. But afterward the people of the Gentiles broke forth, on whose account it is said to have been destroyed many times, and the middle wall which had stood between the Jews and the Gentiles to have been broken down, so that there might be one flock and one shepherd, and glory and honor and peace to everyone who works good, to the Jew first and to the Greek.
Against Heresies Book III

From many other instances also, we may discover that the apostle frequently uses a transposed order in his sentences, due to the rapidity of his discourses, and the impetus of the Spirit which is in him. An example occurs in the [Epistle] to the Galatians, where he expresses himself as follows: "Wherefore then the law of works? It was added, until the seed should come to whom the promise was made; [and it was] ordained by angels in the hand of a Mediator." For the order of the words runs thus: "Wherefore then the law of works? Ordained by angels in the hand of a Mediator, it was added until the seed should come to whom the promise was made,"-man thus asking the question, and the Spirit making answer.
Against Heresies Book V

He has therefore, in His work of recapitulation, summed up all things, both waging war against our enemy, and crushing him who had at the beginning led us away captives in Adam, and trampled upon his head, as thou canst perceive in Genesis that God said to the serpent, "And I will put enmity between thee and the woman, and between thy seed and her seed; He shall be on the watch for (observabit) thy head, and thou on the watch for His heel." For from that time, He who should be born of a woman, [namely] from the Virgin, after the likeness of Adam, was preached as keeping watch for the head of the serpent. This is the seed of which the apostle says in the Epistle to the Galatians, "that the law of works was established until the seed should come to whom the promise was made." This fact is exhibited in a still clearer light in the same Epistle, where he thus speaks: "But when the fulness of time was come, God sent forth His Son, made of a woman." For indeed the enemy would not have been fairly vanquished, unless it had been a man [born] of a woman who conquered him. For it was by means of a woman that he got the advantage over man at first, setting himself up as man's opponent. And therefore does the Lord profess Himself to be the Son of man, comprising in Himself that original man out of whom the woman was fashioned (ex quo ea quae secundum mulierem est plasmatio facta est), in order that, as our species went down to death through a vanquished man, so we may ascend to life again through a victorious one; and as through a man death received the palm [of victory] against us, so again by a man we may receive the palm against death.
The Stromata Book 1

Whence the law was rightly said to have been given by Moses, being a rule of right and wrong; and we may call it with accuracy the divine ordinance, inasmuch as it was given by God through Moses. It accordingly conducts to the divine. Paul says: "The law was instituted because of transgressions, till the seed should come, to whom the promise was made." Then, as if in explanation of his meaning, he adds: "But before faith came, we were kept under the law, shut up," manifestly through fear, in consequence of sins, "unto the faith which should afterwards be revealed; so that the law was a schoolmaster to bring us to Christ, that we should be justified by faith."
Pseudo-Tertullian Against All Heresies

For he, too, says that the world was originated by those angels; and sets forth Christ as born of the seed of Joseph, contending that He was merely human, without divinity; affirming also that the Law was given by angels; representing the God of the Jews as not the Lord, but an angel.
Hippolytus Refutation of All Heresies Book VII

Marcion, adopting these sentiments, rejected altogether the generation of our Saviour. He considered it to be absurd that under the (category of a) creature fashioned by destructive Discord should have been the Logos that was an auxiliary to Friendship-that is, the Good Deity. (His doctrine,) however, was that, independent of birth, (the Logos) Himself descended from above in the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, and that, as being intermediate between the good and bad Deity, He proceeded to give instruction in the synagogues. For if He is a Mediator, He has been, he says, liberated from the entire nature of the Evil Deity. Now, as he affirms, the Demiurge is evil, and his works. For this reason, he affirms, Jesus came down unbegotten, in order that He might be liberated from all (admixture of) evil. And He has, he says, been liberated from the nature of the Good One likewise, in order that He may be a Mediator, as Paul states, and as Himself acknowledges: "Why call ye me good? there is one good." These, then, are the opinions of Marcion, by means of which he made many his dupes, employing the conclusions of Empedocles. And he transferred the philosophy invented by that (ancient speculator) into his own system of thought, and (out of Empedocles) constructed his (own) impious heresy.
Homily on Galatians 3

This remark again is not superfluous; observe too how he glances round at every thing, as if he had an hundred eyes. Having exalted Faith, and proved its elder claims, that the Law may not be considered superfluous, he sets right this side of the doctrine also, and proves that the Law was not given without a view, but altogether profitably. "Because of transgressions;" that is to say, that the Jews might not be let live carelessly, and plunge into the depth of wickedness, but that the Law might be placed upon them as a bridle, guiding, regulating, and checking them from transgressing, if not all, at least some of the commandments. Not slight then was the advantage of the Law; but for how long?

"Till the seed should come to whom the promise hath been made."

This is said of Christ; if then it was given until His advent, why do you protract it beyond its natural period?

"And it was ordained through Angels by the hand of a Mediator."

He either calls the priests Angels, or he declares that the Angels themselves ministered to the delivery of the Law. By Mediator here he means Christ, and shows that He was before it, and Himself the Giver of it.
Commentary on Galatians

What then? The Law was set down because of transgressions, until the seed should come to whom it had been promised, ordained through angels in the hand of a mediator. Now a mediator is not of one, but God is one.

Since, while the promise that had been made to Abraham still stood, the Law given afterwards through Moses seemed to have been brought in to no purpose, he explains why it was given: because of transgressions, he says. For after the offense of the people in the desert, after the worship of the calf and the murmuring against the Lord, the Law followed to forbid transgressions. "For the law is not set down for the righteous man, but for the unjust and the unsubmissive, for the ungodly and sinners" (1 Tim. 1:9). And, to go back further: after the idolatry to which they had been enslaved in Egypt, so that they forgot the God of their fathers and afterwards said, "These are your gods, Israel, who brought you out of the land of Egypt", the rite of worshipping God and the punishment of offenders were ordained in the hand of the mediator Christ Jesus, because all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made: not only heaven, earth, sea and all the things that we see, but also those things that were laid through Moses upon a hard people as the yoke of the Law (John 1). It is also written to Timothy: "For there is one God, and one mediator also of God and men, the man Christ Jesus" (1 Tim. 2:5). After the mediator of God and men, the man Christ Jesus, deigned for our salvation to be born from the Virgin's womb, he was called the go-between (sequester). But before he took up a human body, while he was with the Father in the beginning as God the Word, toward all the saints to whom the word of God came, namely Enoch, Noah, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and afterwards Moses and all the Prophets whom Scripture records, he is called only mediator, without the addition of the man, whom he had not yet assumed. And when he says, the Law ordained through angels, he wants this to be understood: that throughout the Old Testament, where an angel is first reported to have been seen and is afterwards introduced as if God were speaking, an angel indeed, whichever one of the many ministers it may be, was truly seen, but in him the mediator speaks, who says: "I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob" (Exod. 3:6). Nor is it surprising if God speaks in angels, since God also speaks in the prophets through the angels who are in men, as Zechariah says: "And the angel who spoke in me said" (Zech. 2:3); and next adds: "Thus says the Lord almighty". For the angel who had been said to be in the prophet did not dare to say in his own person: "Thus says the Lord almighty". By the hand of the mediator we ought to understand his power and might. Though according to God he is himself one with the Father, according to the office of mediator he is understood as other than he.
Commentary on Galatians

But since the order of the reading is confused and thrown into disorder by a hyperbaton, it seems to us that it should be restored thus: The Law was set down through angels in the hand of a mediator, ordained through angels because of transgressions, until the seed should come to whom the promise had been made. Now there is no doubt that the seed signifies Christ, who is shown by the opening of Matthew also to be the son of Abraham, as Scripture relates: "The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham".
QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 57: ON THE MEDIATOR AND THE ONE GOD (GAL. 3:20)

WHAT NEED WAS THERE FOR THE APOSTLE, WHEN REBUKING THE GALATIANS, TO INSERT THIS STATEMENT? FOR TO THE GALATIANS, WHO AFTER THE GOSPEL WERE TAKING REFUGE IN THE LAW, HE SAYS AMONG OTHER THINGS: “NOW A MEDIATOR IS NOT OF ONE, BUT GOD IS ONE” (Gal. 3:20), AS THOUGH THE GALATIANS DENIED THAT GOD IS ONE. YET IT WAS PRECISELY BY THIS LINE OF REASONING THAT THEY HAD BEEN LED INTO THE LAW: SO THAT THEY MIGHT BELIEVE IN ONE, UNIQUE GOD; AND THAT CHRIST HAD COME ONLY AS A MINISTER BY PREDESTINATION, TO DISPENSE THE GIFT OF GOD’S GRACE. — It is clear that the Galatians were therefore drawn into the Law in such a way that they did indeed profess Christ, but not as he ought to be confessed; rather, in the manner of Photinus, so that, since the Law proclaims one God, it would be contrary to the Law if Christ were called God. This is the device of the Jews, who, overcome by the great deeds of power, believed after the cross of Christ in such a way that, while professing Christ, they nevertheless kept the Law, as though all hope ought not to be placed in Christ. These are the ones whom the Apostle calls “false brethren” (Gal. 2:4; and 2 Cor. 11:26). These, therefore, after the tradition of the Apostles, corrupted the understanding of the Galatians, so that they made them Jews under the name of the Savior. Therefore the Apostle says that Christ came as mediator of the circumcision and the foreskin, as he says to the Ephesians: “making peace in one new man” (Eph. 2:15). If, then, Christ came as mediator, a mediator makes peace between two in such a way that he lays down a new rule, taking away the professions of both, and reconciles them, so that, following his decision, they lose their former discord. For when the Jew insists on circumcision and the Gentile on uncircumcision, there is discord; but when this is taken away from both, there is peace. If, therefore, things stand therefore, how is it, he says, that you Galatians, having become Jews, corrupt the mediation of Christ? Therefore he said to them: “You have been severed from Christ.” (Gal. 5:4) For, despising the right of reconciliation which he had established between them, they turned back to the former way of thinking of the Jews, thereby accusing both themselves and their reconciler. For whatever displeases is accused. And because this matter forced the Galatians to turn to the Law, so that they confessed one God without the mystery, as though it were hostile to the Law if Christ were called God, he says: “The mediator,” that is, the go-between, “is not of one, but of two, of course; but you, turning to the Law, have rejected the mediator; yet God is one.” By saying this, he shows that he proclaims Christ as God in such a way that he does not make him another God, nor confess two, but one God, as is also said in the Law. For when Christ is proclaimed as God from God, this does not result in another God; because that which is from God does not allow itself to be called another God. For whether he is God, or what is from God, he is one God. For there is in fact no difference between God and that which is from God. Yet he is “another.” He is “another” on account of the person by which he is called the Son; but he is the same on account of the unity of substance. Let it not seem blameworthy that I have said “person”; for some are accustomed to reject this. How do I now wish to be with you, to change my voice, to exhort you, to reprehend you, to use all ways and means to regain you to Christ? --- I am in confusion about you,[2] I am perplexed, as the Greek signifies, as not knowing what to say or do. (Witham)

It is written in the law, that is, in Genesis, (chap. xvi. and chap. xxi.) that Abraham had two sons, &c. that his two sons, Ismael, born of his servant, Agar, and Isaac of his wife, Sara, in an allegorical sense, represent the two testaments or covenants, which God made with his people: that by Ismael was represented that covenant of the former law delivered to Moses on Mount Sina, by which the Jews were made his elect people, yet as it were his servants, to be kept to their duty by fear of punishments; but by Isaac is represented the new covenant or testament of Christ, given at Jerusalem, where he suffered, where the new law was first published; by which law, they who believe in Christ were made the spiritual children of Abraham, the sons of God, and heirs of the blessings promised to Abraham: that Sina, the mountain in Arabia, hath[3] an affinity with Jerusalem, and with her children, who remain under the servitude of the law of Moses: we cannot understand a conjunction, or an affinity, as to place and situation, Sina and Jerusalem being near twenty days' journey distant from each other; therefore it can only be an affinity in a mystical signification, inasmuch as Jerusalem was the capital of the Jews, where the children of those who received the law on Mount Sina lived still under the servitude of the same law: but Christians, who believe in Christ, must look upon themselves as belonging to Jerusalem, and not to the city of Jerusalem upon earth, but to the celestial Jerusalem in heaven, which is our mother, now no longer servants and slaves to the former law, but free, being made the sons of God by the grace of Christ, and heirs of heaven. And these blessings were promised to all nations, not only to the Jews, of which the much greater part remained obstinate, and refused to believe in Christ, but also particularly to the Gentiles, according to the prophecy of Isaias, (chap. liv.) rejoice thou that hast been barren, like Sara, for a long time; i.e. rejoice, you Gentiles, hitherto left in idolatry, without the knowledge or worship of the true God, now you shall have more children among you than among the Jews, who were his chosen people. (Witham)

St. Paul makes another observation upon this example of Ismael and Isaac: that as Ismael was troublesome to Isaac, for which he and his mother were turned out of the family, so also now the Jews insulted and persecuted the Christians, who had been Gentiles; but God will protect them as heirs of the blessings promised: they shall be accounted the spiritual children of Abraham, while the Jews, with their carnal ceremonies, shall be cast off. "Since, when we were children," says the same apostle, "we were kept in bondage under the rudiments of the world. And the child, though heir, differeth nothing from a servant, till the time appointed of the father." Philosophers, then, are children, unless they have been made men by Christ. "For if the son of the bond woman shall not be heir with the son of the free," at least he is the seed of Abraham, though not of promise, receiving what belongs to him by free gift.
Homily on Galatians 4

The word "child" in this place denotes not age but understanding; meaning that God had from the beginning designed for us these gifts, but, as we yet continued childish, He let us be under the elements of the world, that is, new moons and sabbaths, for these days are regulated by the course of sun and moon. If then also now they bring you under law they do nothing else but lead you backward now in the time of your perfect age and maturity. And see what is the consequence of observing days; the Lord, the Master of the house, the Sovereign Ruler, is thereby reduced to the rank of a servant.
Commentary on Galatians

Now I say, as long as the heir is a little child, he differs nothing from a slave, though he is Lord of all, but he is under guardians and stewards until the time appointed beforehand by the father.

This little heir, who differs nothing from a slave though he is Lord of all, but is under guardians and stewards until the time appointed beforehand by the father, signifies the whole human race up to the coming of Christ, and, to say more, up to the consummation of the world. For just as all die in Adam, the first-formed man, though not yet born, so also all, even those who were born before the coming of Christ, are made alive in the second Adam. And so it comes about both that we served the Law in the fathers, and that they are saved by grace in the sons. This understanding accords with the Catholic Church, which asserts one providence of both the Old and the New Testament, and does not separate in time those whom it has joined in condition. We are all built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ our Lord, the cornerstone, holding us together, who made both one, and, breaking down the middle wall, destroyed in his flesh the enmity of both peoples, and changed the difficulty of the ancient Law by the integrity of the Gospel doctrines (Eph. 2:20). Truly in Christ we are all one bread, and we two have agreed upon earth. And just as we are founded upon the prophets, so too the patriarchs have stood upon the foundation of the apostles. Now the guardians and stewards can also be taken to be the prophets, by whose words we were daily instructed toward the coming of the Savior, just as the Law of Moses was discussed above as a pedagogue; and the angels of the little ones, who daily see the face of the Father and intercede for them. Of these it was said: "He will send the angels of the Lord round about those who fear him, and will deliver them" (Ps. 33:8). The priests and princes too can be understood, who then ruled over the people and are now held to provide a pattern. And rightly are those said to be under guardians and stewards who, having the spirit of fear, have not yet deserved to receive the spirit of freedom and adoption. For the age of infancy trembles at sins, fears the pedagogue, and does not trust that it is free, although by nature it is mistress. And according to both understandings, by which we have said that the guardians and stewards are either the prophets or the angels, this little one is under stewards and guardians for as long as it takes him to complete the lawful time of the perfect man. Now just as the lawful time under the Roman laws is bounded by a span of twenty-five years, so for the perfection of the human race the coming of Christ is reckoned as that time. As soon as he has come, and we have all grown up into the perfect man, the pedagogue and guardian depart from us. Then we shall fully enjoy the authority of the Lord and the possession of the inheritance, in which we, born earlier, were in a manner regarded as strangers.
QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 82: ON BONDAGE UNDER THE ELEMENTS

THERE IS NO DOUBT THAT THE PAGANS ARE SUBJECT TO THE ELEMENTS; WHAT, THEN, DOES THE APOSTLE MEAN WHEN HE SAYS, “WE TOO WERE IN BONDAGE UNDER THE ELEMENTS OF THIS WORLD”? (Gal. 4:3). IF, THEREFORE, THE JEWS ALSO WERE SERVING UNDER THE ELEMENTS, HOW WERE THEY DIFFERENT FROM THE PAGANS? — It is clear that by the addition, omission, or alteration of a single syllable the sense is distorted. Therefore it is known to all that the pagans worship the elements; but the Jews did not worship the elements, rather they served God under the elements, on account of the new moons, and the sabbaths, and circumcision, and such things; for these are carnal. For whatever is visible is carnal and belongs to the elements. But because it was by the command of God, they were serving God, so that from the visible they might come to the invisible, and for this reason make progress to the reception of greater things, so that by meditating on these they might become worthy of spiritual promises. From that aspect, therefore, which I mentioned above, the Jews served under the elements; from another aspect they had a spiritual law, which both forbids sin and exhorts to the love of the Lord God, who was promised to come to them for the forgiveness of sins.
QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 59: ON BONDAGE UNDER THE ELEMENTS

THERE IS NO DOUBT THAT PAGANS ARE UNDER THE ELEMENTS. WHAT THEN DID THE APOSTLE MEAN WHEN HE SAID, “WE TOO WERE SERVING UNDER THE ELEMENTS OF THIS WORLD”? (Gal. 4:3) IF THEREFORE THE JEWS ALSO WERE UNDER THE ELEMENTS, HOW DO THEY DIFFER FROM THE PAGANS? — The pagans do not serve under the elements, but the elements themselves. For they worship the stars, the sun, the moon, and the constellations in the firmament; and among the lower things, the earth and the water; in the sea, Neptune; in the underworld, Pluto: they openly worship the created world, while passing over the Creator. Now the Jews in this way served under the elements, yet they served God, who had given these very commands. For they observed the new moons, the sabbaths, the sacrifices of cattle; at the beginning of the seventh month they blow the trumpet, and on the fifteenth day of the seventh month they carry about palm-marrow and thick branches of trees and branches of willows, and dwell in booths for seven days. Therefore, as they observed these things, they are rightly said to have served under the elements; for these things are from the elements. Christians, however, do not serve under the elements, but above the elements they serve God, hurrying toward the heavenly Jerusalem; they adore God in spirit, not in visible and worldly things, but having the worship of God in the mind, serving the invisible in an invisible manner, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “The hour is coming when the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and in truth” (Jn. 4:23). This, then, is the truth: to serve God in spirit, in mind rather than in body, so that, because God is spirit, he may be worshiped spiritually. From this side he says that the Jews were subject under the elements, as I mentioned above; but from another side, the principle of the Law was spiritual, by which he both forbade sin and commanded that the Lord be loved with all the heart, and that hope be placed in Christ. But when the Apostles preached these things, they clung more strongly to what had been given carnally. The Apostle recalls these matters in order to stun the Jews, who, disapproving the spiritual Law, were subject to visible things; and to show that these are truly weak in comparison with the law of faith, he also indicates this by introducing his own person, who had once been their zealous imitator. But once he had come to know Christ, he judged these things to be worthy of contempt, because the grace of God through Christ differs greatly from the Law of works.
Commentary on Galatians

So we also, when we were little children, were in bondage under the elements of this world.

He has called the elements of the world the same ones whom above he had called guardians and stewards: because, set first under these very overseers, since we could not yet grasp the coming of the Son of God to us, we were being instructed in the meantime. Some think that they are angels who preside over the four elements of the world, namely earth, water, fire and air, and that it is necessary that, before anyone believes in Christ, he be governed by those as his overseers. Many think that heaven and earth, and the things that are within them, are called the elements of the world: because, namely, the wise men of Greece, and the barbarian nations, and the Romans, the cesspool of all superstitions, worship the sun, the moon, the seas, and the gods of the forests and the mountains; from which we are set free when Christ has come, understanding that they are creatures, not divinities. Others interpret the elements of the world as the Law of Moses and the utterances of the prophets: because through these, as through the beginnings and first rudiments of letters, we take up the fear of God, which is the beginning of wisdom. Finally, to those who ought already to have been perfect, and who, having neglected the truth, still clung to the first principles of instruction, the Apostle writes in the Epistle to the Hebrews: "For when by reason of the time you ought to be teachers, you have need again to be taught what are the elements of the beginning of the words of God" (Heb. 5:12). On the contrary, it can be objected to us that Paul the apostle, writing to the Colossians, has named other things the elements of the world: "See", he says, "that no one plunder you through philosophy and empty deceit, according to the tradition of men, according to the elements of the world, and not according to Christ" (Col. 2:8). But from what he added, "according to the tradition of men, and empty deceit", he shows that the same elements are not named to the Colossians and to the Galatians. For from these elements, after the fullness of time has come, we are redeemed, and, advancing to greater things, we receive the adoption of sons. But of those nothing of the kind is said as something that follows; rather, the elements are taken simply for letters. Therefore, as we have said, the Law of Moses and the prophets can be taken for the elements of letters, because through them syllables and names are joined, and they are learned not so much for their own usefulness as for that of something else: so that we may be able to read connected discourse, in which the sense and the order of the words, rather than the first principles of the letters, are considered. And as for our having interpreted the Law and the prophets as the elements of the world, the world is commonly taken for those who are in the world, as the same Paul says: "God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself" (2 Cor. 5:19). And in the Gospel: "And the world was made through him, and the world does not receive him" (John 1:10). Some, moreover, range more freely in this matter: so that, since the Law has a shadow of good things to come, they inquire whether in another world, of which the Savior says: "I am not of this world" (John 8:23), we are first little children and, set under the elements of the beginnings, advance little by little to the highest point, and receive again the place of adoption which we once lost.

Paul, when writing to the Romans, has explained this very point: "Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ, predestinated unto the Gospel of God, which He had promised by His prophets in the holy Scriptures, concerning His Son, who was made to Him of the seed of David according to the flesh, who was predestinated the Son of God with power through the Spirit of holiness, by the resurrection from the dead of our Lord Jesus Christ." And again, writing to the Romans about Israel, he says: "Whose are the fathers, and from whom is Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed for ever." And again, in his Epistle to the Galatians, he says: "But when the fulness of time had come, God sent forth His Son, made of a woman, made under the law, to redeem them that were under the law, that we might receive the adoption;" plainly indicating one God, who did by the prophets make promise of the Son, and one Jesus Christ our Lord, who was of the seed of David according to His birth from Mary; and that Jesus Christ was appointed the Son of God with power, according to the Spirit of holiness, by the resurrection from the dead, as being the first begotten in all the creation; the Son of God being made the Son of man, that through Him we may receive the adoption,-humanity sustaining, and receiving, and embracing the Son of God.
Against Heresies Book III

With Him is nothing incomplete or out of due season, just as with the Father there is nothing incongruous. For all these things were foreknown by the Father; but the Son works them out at the proper time in perfect order and sequence. This was the reason why, when Mary was urging [Him] on to [perform] the wonderful miracle of the wine, and was desirous before the time to partake of the cup of emblematic significance, the Lord, checking her untimely haste, said, "Woman, what have I to do with thee? mine hour is not yet come"-waiting for that hour which was foreknown by the Father. This is also the reason why, when men were often desirous to take Him, it is said, "No man laid hands upon Him, for the hour of His being taken was not yet come;" nor the time of His passion, which had been foreknown by the Father; as also says the prophet Habakkuk, "By this Thou shalt be known when the years have drawn nigh; Thou shalt be set forth when the time comes; because my soul is disturbed by anger, Thou shalt remember Thy mercy." Paul also says: "But when the fulness of time came, God sent forth His Son." By which is made manifest, that all things which had been foreknown of the Father, our Lord did accomplish in their order, season, and hour, foreknown and fitting, being indeed one and the same, but rich and great. For He fulfils the bountiful and comprehensive will of His Father, inasmuch as He is Himself the Saviour of those who are saved, and the Lord of those who are under authority, and the God of all those things which have been formed, the only-begotten of the Father, Christ who was announced, and the Word of God, who became incarnate when the fulness of time had come, at which the Son of God had to become the Son of man.
Against Heresies Book III

Those, therefore, who allege that He took nothing from the Virgin do greatly err, [since,] in order that they may cast away the inheritance of the flesh, they also reject the analogy [between Him and Adam]. For if the one [who sprang] from the earth had indeed formation and substance from both the hand and workmanship of God, but the other not from the hand and workmanship of God, then He who was made after the image and likeness of the former did not, in that case, preserve the analogy of man, and He must seem an inconsistent piece of work, not having wherewith He may show His wisdom. But this is to say, that He also appeared putatively as man when He was not man, and that He was made man while taking nothing from man. For if He did not receive the substance of flesh from a human being, He neither was made man nor the Son of man; and if He was not made what we were, He did no great thing in what He suffered and endured. But every one will allow that we are [composed of] a body taken from the earth, and a soul receiving spirit from God. This, therefore, the Word of God was made, recapitulating in Himself His own handiwork; and on this account does He confess Himself the Son of man, and blesses "the meek, because they shall inherit the earth." The Apostle Paul, moreover, in the Epistle to the Galatians, declares plainly, "God sent His Son, made of a woman." And again, in that to the Romans, he says, "Concerning His Son, who was made of the seed of David according to the flesh, who was predestinated as the Son of God with power, according to the spirit of holiness, by the resurrection from the dead, Jesus Christ our Lord."

He has therefore, in His work of recapitulation, summed up all things, both waging war against our enemy, and crushing him who had at the beginning led us away captives in Adam, and trampled upon his head, as thou canst perceive in Genesis that God said to the serpent, "And I will put enmity between thee and the woman, and between thy seed and her seed; He shall be on the watch for (observabit) thy head, and thou on the watch for His heel." For from that time, He who should be born of a woman, [namely] from the Virgin, after the likeness of Adam, was preached as keeping watch for the head of the serpent. This is the seed of which the apostle says in the Epistle to the Galatians, "that the law of works was established until the seed should come to whom the promise was made." This fact is exhibited in a still clearer light in the same Epistle, where he thus speaks: "But when the fulness of time was come, God sent forth His Son, made of a woman." For indeed the enemy would not have been fairly vanquished, unless it had been a man [born] of a woman who conquered him. For it was by means of a woman that he got the advantage over man at first, setting himself up as man's opponent. And therefore does the Lord profess Himself to be the Son of man, comprising in Himself that original man out of whom the woman was fashioned (ex quo ea quae secundum mulierem est plasmatio facta est), in order that, as our species went down to death through a vanquished man, so we may ascend to life again through a victorious one; and as through a man death received the palm [of victory] against us, so again by a man we may receive the palm against death.

A certain person thought that he had cleverly solved this question: that Mary was called a woman by the angel and the apostle because she was already betrothed. For a betrothed is in some sense a bride. Yet between "in some sense" and "truly" there is a great distance.… He spoke of one who was a virgin and was called woman according to a proper usage of this term with respect to the basic quality of a virgin, which is therefore vindicated by the generic term woman.

"But when the fulness of time was come, God sent forth His Son" -the God, of course, who is the Lord of that very succession of times which constitutes an age; who also ordained, as "signs" of time, suns and moons and constellations and stars; who furthermore both predetermined and predicted that the revelation of His Son should be postponed to the end of the times.

Since, then, the Creator promised the gift of His Spirit in the latter days; and since Christ has in these last days appeared as the dispenser of spiritual gifts (as the apostle says, "When the fulness of the time was come, God sent forth His Son; " and again, "This I say, brethren, that the time is short" ), it evidently follows in connection with this prediction of the last days, that this gift of the Spirit belongs to Him who is the Christ of the predicters.

But Paul, too, silences these critics when he says, "God sent forth His Son, made of a woman." Does he mean through a woman, or in a woman? Nay more, for the sake of greater emphasis, he uses the word "made" rather than born, although the use of the latter expression would have been simpler.

"Still," He said, "I have many things to say to you, but ye are not yet able to bear them: when that Spirit of truth shall have come, He will conduct you into all truth, and will report to you the supervening (things).

But if someone clever should come up against us and say that Mary too is named "a woman" in the Scriptures — for so the Apostle says: "But when the fullness of the times was come, God sent his Son, made of a woman, made under the law, that he might redeem them that were under the law" — we shall answer him that in this the Apostle named her "a woman" not for corruption, but as an indication of sex; so that, since he was saying that "God's Son was sent," he might at the same time also set forth that he had come into this world by the common entrance of all. Moreover, this word is also one of age — namely, of that age at which the female sex passes beyond the years of puberty and crosses over to that time at which she seems fit for a man.

And just as the time for the heir, having come to be at the stature of a man, to receive the paternal possession might in some way be named the fullness of his time or of his season, so a man would come to be in the fullness of the times who, through the ways and advancements that bear toward perfection, has arrived at being able to receive the things predestined and purposed by God for the saints.

QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 58: WHY DID CHRIST NOT COME EARLIER

If salvation and true and perfect knowledge are through Christ, why did he not come earlier, so that our predecessors who were in ignorance might learn the truth? Indeed, after the coming of Christ many have been saved more than before; whereas, if he had come earlier, far more would have been saved. If this is so, it appears open to criticism. — If help is given beforehand to someone upon whom necessity is about to press, he will indeed be grateful, yet he will not be very able to recognize what has been done for him. But if you bring help to someone placed in the very midst of necessity, he will know what kind of benefit he has obtained. For one who is delivered from tribulation gives greater thanks; just as when you offer bread to one who is hungry: but if you offer it to one who is not hungry, what thanks will there be? Therefore it was rightly arranged that the Lord did not come earlier. First, he allowed the human race to use its own free will, yet not without a witness of himself: for from the very structure of the world, through the yearly gifts which he decreed should be supplied for human use by the ministry of the elements, he willed that his divinity be known and feared. Later, however, when the knowledge of God on earth grew dim and morals were changed, he consented to visit the human race, so that by giving the Law, or rather renewing it (for it existed in nature, but had begun to be neglected), he might restore both the knowledge of himself and the authority of the Law; so that, having recognized God and recalled the Law, they might begin to fear: being certain that the one who gave the Law would be the judge of human deeds. And because, after receiving the Law, they were unable to restrain themselves from sins, although they could have done so, and after being long admonished even through the Prophets, God, moved by mercy, sent his Son, who, offering himself for them and destroying death, granted them the remission of sins, that he might present them, justified, to God the Father; so that, knowing from what danger they have been rescued, they may give thanks to God without ceasing; so that even if necessity should require that they pour out their blood for him, they may still profess that they do not thereby repay him in kind. How pleasing and precious, then, do they deem that benefit which they do not think can be repaid even by death? But perhaps it will be argued on the other side: If many before the Law, and after the Law, weighed down by sins, gave themselves wholly over to the flesh, there were without doubt some who, devoted to God the Creator, restrained themselves from vices. Come, did these, once removed from life, not descend into hell? But if Christ had come immediately after the death of Adam, and, having freed Adam, who was held by his own sin, from death, had made a way to heaven for the rest who believed, so that, because they had lived well here, they might be received after death into heaven by their gracious Creator and Restorer. Therefore, is it a loss because Christ did not come earlier? It is clearly a loss. But ask whether it is just or unjust. For losses are often just. When a thief is caught and condemned to pay fourfold according to the Law, does he not suffer loss? Yet it is just; and therefore what the human race has suffered, having come about justly, is therefore permitted. For this reason the Savior ought not to have come at the very beginning. For when the Devil grew proud, and man, made by God, was set up as his enemy, so that, strengthened by God's help, for he was unequal in strength, he might resist him by the command that he had received, being the image of the one God on earth to remove error, by the fact that one was made by the One, from whom the others came, he might show this. But the Devil, with his usual subtlety, pretended not to know what had been commanded by God, and found Eve unpredictable; then, promising them that if they tasted what was forbidden they would become gods, he deceived them. Therefore the Devil, having conquered man, triumphed; the defeated man sold his race to sin. It was therefore not just to snatch away the spoils from the victor by force at once, because whatever God does, he does justly. Moreover, since man had sinned grievously, for by consenting to become a god he committed idolatry, that is, he sinned against God, he ought not at once to have been helped, since he did not even repent. Later, however, Satan brought many evils upon the righteous: upon Job, Joseph, Jeremiah, Isaiah, Zechariah, and the other prophets and righteous ones. Therefore Christ was entrusted by God his Father to overcome him and to reveal himself, taking away his kingdom by reason, not by sheer power; although God can do all things, yet he does what is in harmony with reason, so that he may remain above blame.
QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 44: ON CHRIST BEING MADE FROM THE SEED OF DAVID

AS WE CONFESS THAT THE SAVIOR WAS BORN, WHAT DOES IT MEAN THAT THE APOSTLE SAYS HE WAS MADE FROM THE SEED OF DAVID (Rom. 1:3), SINCE TO BE MADE IS ONE THING AND TO BE BORN ANOTHER? — Although in this place “making” can be understood as “birth”: for “making” does indeed differ from “generation,” but only in other contexts, not where the matter concerns flesh and body. Yet the Apostle did not use such words without reason; for in another place he says, “made of a woman” (Gal. 4:4). Therefore he meant something by this expression. For the flesh of the Lord in the Virgin’s womb was not formed and the body brought into being by human seed, but by the operation and power of the Holy Spirit; that is why the Apostle spoke in this way. It is one thing to thicken blood with mingled seed and therefore to generate, and another to bring forth, not by mixture, but by power. Therefore he said “made” rather than “begotten.”
QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 83: WHY DID CHRIST NOT COME EARLIER?

IF SALVATION AND TRUE AND PERFECT KNOWLEDGE ARE THROUGH CHRIST, WHY DID HE NOT COME EARLIER, SO THAT OUR PREDECESSORS WHO WERE IN IGNORANCE MIGHT LEARN THE TRUTH? INDEED, AFTER THE COMING OF CHRIST MANY HAVE BEEN SAVED, MORE THAN BEFORE. WHENCE, IF HE HAD COME EARLIER, MANY MORE WOULD HAVE BEEN SAVED. IF THIS IS SO, IT SEEMS BLAMEWORTHY. — Yet no one who shows mercy ought to be slandered. For it is in the power of the giver when and how much he wishes to have mercy. Such a one must be encouraged and moved by prayers, not drawn back from a good work by disagreement. Perhaps there would be no objection if some return were made to Him in exchange for this mercy. Will anyone accuse a physician who bestows his remedies and his service freely? Or will his slowness be blamed by those who did not ask for him? We have said this according to reason, but the kindness of the Savior does not regard such calculations because of human weakness: He follows His own nature in showing mercy. Therefore He came when He ought to have come, following the counsel of His own will, not our merits. For if you weigh our merits, He ought not to have come. He came, then, when He knew both that help was needed, and that the benefit would be welcomed. If someone in danger is helped beforehand, the benefit will indeed be welcome; yet he will not be able to recognize very clearly what has been granted to him. But if you bring help to one when he is in the very midst of necessity, he will know what kind of benefit he has obtained. Being delivered from tribulation, he will give greater thanks, just as if you offer bread to a hungry man; if you offer it when he is not hungry, it will certainly not be as welcome. Therefore it was rightly done that the Lord did not come earlier. First He allowed the human race to use its own will, yet not without testimony of Himself; for from the very structure of the world, through the yearly gifts which He decreed should be supplied to human use by the ministry of the elements, He wished His divinity to be understood and feared. Indeed, from the stock of the first man, and then in Enoch and Noah, His knowledge was on earth. But when, through a kind of sickness of the human race, the knowledge of God among men began to fade, and morals were being changed, He agreed to choose Abraham, in whom there might be a pattern of renewed knowledge of God and of conduct. And when reverence was still sluggish, afterward through Moses He gave the Law in writing, which neither could fade away and which inspired greater fear. For fear is greater where authority is revealed. And because the nations rejected the Law they had received, not subjecting themselves to it, and even those who received it did not keep it, the Lord, moved by mercy, sent His Son, who, offering Himself for them, destroying death, and granting remission of sins to all, might present them justified to God the Father. For He could not descend to the lower regions except through death. Neither order nor reason demanded that one who had not died should enter the gates of Tartarus. If someone wishes to deceive barbarians in his own land, does he not change his appearance to match theirs, so that he may be thought one of them, and therefore find out how to overthrow them? So it was with the Devil: because he had overthrown man by evil cunning, so that man would not remain in death, a remedy was found by which he might lose those whom he held unjustly, and be taken unawares; and the one whom he thought he had killed as a mere man, he found to be God in the lower regions. When this happened, found guilty, he lost all those whom he held, and thereafter the way to heaven was opened. See how greatly the coming of the Savior has profited, so that men, knowing from what peril they have been freed, might unceasingly give Him thanks. But perhaps it may be said on the contrary: If many before the Law and after the Law, pressed down by sins, gave themselves entirely to the flesh and were worthy to remain in Tartarus, surely there were also those who, by devotion and reverence for the Creator, restrained their lives by the law of nature: were not these too, stripped of this life, detained in the lower regions? If He had come earlier, after the death of Adam, having freed Adam who first sinned, would He not have opened the way to heaven for the others, so that those who had lived well, having known the Creator, might be received into heaven after their death? Is it then a loss because Christ did not come earlier? It is clearly a loss; but ask whether it is just or unjust. For losses are often just, and about these one may not complain. Has a thief caught in the act and condemned fourfold according to the law ever dared to complain? Therefore the loss which the human race has suffered was justly done, and therefore was allowed. For this reason too the Savior ought not to have come at the very beginning. For when the Devil was exalting himself, man made by God was set as his enemy, that, strengthened by the help of God, for he was not his equal, he might resist him after receiving a command. But the Devil, with his usual subtlety, pretended not to know what had been commanded by God, and he found Eve unstable; then, promising her that if they touched what was forbidden it would confer divinity on them, he deceived them. Then the Devil, having overcome man, triumphed; the conquered man subjected his race to sin. Therefore it would have been unjust to take the spoils from the victor by force, since whatever God does He does justly. Moreover, since man grievously sinned by consenting to him, against the command of the Creator, to make himself God, he committed idolatry, by which he sinned against God; therefore help ought not to have been granted him at once; for neither would he have repented, nor would mercy have been welcome to him, if he had not known what he deserved. Although God can do all things, He does what is in harmony with reason, so that He may remain beyond blame.

He says "his Son," not one of many, not "a Son" but his own. When he says "his own" he confirms that he has the property of eternal generation. This is the one whom he subsequently declares to have been born from a woman, so as to ascribe the fact of being born not to the Godhead but to the assumed body. He was made from a woman by assuming flesh and made under the law by observing the law. But that heavenly birth of his is prior to the law, while the incarnation happens later.

Here he states two objects and effects of the Incarnation, deliverance from evil and supply of good, things which none could compass but Christ. They are these; deliverance from the curse of the Law, and promotion to sonship. Fitly does he say, that we might "receive," "[be paid,]" implying that it was due; for the promise was of old time made for these objects to Abraham, as the Apostle has himself shown at great length. And how does it appear that we have become sons? he has told us one mode, in that we have put on Christ who is the Son; and now he mentions another, in that we have received the Spirit of adoption.
