But when the fullness of time came, God sent his Son, made of a woman, made under the Law, that he might redeem those who were under the Law, that we might receive back the adoption of sons.

Pay careful attention to the fact that he did not say made through a woman, as Marcion and the other heresies would have it, which pretend that the flesh of Christ was merely apparent, but of a woman, so that he may be believed to have been born not through her but of her. And as for his calling the holy and blessed Mother of the Lord woman (mulierem), not Virgin (Virginem), this same thing is written also in the Gospel κατὰ Ματθαῖον (according to Matthew), where she is called the wife of Joseph (Luke 2), and where she is rebuked by the Lord himself as a woman (John 2). For it was not necessary always to say Virgin, as if cautiously and timidly, since woman (mulier) signifies the sex rather than union with a man; and according to the sense of the Greek language, γυνή can be translated as either wife or woman. But to pass over all this: just as he was made under the law that he might redeem those who were under the law, so for the sake of those who had been born of a woman he willed to be born of a woman. For this is also why he received baptism in the stream of the Jordan as if he were a penitent, though he was free from sins: to teach the rest that they must be cleansed through baptism and be begotten as sons by the new adoption of the Spirit. John the Baptist, by no means understanding this, tried to keep him from coming to the washing, saying: "I ought to be baptized by you" (Matt. 3:14). And at once the mystery is taught: "Permit it now; for thus it befits us to fulfill all righteousness", so that he who had come for the salvation of men should not pass over anything of the manner of life of men. Someone may ask and say: If he was made under the Law for this reason, that he might redeem those who were under the Law (since, evidently, it would have been impossible for those who were under the Law to be redeemed unless he himself had been made under the Law), then either he was made without the Law, that he might redeem those who were not under the Law; or, if he himself was not made without the Law, he does not redeem those who had not been under the Law. But if it was possible for those who were without the Law to be redeemed in such a way that he himself did not become without the Law, then he was made under the Law superfluously in order to redeem those who were under the Law. One will resolve this question briefly if one uses that example: "and he was reckoned with those who were without the Law". For although in the Latin manuscripts, owing to the simplicity of the translators, it has been badly rendered: "And he was reckoned with the iniquitous" (Luke 22:37), yet one must know that among the Greeks ἄνομον, which is written here, means one thing, and ἄδικον, which is found in the Latin volumes, another. For ἄνομος is said of one who is without law and is bound by no right, whereas ἄδικος means iniquitous, or unjust. Hence the Apostle himself too, in another place: "since I was not", he says, "without the Law of God, but was in the Law of Christ" (1 Cor. 9); and certainly in this testimony also ἄνομος is written in the Greek; and he who translated well here could have translated the same word likewise there too, had the ambiguity not deceived him.
Commentary on Galatians

But what shall we do about that passage of Paul, where he says: "But when the fullness of time came, God sent his Son, made of a woman, made under the Law, that he might redeem those who were under the Law" (above)? For if Christ was under the Law, and not as if under the Law, that whole preceding discussion will become empty. But this objection too will be resolved from its own passage. For he who was made under the Law for this reason, that he might redeem those who were under the Law, surely, since he was free from the Law, subjected himself to the Law of his own will; and he was far freer than Paul, who testified that he had been not under the Law but as if under the Law. And just as he went down into the mire and abyss of death for our sake, who were praying and saying: "Who will deliver me from the body of this death" (Rom. 7:24)? so too he willed to be born of a woman and to be under the Law, that he might save those who had been born of a woman and under the Law. And certainly he was not born of a woman, that is, of a married woman, but of a virgin. But the virgin was called a woman by a loose use of the word, on account of those who did not know that she had been a virgin. So, then, just as "woman" was put for "virgin" on account of those who thought that holy Mary had a husband, so, on account of those who supposed that Christ was under the Law, not knowing that to those who were under the Law he had become as if under the Law, he too is said to have been made under the Law.

But this is God's kindness to man, that of whom He is Maker, of them according to grace He afterwards becomes Father also; becomes, that is, when men, His creatures, receive into their hearts, as the Apostle says, 'the Spirit of His Son, crying, Abba, Father.' And these are they who, having received the Word, gained power from Him to become sons of God; for they could not become sons, being by nature creatures, otherwise than by receiving the Spirit of the natural and true Son. Wherefore, that this might be, 'The Word became flesh,' that He might make man capable of Godhead. This same meaning may be gained also from the Prophet Malachi, who says, 'Hath not One God created us? Have we not all one Father?' for first he puts 'created,' next 'Father,' to shew, as the other writers, that from the beginning we were creatures by nature, and God is our Creator through the Word; but afterwards we were made sons, and thenceforward God the Creator becomes our Father also. Therefore 'Father' is proper to the Son; and not 'creature,' but 'Son' is proper to the Father. Accordingly this passage also proves, that we are not sons by nature, but the Son who is in us; and again, that God is not our Father by nature, but of that Word in us, in whom and because of whom we 'cry, Abba, Father.' And so in like manner, the Father calls them sons in whomsoever He sees His own Son, and says, 'I begat;' since begetting is significant of a Son, and making is indicative of the works. And thus it is that we are not begotten first, but made; for it is written, 'Let Us make man;' but afterwards, on receiving the grace of the Spirit, we are said thenceforth to be begotten also; just as the great Moses in his Song with an apposite meaning says first 'He bought,' and afterwards 'He begat;' lest, hearing 'He begat,' they might forget their own original nature; but that they might know that from the beginning they are creatures, but when according to grace they are said to be begotten, as sons, still no less than before are men works according to nature.

And because you are sons of God, God sent the spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, Abba, Father.

The apostle Paul plainly names three spirits: the Spirit of the Son of God, as in the present passage, "God sent the Spirit of the Son into our hearts" (Rom. 8:14); and the Spirit of God, as in that passage: "As many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are sons of God"; and the Holy Spirit, as there: "Your bodies are a temple of the Holy Spirit, who is in you" (1 Cor. 6:19). That the Holy Spirit is other than the Son of God is plainly proved in the Gospel as well: "Whoever speaks a word against the Son of man, it will be forgiven him. But whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit, it will not be forgiven him, neither here nor in the age to come" (Luke 12:10). I say this for the following reason: because many, through ignorance of the Scriptures (as Firmianus also does in the eighth book of his Letters to Demetrianus), assert that the Holy Spirit is often named the Father, often the Son. And although we clearly believe in the Trinity, they take away the third Person and will have him to be not a substance but a name. But not to be long (for it is a commentary, not a dialogue, that is being written), I shall show briefly from the fiftieth psalm that three spirits are named, the prophet saying: "Create a clean heart in me, O God, and renew a right spirit in my inward parts. Do not cast me away from your face, and do not take your Holy Spirit from me. Restore to me the joy of your salvation, and strengthen me with a princely spirit". By the princely spirit he means the Father, because the Son is from the Father, and not the Father from the Son. But by the right spirit, the spirit of truth and righteousness, he signifies Christ the Lord: "For the Father has given all judgment to the Son" (John 5:22), as David says: "O God, give your judgment to the king, and your power to the king's son" (Ps. 71:1). Further, he calls the Holy Spirit by his open name. And though these differ in names and persons, they are joined in substance and nature; and, because of the fellowship of nature, the same Spirit is said without distinction to be now of the Father, now of the Son. Now the argument by which he is trying to assert that we are no longer under the Law but under the grace of the Lord Jesus, he concludes with an ending of this kind. Above he had said, "that we might receive the adoption of sons"; now he proves that we are sons of God from the spirit which we have within us. For we should never dare, he says, to say: "Our Father, who are in heaven, hallowed be your name", except from the consciousness of the Spirit dwelling in us and crying with a great voice of understanding and of doctrines: "Abba, Father" (Rom. 8:15). Abba is Hebrew, meaning the very same thing as Father. And Scripture keeps this custom in many places, setting a Hebrew word together with its interpretation: Bartimaeus, "son of Timaeus"; Asher, "riches"; Tabitha, "Dorcas" (Acts 9); and in Genesis, Mesech, "home-born slave" (Gen. 15), and other things like these. But since Abba means Father in the Hebrew and Syriac tongue, and our Lord in the Gospel commands that no one is to be called father except God (Matt. 23), I do not know by what license in the monasteries we either call others by this name or consent to be called by it ourselves. And certainly he gave this command who had said that one must not swear (Matt. 5). If we do not swear, let us not name anyone father either. If we interpret the saying about a father otherwise, we shall be compelled to think otherwise about swearing as well. It should be noted also that in the Scriptures a cry is to be understood not as the emitting of a loud voice but as the greatness of knowledge and of doctrines. For in Exodus too the Lord answered Moses: "Why do you cry to me" (Exod. 14:15)? although no voice of Moses at all had gone before. But Scripture called a cry his heart, pierced with compunction and groaning tearfully for the people. Just as, therefore, he who has the Spirit of the Son of God is a son of God, so conversely he who does not have the spirit of the Son of God cannot be called a son of God.

Now the same elements which he has now called weak and needy he set down above simply as the elements of the world. And where they were called elements of the world, weak and needy was not added there. Here again, where they are called weak, the name "of the world", as we said above, is passed over in silence. I think, therefore, that as long as someone is a little child and has not completed the time fixed by the father, so that he can be called son and heir, he is under the elements of the world, that is to say, the Law of Moses. But when, after the freedom owed to the son, he has gone back again to the Law, wishing to be circumcised and to follow the whole letter of the Jewish superstition, then the things which before had been for him only the elements of the world are also called weak and needy beginnings. For they are of so little profit to their worshippers that they cannot even offer them what they had provided before, since Jerusalem, the temple and the altar have been destroyed. Someone may answer and say: If the law and the precepts written in the Law are weak and needy elements, and those who have known God, or rather have been known by him, ought not to observe the Law (lest they begin not so much to worship the God by whom they have been known as to go back to those who by nature are not gods), then either Moses and the prophets observed the Law and did not know God, nor were known by him; or, if they knew God, they did not at all fulfill the commandments of the Law. Either of these is dangerous to say: either that they did not do the things of the Law, and so knew God; or that they did not know God, while they kept the weak and needy elements of the Law. This can indeed be resolved in this way, by saying that, just as Paul became a Jew to the Jews in order to win the Jews (1 Cor. 9), and at Cenchreae cut his hair in fulfillment of a vow (Acts 18), and at Jerusalem in the temple practiced the going barefoot and the shaving of the head, in order to calm the ill will of those who had been instructed about him that he was acting against the Law of Moses and the God of the prophets: so also the holy men did indeed do the things that belonged to the Law, but followed the sense of the Law rather than the letter. They, no less than Abraham, with the veil taken from their face, desired to see the day of Christ, and they saw it and were glad: they became weak to a weak people, in order to win the weak (1 Cor. 9), and to those who were under the Law as though they themselves were under the Law, in order to separate them from the idols to which they had grown accustomed in Egypt. For it is absurd that Moses and the others who conversed with God should have been in such a condition that we do not believe that for them too the time fixed by the Father had come, and that they were redeemed from legal slavery, and obtained the adoption of sons, and received the inheritance with Christ. For whatever the wisdom of God has granted to the whole human race as to one Son, this same it has always bestowed on each of the saints in his own order and dispensation. When we call the Law of Moses weak and needy elements, the heretics find an occasion to disparage the Creator, because he founded the world and established the Law. To them we shall answer what we said above: that the elements are weak and needy for those who go back to them after the grace of the Gospel. But before the time fixed by the Father came, the elements were called not so much weak and needy as elements of the world. In short, before the Gospel of Christ shone out in the whole world, the precepts of the Law had their own brightness; but after the greater light of the grace of the Gospel shone forth, and the sun of righteousness showed itself to the whole world, the light of the stars was hidden and their rays grew dim, so that the Apostle says in another place: "For what was glorified in this respect was not glorified, because of the surpassing glory" (2 Cor. 3). This he now says in other words, meaning that the Law of Moses, which before the Gospel was rich and wealthy and splendid, after the coming of Christ, by comparison with him, as being weak and needy, has been diminished and destroyed by him who was greater than Solomon, and the temple, and Jonah. For what is written, "He must increase, but I must decrease" (John 3:30), I think was said not so much in the person of John as in the person of the Law, because lesser things always give way to greater, and perfect things are set before beginnings. In another way, however, we shall affirm that the weak and needy elements are the traditions of the Jews and the base understanding according to the letter, which are statutes that are not good and precepts that are not good. For the spiritual understanding of the Law is strong and rich (Ezek. 20), so that either it ought not to be called an element at all, or it is indeed an element by comparison with the age to come and with the life in Christ Jesus, by which the angels and the heavenly powers now live. But compared with the Jewish sense, it should be called not so much an element, that is, a beginning, as perfection. And when he says: But now, knowing God, or rather being known by him, this shows that after the worship of idols the Galatians came to understand God, or rather that they themselves were judged worthy of his knowledge. Not that God, the Creator of all things, is ignorant of anything; but that he is said to know only those who have exchanged error for piety. "The Lord knows those who are his" (2 Tim. 2:19). And the Savior in the Gospel: "I am", he says, "the good shepherd, and I know mine, and mine know me" (John 10:14). On the contrary, to the ungodly: "I do not know you; depart from me, workers of iniquity" (Luke 13:27). And to the foolish virgins: "I do not know who you are" (Matt. 25:12).
Against Marcion Book V

He tells us himself clearly enough what he means by "elements," even the rudiments of the law: "Ye observe days, and months, and times, and years" -the sabbaths, I suppose, and "the preparations," and the fasts, and the "high days.
On Fasting

(Inburnt?) With what fires, prithee? The fires, I ween, which lead us to repeated contracting of nuptials and daily cooking of dinners! Thus, too, they affirm that we share with the Galatians the piercing rebuke (of the apostle), as "observers of days, and of months, and of years." Meantime they huff in our teeth the fact that Isaiah withal has authoritatively declared, "Not such a fast hath the Lord elected," that is, not abstinence from food, but the works of righteousness, which he there appends: and that the Lord Himself in the Gospel has given a compendious answer to every kind of scrupulousness in regard to food; "that not by such things as are introduced into the mouth is a man defiled, but by such as are produced out of the mouth; " while Himself withal was wont to eat and drink till He made Himself noted thus; "Behold, a gormandizer and a drinker: " (finally), that so, too, does the apostle teach that "food commendeth us not to God; since we neither abound if we eat, nor lack if we eat not.
On Fasting
Being, therefore, observers of "seasons" for these things, and of "days, and months, and years," we Galaticize.
Homily on Galatians 4
Hence is plain that their teachers were preaching to them not only circumcision, but also the feast-days and new-moons.
Commentary on Galatians

You observe days, and months, and times, and years; I fear you, lest perhaps I have labored in vain among you.

He who does not worship the Father in spirit and truth does not know the sabbath rest laid up for the saints, of which God speaks: "If they shall enter into my rest" (Ps. 94:11); and he does not remember those times of which it is written: "Remember the days of the age" (Isa. 46:9). And elsewhere: "I remembered the ancient days, and I had the eternal years in mind" (Ps. 76:6). He observes Jewish days, and months, and times, and years. Days, such as those of the sabbath and of the new moon, and from the tenth of the first month to the fourteenth, on which the bodily lamb is kept for sacrifice, and from the fourteenth to the twenty-first of the same month, when unleavened bread is eaten, not that of sincerity and truth, but in the old leaven of the malice and wickedness of the Pharisees. He too who, by the Jewish rite, counts seven weeks after the unleavened bread keeps the days of the Israelite Pentecost; and likewise the blast of trumpets in the seventh month, on the first of the month. Those too who keep the tenth of the same month, the expiation and the fast, and who pitch the booths of the Feast of Tabernacles according to custom, observe Jewish days. And they keep months who observe the first and the seventh month, not understanding the mystery of the truth. They also keep times who, coming to Jerusalem three times every year, think they are fulfilling the precept of the Lord, who says: "Three times in the year you shall keep a feast day to me: the solemnity of unleavened bread, and the solemnity of the harvest of the firstfruits, and the solemnity of the completion at the going out of the year" (Exod. 23:14 ff.). And elsewhere: "Three times in the year your male shall appear in the sight of the Lord your God" (Exod. 23:17). But as for his saying and years, I think it is said of the seventh year, that of remission, and of the fiftieth, which they call the Jubilee. The Apostle explains this passage more fully to the Colossians, saying: "Let no one therefore judge you in food, or in drink, or in part of a feast day, or of a new moon, or of sabbaths, which are a shadow of things to come" (Col. 2:16). He put "part of a feast day" here to distinguish it from the perpetual festival, so that we may hold not a brief one and, so to speak, some small particle of the whole body, but the whole span of our life as a perpetual solemnity in Christ. And, to connect the earlier with the later, what he thinks of the law of Moses and of superfluous fussiness about foods in this same Epistle he at once adds, saying: "For if you have died with Christ from the elements of this world, why do you still, as though living in this world, lay down decrees? Do not touch, nor taste, nor handle, which things all are for destruction by the very use, according to the precepts and doctrines of men". Someone may say: If it is not permitted to observe days, and months, and times, and years, we too incur a similar charge when we observe the fourth day of the week, and the Preparation, and the Lord's day, and the fast of Lent, and the festival of the Pasch, and the gladness of Pentecost, and the various times appointed, according to the variety of regions, in honor of the martyrs. He who answers this simply will say that the days of the Jewish observance are not the same as ours. For we do not celebrate a pasch of unleavened bread, but of the resurrection and of the cross. Nor do we number seven weeks at Pentecost after the custom of Israel, but we venerate the coming of the Holy Spirit. And lest a disorderly gathering of the people should diminish faith in Christ, for that reason certain days have been appointed, so that we might all come together into one place. Not that the day on which we assemble is more festive, but that, on whatever day we are to assemble, a greater joy may arise from the sight of one another. He, however, who tries to answer the opposing question more acutely affirms this: that all days are equal, and that Christ is not crucified only on the Preparation and does not rise only on the Lord's day, but that it is always the holy day of the resurrection and always one may feed on the Lord's flesh; and that fasts and assemblies on days in between were appointed by prudent men on account of those who are more free for the world than for God, and who cannot, or rather will not, gather in the church through the whole time of their life and, before their human business, offer to God the sacrifice of their prayers. For how many are there who always practice even these few things that have been appointed, the times either of praying or of fasting? And so, just as it is permitted to us either to fast always or always to pray, and, rejoicing, to celebrate the Lord's day unceasingly, having received the Lord's body, it is not likewise lawful for the Jews to sacrifice the lamb at all times, to keep Pentecost, to pitch tabernacles, to fast daily.
Homily on Galatians 4

Observe the tender compassion of the Apostle; they were shaken and he trembles and fears. And hence he has put it so as thoroughly to shame them, "I have bestowed labor upon you," saying, as it were, make not vain the labors which have cost me sweat and pain. By saying "I fear," and subjoining the word "lest," he both inspires alarm, and encourages good hope. He says not "I have labored in vain," but "lest," which is as much as to say, the wreck has not happened, but I see the storm big with it; so I am in fear, yet not in despair; ye have the power to set all right, and to return into your former calm...
Commentary on Galatians

Quite cautiously, however, has he tempered his words between the authority of the Apostle and the gentleness of a holy man, adding: I fear you, lest perhaps I have labored in vain among you. For had he wished to condemn them abruptly, he would certainly have said: I fear you: for I have labored in vain among you. But now, seeing that they have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge, he neither wholly despaired of the salvation of those who had been deceived by a pious error, nor, on the other hand, did he leave them unreproved, lest he should give both to them an occasion of persevering in error and to the rest likewise an occasion of erring. But I fear you, he set down in place of I fear for you. A teacher labors in vain when he himself calls his disciples on to greater things, and they, slipping back, roll down again to lesser and lowly things.
Discourse to the Greeks, Chapter V

O trumpet of peace to the soul that is at war! O weapon that puttest to flight terrible passions! O instruction that quenches the innate fire of the soul! The Word exercises an influence which does not make poets: it does not equip philosophers nor skilled orators, but by its instruction it makes mortals immortal, mortals gods; and from the earth transports them to the realms above Olympus. Come, be taught; become as I am, for I, too, was as ye are.
QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 60: ON BE AS I AM (GAL. 4:12)

When the Apostle says to the Galatians, whom he rebukes and reproves throughout the whole epistle, Be as I am, because I am as you are (Gal. 4:12): if therefore he had made himself such as they were, it was unnecessary to say, Be as I am. Or perhaps in some things he had begun to be an imitator of them, and in others he wishes them to become like him? — What of theirs could the Apostle imitate? Or what was lacking to the teacher of the Gentiles? Rather, he exhorts them to be his imitators; and since it is not impossible, he reproves them in this way when he says, Because I am what you are: for you are human, just as I am; therefore do what I do. It can also be referred to that statement where he says that he became all things to all by agreeing with them in those points where they did not differ from the truth, especially the Gentiles (1 Cor. 9:22). For there was nothing of theirs, which ought no longer to be done, that had not previously been rightly done, such as circumcision, the observance of sabbaths, new moons, foods. But if he approved anything of the Gentiles, he did not show that it should still continue. For they say that the world was made by God and by men: this always stands. If therefore in these matters, by consenting to them, he was made as they were, he exhorts them that in a similar way they too should become as he is, agreeing with his doctrine.
Homily on Galatians 4

This is addressed to his Jewish disciples, and he brings his own example forward, to induce them thereby to abandon their old customs. Though you had none other for a pattern, he says, to look at me only would have sufficed for such a change, and for your taking courage. Therefore gaze on me; I too was once in your state of mind, especially so; I had a burning zeal for the Law; yet afterwards I feared not to abandon the Law, to withdraw from that rule of life. And this ye know full well how obstinately I clung hold of Judaism, and how with yet greater force I let it go. He does well to place this last in order: for most men, though they are given a thousand reasons, and those just ones, are more readily influenced by that which is like their own case, and more firmly hold to that which they see done by others.

Observe how he again addresses them by a title of honor, which was a reminder moreover of the doctrine of grace. Having chid them seriously, and brought things together from all quarters, and shown their violations of the Law, and hit them on many sides, he gives in and conciliates them speaking more tenderly. For as to do nothing but conciliate causes negligence, so to be constantly talked at with sharpness sours a man; so that it is proper to observe due proportion everywhere. See then how he excuses to them what he has said, and shows that it proceeded not simply because he did not like them, but from anxiety. After giving them a deep cut, he pours in this encouragement like oil; and, showing that his words were not words of hate or enmity, he reminds them of the love which they had evinced toward him, mixing his self-vindication with praises. Therefore he says, "ye did me no wrong."
Commentary on Galatians

Be as I also am, because I also am as you.

What he says is this: just as I became weak to you who were weak, and could not speak to you as to spiritual men but as to carnal men and little ones in Christ, and, because you were not yet able to feed on solid food, gave you only the milk of the Gospel to drink, not wishing you to remain forever in the age of infancy but to lead you little by little on to adolescence and youth, so that you might be able to take solid food: so you too ought to be as I also am, namely to have a taste for more perfect things and, leaving milk behind, to pass on to stronger foods and to greater pastures. And he says this as an imitator of the Savior, who did not think it robbery to be equal to God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a slave; and was found in habit as a man, so that we might become gods from men and no longer die; but, rising together with Christ, might be called his friends and brothers, and so that the disciple might be as the teacher, and the slave as the master. But it can also be understood thus: I beseech you, he says, brothers, that, despising the Jewish observance of days, months, seasons and years, which are shadows of things to come, you imitate me, who, having lived without reproach in the Law, counted all things as refuse and rubbish, that I might gain Christ. For I too was as you now are, when I was held bound by the same observances, and, because the Church of Christ did not do these things, I persecuted it and laid it waste.
Commentary on Galatians

Brothers, I beseech you, you have done me no injury. And you know that through infirmity of the flesh I preached the gospel to you some time ago.

Join what follows to the preceding sentence; and to make this clearer, let the order be the one we construct: I beseech you, brothers, be as I am, because I also am as you are. Like this is that saying: "We entreat on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God" (2 Cor. 5:20). And elsewhere too: "I beseech that first of all supplications, prayers, petitions, thanksgivings be made" (1 Tim. 2:1). So also the words of Peter, who says: "The elders among you I entreat, who am myself a fellow elder and a witness of the sufferings of Christ" (1 Pet. 5:1). These words indeed both summon us to humility and strike down the haughty brow of bishops who, as though set upon some lofty watchtower, scarcely deign to look at mortals and to speak to their fellow slaves. Let them learn from the Apostle that the erring and unwise Galatians are called brothers. Let them learn from him who, after rebuke, speaks gentle words: "I beseech you" (1 Cor. 11). And what he beseeches is this, that they be imitators of him, as he himself is of Christ; or rather, to keep to the present passage, what he asks is nothing great: that just as he himself for their sake was made lesser from greater, so they should climb up from lesser things to greater. In nothing, he says, have you injured me. A disciple injures his master if through his own negligence he wastes his precepts and his labor. The Galatians had not injured the Apostle, since up to the present time they were keeping his Gospel and his commandments. Or certainly thus: When I first announced the Gospel to you, and on account of the infirmity of your flesh, because you could not receive the greater mysteries, I preached to you as to little children, and pretended that I myself was weak, so that I might gain you who were weak: did you not receive me as an angel, as Christ Jesus? Since, then, you did me no injury in anything at that time, and thought me, humble and cast down for your sake, like the Son of God, how is it that, when I summon you to greater things, I am injured by you, through the waste of my labor, and that you now mourn, with the work made void, that dispensation by which I had pretended to be a little one?
Homily on Galatians 4

Not to have injured one is indeed no great thing, for no man whatever would choose to hurt wantonly and without object to annoy another who had never injured him. But for you, not only have ye not injured me, but ye have shown me great and inexpressible kindness, and it is impossible that one who has been treated with such attention should speak thus from any malevolent motive. My language then cannot be caused by ill-will; it follows, that it proceeds from affection and solicitude. "Ye did me no wrong; ye know that because of an infirmity of the flesh I preached the Gospel unto you." What can be gentler than this holy soul, what sweeter, or more affectionate! And the words he had already used, arose not from an unreasoning anger, nor from a passionate emotion, but from much solicitude. And why do I say, ye have not injured me? Rather have ye evinced a great and sincere regard for me. For "ye know," he says, "that because of an infirmity of the flesh I preached the Gospel unto you; and that which was a temptation to you in my flesh ye despised not, nor rejected." What does he mean? While I preached to you, I was driven about, I was scourged, I suffered a thousand deaths, yet ye thought no scorn of me; for this is meant by that which was a temptation to you in my flesh ye despised not, nor rejected." Observe his spiritual skill; in the midst of his self-vindication, he again appeals to their feelings by showing what he had suffered for their sakes. This however, says he, did not at all offend you, nor did ye reject me on account of my sufferings and persecutions; or, as he now calls them, his infirmity and temptation.

But ye received me as an Angel of God. Was it not then absurd in them to receive him as an Angel of God, when he was persecuted and driven about, and then not to receive him when pressing on them what was fitting?
Commentary on Galatians

Now Paul announces the Gospel to the Galatians through the infirmity of the flesh, not his own but that of his hearers, who could not subject the flesh to the word of God, but, being as it were fleshly, received nothing of spiritual understanding. To make this more evident, let us set out an example. He teaches through the infirmity of the flesh who says: "If they do not contain themselves, let them marry". And: "A woman, if her husband has died, is free: let her marry whom she will, only in the Lord" (1 Cor. 7:9, 39). But he by no means teaches through the infirmity of the flesh when he records these things: "You are loosed from a wife: do not seek a wife". And: "It is time that those who have wives be as though they had none" (ibid. 27, 29). For some precepts are given to the spiritual, others to the fleshly. And it is one thing that is commanded by way of command, another by way of indulgence.
Commentary on Galatians

And your temptation, which was in my flesh, you did not despise nor reject; but you received me as an angel of God, as Christ Jesus.

An obscure passage, and one to be attended to more keenly. I, he says, long ago preached the Gospel to you as to little ones and sucklings, because of the weakness of your flesh, beginning from the lesser things and (so to speak) almost stammering among you. This dispensation and pretense of a weak preaching was indeed my management; but it was your temptation, to see whether those things would please you and seem great which in their own condition were lesser, and were brought forth by me as if lowly. And you, taking them not as small but as great, admired them so much that you welcomed me, who spoke them, as an angel and, to say more, as the Son of God. This temptation of yours, then, by which I was tempting you in the carnal proclamation of my discourse, was not despised, nor was it held cheap; but it had more dignity than I reckoned. This passage can also be explained thus: when I came to you, I did not come in the word of wisdom, but as a lowly and despised man, bringing nothing great: the Crucified. When, therefore, you saw me placed in a body subject to infirmities, promising the heavenly kingdoms, you did not laugh at me, nor did you reckon me worthy of contempt: for you understood that the lowliness of my flesh and the meanness of my very bearing came about for your temptation, namely, whether you would despise him who was thought pitiable by unbelievers; but on the contrary you welcomed that lowly, mean and despised man as an angel, and more than an angel. Or surely we can suspect that the Apostle, at the time when he first came to the Galatians, was sick; and that, though held back by some infirmity of his poor body, he nevertheless did not cease nor hold back his voice in silence from preaching the Gospel he had begun. For they relate that he often suffered a most severe pain of the head, and that this is the angel of Satan who was set upon him to buffet him in the flesh, lest he be lifted up. This infirmity and this sickness of the body was a temptation for those to whom the Gospel was proclaimed: whether they would despise him who promised sublime things, whom they saw subject to the sicknesses of the body. It can also be said that at the beginning of his coming to the Galatians he endured insults and persecutions and blows on his body from those who opposed the Gospel; and that this was the very greatest temptation for the Galatians, seeing the Apostle of Christ beaten. But when he says, as an angel, as Christ Jesus you welcomed me, he both shows that Christ is greater than an angel, Christ whom the Psalmist had sung as lesser according to the dispensation of the body, saying: "You have made him a little less than the angels" (Ps. 8:6); and he demonstrates that his own words at the beginning had such force that they were thought to be those of an angel and of Christ.
Homily on Galatians 4

Here he shows perplexity and amazement, and desires to learn of themselves the reason of their change. Who, says he, hath deceived you, and caused a difference in your disposition towards me? Are ye not the same who attended and ministered to me, counting me more precious than your own eyes? what then has happened? whence this dislike? whence this suspicion? Is it because I have told you the truth? You ought on this very account to pay me increased honor and attention; instead of which "I am become your enemy, because I tell you the truth,"-for I can find no other reason but this. Observe too what humbleness of mind appears in his defence of himself; he proves not by his conduct to them, but by theirs to him that his language could not possibly have proceeded from unkind feeling. For he says not; How is it supposable that one, who has been scourged and driven about, and ill-treated a thousand things for your sakes, should now have schemes against you? But he argues from what they had reason to boast of, saying, How can one who has been honored by you, and received as an Angel, repay you by conduct the very opposite?
Commentary on Galatians

Where then is your blessedness? For I bear you witness that, if it could have been done, you would have plucked out your eyes and given them to me. Have I then become your enemy, telling you the truth?

Blessed is he who walks in the way of the virtues, but only if he arrives all the way to the virtues. Nor does it profit to have withdrawn from vices unless you lay hold of the best things. For in good pursuits it is not so much the beginnings that are to be praised as the end. For just as in the vineyard there are many stages of the grape up to the press: first the vine must bud into leafy shoots and hold out hope in its blossoms; then, once the flower has fallen, the form of the future cluster is shaped, and little by little the grape, swelling, comes to its birth, so that, pressed in the winepresses, it may sweat out sweet must. So also in teaching there are single advances of blessedness: that someone hears the word of God, that he conceives it, that it grows in the womb of his soul and comes all the way to birth; that, when he has brought it forth, he nourishes it with milk and leads it through infancy, boyhood, adolescence and youth all the way to the perfect man. Since, then, the single stages, as we have said, have their blessedness according to their advances, if the end, and, so to speak, the finishing hand is lacking to the work, all the labor will become void; and it will be said: Where then is your blessedness? Although, he says, at the time when you received the Gospel according to the flesh I called you blessed because you were fervent in the beginnings, yet now, because I do not see the roof set upon the building, and the foundations hardly laid at all, I am compelled to say: Where then is your blessedness, for which, judging you blessed, I used to praise you before? For truly I myself also confess that you so loved me in the beginning, when I preached lowly things to you and was beset by persecutions, that, if it could have been done (and what he says is to be taken as hyperbole), you would have plucked out your eyes and given them to me, so that I might see more with the lights of all of you. For you wished to be blind yourselves through an ineffable love toward me, so that the light of the Gospel might rise more fully in my heart; you wished my gain to grow by your losses: and this at that time when, whether because of the weakness of your flesh I announced small and lowly things to you as to little ones and sucklings, or because of the injuries of my own flesh, I did not seem worthy of belief.
The Instructor Book 1

Wherefore the apostle himself also in every case uses stringent language to the Churches, after the Lord's example; and conscious of his own boldness, and of the weakness of his hearers, he says to the Galatians: "Am I your enemy, because I tell you the truth?" Thus also people in health do not require a physician, do not require him as long as they are strong; but those who are ill need his skill. Thus also we who in our lives are ill of shameful lusts and reprehensible excesses, and other inflammatory effects of the passions, need the Saviour. And He administers not only mild, but also stringent medicines. The bitter roots of fear then arrest the eating sores of our sins. Wherefore also fear is salutary, if bitter.
Epistle LXI

Therefore, dearest brother, endeavour that the undisciplined should not be consumed and perish, that as much as you can, by your salutary counsels, you should rule the brotherhood, and take counsel of each one with a view to his salvation. Strait and narrow is the way through which we enter into life, but excellent and great is the reward when we enter into glory. Let those who have once made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven please God in all things, and not offend God's priests nor the Lord's Church by the scandal of their wickedness. And if, for the present, certain of our brethren seem to be made sorry by us, let us nevertheless remain in our wholesome persuasion, knowing that an apostle also has said, "Am I therefore become your enemy because I tell you the truth? " But if they shall obey us, we have gained our brethren, and have formed them as well to salvation as to dignity by our address. But if some of the perverse persons refuse to obey, let us follow the same apostle, who says, "If I please men, I should not be the servant of Christ." If we cannot please some, so as to make them please Christ, let us assuredly, as far as we can, please Christ our Lord and God, by observing His precepts.
Commentary on Galatians

But now, because I have begun to call you on from the elements and syllables and the reading of boys to greater studies, so that you may hold books in your hands and may learn words full of learning and of meanings, you kick back, you are angry, the perfection of teachings seems burdensome to you; and you are changed to other feelings to such a degree that me, whom you had received as an angel and as Christ, to whom you wished to hand over your eyes, you now hold as an enemy, because I announce to you the full truth. And he has elegantly ended the sentence, saying: Have I then become your enemy, telling you the truth? in order to show that the beginnings of the preaching were not so much the truth as the shadow and image of the truth. Like this is that famous sentence of the poet among the Romans (Terence, Andria 1.1): Compliance begets friends, truth hatred. But see how much better the one here is than that one; for the Apostle tempered this sentence for those whom he had called foolish, whom he had named little ones, and made it particular, since he directed it properly to the persons and to the Galatians. But that one, declaring it both general and as holding so among all men, erred badly. For compliance, by which he thought friends are made, once truth is taken away, is not so much compliance as flattery and fawning; and it is plain that these ought to be called hidden enmities rather than friendships. At the same time this too must be considered, that today also, so long as we explain the Scriptures according to the letter to little ones and sucklings, and to those in whose hearts Christ never grows up nor advances in age and wisdom and grace with God and men, we are praised, looked up to, held in admiration. But when we have begun a little to call them on to pass over to greater things, from being our heralds they become enemies, and they would rather follow the Jews than the apostles, who, withdrawing from the teaching and traditions of the Pharisees, entered into Christ himself, the propitiatory, and the perfection of the Law; nor do they deign to accept the divine word, which bids the teachers of the Church to climb to loftier doctrines, to raise the voice with all their strength, and not to fear the clamor of the little ones barking around them, saying: "Go up on a lofty mountain, you who bring good tidings to Sion. Lift up your voice in strength, you who bring good tidings to Jerusalem. Lift it up, do not fear" (Isa. 40:9).
Homily on Galatians 4

It is a wholesome emulation which leads to an imitation of virtue, but an evil one, which seduces from virtue him who is in the right path. And this is the object of those persons, who would deprive you of perfect knowledge, and impart to you that which is mutilated and spurious, and this for no other purpose than that they may occupy the rank of teachers, and degrade you, who now stand higher than themselves, to the position of disciples. For this is the meaning of the words "that ye may seek them." They emulate you not well: but they wish to shut you out, that you may emulate them. But emulate the good in a good thing always: and not only when I am present with you.

They emulate well who, when they see graces, gifts and powers in certain people, themselves desire to be such: and they strive to imitate the faith, life and diligence of those people, through which they merited those things, so that they too may be able to attain the things that are good and worthy of emulation. Of these the Apostle also says: "Emulate spiritual things: but rather that you may prophesy". And next: "So you also, since you are emulators of spiritual things, seek to abound for the edification of the Church". And again: "Therefore, brothers, emulate to prophesy, and do not forbid to speak in tongues". But they emulate not well who do not so much desire to be better themselves, by imitating those who are worthy of emulation, as wish to make those very people worse, and to drag them backward by a perverse emulation. Let it be said by way of example: someone is a Christian; he reads Moses and the prophets; he knows that all things went before for that people in shadow and in image, but were written for our sake, upon whom the ends of the ages have come down. He understands circumcision not so much of the foreskin as of the ears and of the heart. He has risen with Christ: he seeks the things that are above. He has been freed from the burden and slavery of the Law, which commands: touch not, taste not, defile not. If anyone should wish to persuade this man by the words of the Scriptures to receive the things that are written not through tropology but according to the killing letter, so that he becomes a Jew outwardly, not inwardly, that person emulates him not well: rather he hastens to drag back one who is advancing at a swift pace toward greater things, so that the other may instead emulate him who is going backward; or at the least he keeps him from advancing much further. He speaks, therefore, to the Galatians, who had been induced by the champions of the Law to imitate them, when those men ought rather to have imitated the Galatians.
Commentary on Galatians

This is said of that zeal and perverse emulation of which it is also said elsewhere: "Do not emulate among the evildoers" (Ps. 36:1); and here: They emulate you not well. But we find also another zeal, with which the sons of Jacob were zealous against their brother Joseph (Gen. 37 ff.), and Miriam and Aaron against Moses, the friend of the Lord (Num. 12). For neither the former nor the latter were stirred to zeal in order to become better than Joseph and Moses, but because they grieved that those men were better. This zeal is a near neighbor of envy. It would be a long task if I wished to bring forth from the treasury of the Scriptures all the kinds of zeal, whether good or bad. We read of the good zeal of Phinehas (Num. 25), of Elijah (1 Kings 19), of Mattathias (1 Macc. 2), and of the apostle Judas (but not the traitor), who on account of the remarkable power of zeal in him received also the name of Zealot (Acts 1). And bad zeal, as that of Cain against Abel (Gen. 4), and of others against others. And the zeal of a husband, of which it is written: "And the spirit of zeal come upon him" (Num. 5). Unless perhaps this zeal is intermediate, and can be taken neither in a good nor in a bad sense, but, standing between the two, is rather called jealousy. Otherwise: those who were of the circumcision, seeing that the Galatians from the Gentiles abounded in the powers of the Holy Spirit, while they themselves did not speak in tongues, did not have gifts of healings, nor the grace of prophecy, were spurred on by the goads of zeal and desired to bring them over to the burdens of the Law, so that they too might begin to become like them.

And since it is natural that the greater should be made from the lesser, not the lesser from the greater, he also says: Emulate the good in a good thing, that is, do not imitate the champions of Jewish observance, but imitate the things that are good. For just as one who imitates someone's riches, power and rank emulates not so much good things as things that ought to be shunned, so you, on the contrary, emulate the good in a good thing, seeking spiritual things rather than carnal ones, so that it is not they who teach you to be Jews, but you who teach them to be Christians. And do this always, so that with persevering step you may be able to reach the end of the good work. For indeed you emulated the good in a good thing formerly, when I was with you; but after I departed from you, you lost everything I had handed on to you, drawn away from a sure anchorage and a trusty harbor out again into the deep by the ebbing wave. Nor is it any wonder if, when the Apostle departed, the vessel of election, in whom Christ the Lord spoke, the Galatians were changed, since even now we see the very same thing happen in the churches too. For if ever there happens to be in a church a teacher adorned in speech and in life, who rouses his hearers to virtues as if with certain goads, we see the whole people hasten, burn with fervor and run to and fro over almsgiving, fasting, chastity, the receiving of the poor, the burial of the dead and other such things. But when he has departed, we see it little by little wither away, and, its food withdrawn, grow thin, turn pale and languish, and the ruin follow of everything that had flourished before. Wherefore, since the harvest is great but the laborers are few (Matt. 9:37), let us pray the Lord of the harvest to send laborers to reap, who may reap and gather the ears of the Christian people that stand in the Church, made ready to be the wheat to come, and, carrying them into the barns, may by no means allow them to perish.

That there are also some souls that conceive offspring, the prophet made clear when he said: "from fear of you, Lord, we conceived in the womb and travailed and gave birth to a spirit of salvation which you made upon the earth". For just as in those who are pregnant the seed is formed and shaped, so also in the soul that receives the word, the conception of the word is gradually formed and shaped within it. And this I think is what Paul says to the Galatians: "my children, whom I again bring forth in travail until Christ be formed in you", which is as though he were to say: until the word be formed and made manifest in you. In the epistle to Timothy he says likewise that a woman shall be saved "through the bearing of children, if she abide in faith and love and holiness with chastity". Therefore the souls that have newly received the word and, being still established as pregnant, have not yet borne fruit in it, having it intelligibly in the womb, cannot endure the discourse that stands "in the holy place" opposing the truth, nor stand firm so as not to be seduced by its persuasions.

The pregnant woman is said to be the soul which has recently conceived the word of God. Now concerning such a conception we read it written also in another place: "from fear of you, O Lord, we have conceived in the womb, and we have given birth." Those, therefore, who conceive and immediately give birth—these are to be reckoned not as women, but as men, and perfect men. Hear, finally, also the prophet saying: "if the earth has given birth in one day, and a nation has been born at once." This is the generation of the perfect, which is born immediately, on the same day, as soon as it has been conceived. But lest it seem new to you that we have said men give birth, we have already long since set forth how you ought to take the names of the members, that you may withdraw from bodily senses and grasp the understanding of the inner man. But if you wish that I satisfy you still further in this also from the Scriptures, hear the Apostle saying: "my little children, whom I again bring forth in travail, until Christ be formed in you." Perfect, therefore, and strong men are those who immediately, as soon as they conceive, give birth—that is, those who bring the conceived word of faith forth into works. But the soul which conceives and retains in the womb and does not give birth, this one is called a woman, just as the prophet also says: "the pains of childbirth have come upon her, and the power of giving birth is not in her." This soul, then, which now on account of its weakness is called a woman, when two men are quarreling with one another and in the contest bringing forth stumbling-blocks—which the contention of words is always wont to have—is struck and scandalized, so that it casts out and loses the word of faith which it had faintly conceived; and this is the quarrel and contention "unto the subversion of the hearers." If, therefore, the soul which has been scandalized casts out the word not yet formed, he who scandalized it is said to suffer loss. Do you wish to know that in some the word is formed, in some not yet formed? The word of the Apostle plainly teaches us, which we recalled above, when he says: "until Christ be formed in you"; but Christ is the Word of God. By this he shows that at the time when he was writing, the Word of God was not yet formed in them; if, therefore, it comes forth not yet formed, he shall suffer loss.

Observe his perplexity and perturbation, "Brethren, I beseech you:" "My little children, of whom I am again in travail:" He resembles a mother trembling for her children. "Until Christ be formed in you." Behold his paternal tenderness, behold this despondency worthy of an Apostle. Observe what a wail he utters, far more piercing than of a woman in travail;-Ye have defaced the likeness, ye have destroyed the kinship, ye have changed the form, ye need another regeneration and refashioning; nevertheless I call you children, abortions and monsters though ye be. However, he does not express himself in this way, but spares them, unwilling to strike, and to inflict wound upon wound. Wise physicians do not cure those who have fallen into a long sickness all at once, but little by little, lest they should faint and die. And so is it with this blessed man; for these pangs were more severe in proportion as the force of his affection was stronger. And the offense was of no trivial kind. And as I have ever said and ever will say, even a slight fault mars the appearance and distorts the figure of the whole.

My little children, of whom I travail again, until Christ be formed in you.

With what great difficulties and pain offspring are brought forth from the womb, the first curse declares, saying: "In sorrow you shall bear children" (Gen. 3:16). Wishing therefore to show the solicitude of teachers for their disciples, and what feelings they suffer lest their followers fall away from salvation, Paul says: My little children, of whom I travail again. For he who in another place had said as a father: "Though you have ten thousand pedagogues in Christ, yet not many fathers" (1 Cor. 4:15), now speaks in Christ no longer as a father but as a mother, so that they may recognize in him the anxiety and the tender devotion of both parents. Something of the sort Moses too said of the people: "Did I receive all this people in my womb" (Num. 11:12)? Which of us, do you think, is so anxious for the salvation of his disciples that he is tormented not for a few hours, or at most for two or three days, but for the whole time of his life, until Christ is formed in them? The example he has taken of a pregnant woman, conceiving and forming the seed within herself, must be carefully held to, so that we may understand what is said. Nature is not to be blushed at, but revered. For just as the seed is first cast without form into a woman's womb, so that it clings to its furrows and floor as if with a kind of glue (and the prophet too, remembering his own beginning, says of it: "Your eyes saw my unformed state" (Ps. 138:16)); then through nine months, the blood being held back, the future man is curdled, given a body, nourished and articulated into parts; so that, after it has stirred in the womb, at the appointed time it is poured forth into the light, and is born with as great difficulties as those with which it is afterwards nursed lest it perish: so too the seed of the word of Christ, when it has fallen into the soul of the hearer, grows by its own stages, and, to pass over many things (for we can easily transfer the bodily description to the spiritual understanding), it remains in a precarious state for as long as it takes until he who conceived gives birth. Nor is the end of the effort reached at once in having brought forth; rather, then comes the beginning of another labor: to lead the suckling infancy, with diligent nourishment and pains, up to the full age of Christ. And just as in marriage the husband's seed is often the cause that children are not begotten, sometimes a barren wife does not retain the seed, frequently neither is fit for begetting, and on the contrary both are fruitful: so too among those who sow the word of God this fourfold division holds: either the teacher indeed fulfills his office, but the hearer is barren; or the hearer is of good disposition, but through the teacher's want of skill the seed of the word perishes; or surely the one who is taught is as senseless as the one who instructs; and rarely does it happen that master and disciple are in accord with each other, namely that the one teaches as much as the other can draw in, or that the one taught takes in as much as the teacher pours in. But now we are all judges. We do not know what number a psalm is, what part of prophecy, what chapter of the Law, and by mere facility of speech we boldly interpret what we in no way understand. It is no concern of ours that Christ be formed in the people, that each one, returning to his own home, may have the seed of the word of God, so that when he has conceived it he may say with the prophet: "From fear of you, O Lord, we have conceived and brought forth; we have made children of your salvation upon the earth" (Isa. 26:17, 18). Such people pass over into the apostles, and deserve to hear from the Savior: "Whoever shall do the will of my Father, he is my brother, and sister, and mother" (Matt. 12:50): the diversity of their progress being shown in the different names. Christ is also formed in the heart of believers when all mysteries are laid open to them, and the things that seemed obscure become clear. But this too must be observed: that he who through sin had in a certain manner ceased to be a man is conceived by the master through penitence, and the forming of Christ in him is promised once again. This is against the Novatians, who will not have those whom sins have once crushed formed anew.

Observe his warmth, his inability to refrain himself, and to conceal these his feelings; such is the nature of love; nor is he satisfied with words, but desires to be present with them, and so, as he says, to change his voice, that is, to change to lamentation, to shed tears, to turn every thing into mourning. For he could not by letter show his tears or cries of grief, and therefore he ardently desires to be present with them.

I know not, says he, what to say, or what to think. How is it, that ye who by dangers, which ye endured for the faith's sake, and by miracles, which ye performed through faith, had ascended to the highest heaven, should suddenly be brought to such a depth of degradation as to be drawn aside to circumcision or sabbaths, and should rely wholly upon Judaizers? Hence in the beginning he says, "I marvel that ye are so quickly removing," and here, "I am perplexed about you," as if he said, What am I to speak? What am I to utter? What am I to think? I am bitterly perplexed. And so he must needs weep, as the prophets do when in perplexity; for not only admonition but mourning also is a form in which solicitous attention is often manifested. And what he said in his speech to those at Miletus, "By the space of three years I ceased not to warn every one with tears, he says here also, "and to change my voice." (Acts 20:31.) When we find ourselves overcome by perplexity and helplessness which come contrary to expectation, we are driven to tears; and so Paul admonished them sharply, and endeavored to shame them, then in turn soothed them, and lastly he wept. And this weeping is not only a reproof but a blandishment; it does not exasperate like reproof, nor relax like indulgent treatment, but is a mixed remedy, and of great efficacy in the way of exhortation. Having thus softened and powerfully engaged their hearts by his tears, he again advances to the contest, and lays down a larger proposition, proving that the Law itself was opposed to its being kept. Before, he produced the example of Abraham, but now (what is more cogent) he brings forward the Law itself enjoining them not to keep itself, but to leave off. So that, says he, you must abandon the Law, if you would obey it, for this is its own wish: this however he does not say expressly, but enforces it in another mode, mixing up with it an account of facts.

But I would wish to be with you now, and to change my voice, because I am confounded in you.

Divine Scripture edifies even when it is read; but it profits much more if it is turned from letters into voice, so that he who had taught through the Epistle may, being present, instruct his hearers. For the living voice has great force: a voice resounding from the mouth of its author, which is uttered and articulated with the very delivery with which it was generated in its own man's heart. The Apostle, therefore, knowing that speech addressed to those who are present has greater force, desires to change the epistolary voice, the voice confined in letters, into presence: and, because this was more expedient for those who had been perverted in error, to draw them back to the truth by living speech. And this for the reason that he was confounded in them: which indeed is said more properly in Greek. For Ἀποροῦμαι signifies not so much confusion, which among them is called αἰσχύνη or σύγχυσις, as need and want. This, then, is the sense: I would wish to be with you now, and to utter in person, being present myself, the voice of my letters, because I am in need in you. For I do not have the fruits that teachers are accustomed to have from their disciples; and the seed of teachings has been sown in vain, since I suffer utter destitution in you: so that I could break out in the words of Jeremiah: "I have not profited, nor has anyone profited me" (Jer. 15:10). This passage can also be interpreted another way: Paul the apostle, who had become a Jew to the Jews, that he might gain the Jews (1 Cor. 9), and to those who were under the Law as though he himself were under the Law, and weak to the weak, that he might gain the weak: according to the character of those whom he desired to save, he would change his voice, and, in the manner of actors (for indeed he was made a spectacle to the world, and to angels, and to men [1 Cor. 4]), he would turn his bearing and his voices into various shapes. Not that he was what he pretended to be; but that he only seemed to be what was of profit to the others. He perceives that the Galatians need another teaching, that they must be saved by another way, not by that by which they had first been brought over from heathenism to the faith of Christ: and he is compelled to say: I would wish now to be with you, and to change my voice, because I am confounded in you. I do not see, he says, that I am of profit if I speak the things that I spoke before; because of which, not knowing what to do, and drawn in different directions, I am torn, confounded and rent apart. And just as physicians, when they have seen that the force of their art does not prevail with the first remedy, pass on to another, and go on trying for so long which of several may help, until they arrive at a cure, so that what could by no means be healed by the softness of some plaster may be healed by a more biting powder and a harsher treatment: so I too, because I am confounded in you and am drawn hither and thither by not knowing, would wish, being present, to utter the voice of my letters from my own mouth, so that I myself might rebuke you more severely than usual; since a letter cannot express the voice of one who rebukes; it cannot make the outcry of one who is angry resound, nor unfold the pain of the breast in strokes of the pen. But it can also be understood more simply: I have just now used gentle words with you, saying: "Brothers, I beseech you". And: "My little children, of whom I am again in labor until Christ be formed in you"; but I, gentle and mild, who spoke to you as a father, out of that love by which I do not suffer my sons to perish and to wander perpetually, would wish now to be present, if the chains of my confession did not confine me, and to change my gentle voice into the words of one who rebukes. Nor is it fickleness if I now coax, now grow angry; love impels me, sorrow impels me, to speak with differing feelings. For I do not know into what words I should first break out, and with what remedy I ought to heal you, because I am confounded in you.
