For it is written that Abraham had two sons, one by the bondwoman and one by the free woman. But he who was by the bondwoman was born according to the flesh; but he who was by the free woman, through the promise.

It is a matter of very great difficulty to show that only Isaac, who was born of Sarah, was begotten by promise, and not Ishmael too, who sprang from Hagar, the Egyptian bondwoman. For Scripture relates that when, with Sarah persecuting her, Hagar had fled while with child, and an angel had come to her in the desert and was warning her to submit herself to her mistress's authority, that same angel also spoke these words: "Multiplying I will multiply your seed, and it shall not be numbered for multitude" (Gen. 16:10). And afterward, concerning Ishmael (and no one would doubt that these are certainly words of promise): "He shall be a rustic man, his hand over all, and the hands of all over him, and he shall dwell over against the face of all his brothers". But it can be answered that the promise of an angel is of lesser authority than that of God himself. For just as a star does not glow when the sun has risen, so too the words of the angel, in comparison with the promise of God, are obscured, and vanish, and are counted as nothing. This answer does indeed seem to have some weight; but it is at once crushed by the authority of the Scripture that follows. For it is written: "But Abraham said to God: Let this Ishmael live in your sight" (ibid., 17:18 ff.); and God answered him thus: "Behold, Sarah your wife shall bear you a son, and you shall call his name Isaac, and I will establish my testament with him, for an everlasting testament, and with his seed after him. But concerning Ishmael: Behold, I have heard you, and behold, I have blessed him, and I will increase him, and I will multiply him exceedingly. He shall beget twelve nations, and I will make him a great nation; but my testament I will establish with Isaac, whom Sarah shall bear to you at this time, in the coming year". From these words it is evident, by the very speech of God as well, that Ishmael was begotten according to promise. But this too is resolved thus: the promise is properly fulfilled in the giving of the testament, and it is one thing to bless, to increase, to multiply exceedingly, which is written of Ishmael, and another to make an heir through a testament, which is said of Isaac: "I will establish my testament with him, for an everlasting testament, and with his seed after him". And in what follows: "But my testament I will establish with Isaac, whom Sarah shall bear to you" (Gen. 17:19). And just as gifts are one thing and the substance another, legacies one thing and the inheritance another (for we read that gifts were handed over to the sons of Abraham's concubines, but to the son of Sarah was left the inheritance of the whole substance), so, as we have said, blessing and legacies are one thing, the testament another. And this too can be said: that concerning Ishmael either the angel or God spoke after he had been conceived, whereas concerning Isaac God made the promise before he was conceived in Sarah's womb. Let this be said for the present, as far as the mediocrity of our talent allows. But if anyone can find something greater, as to how Ishmael, who was born of the bondwoman, is not the son of promise, but Isaac, who was born of the free woman, is, he should rather be listened to. "And if", says the Apostle, "you think anything otherwise, God has revealed this also to you". Now we must briefly reach toward higher things, so as to say that each one of us is at first not born according to promise, as long as he is instructed by the simple words of the Scriptures and still delights in Jewish expositions; but when he has crossed over to more sublime things and has understood the Law as spiritual, then he is begotten of promise; and, to speak more plainly, those who do the works of Abraham are born of Abraham daily. But those who have the spirit of slavery again in fear are begotten of the Egyptian bondwoman, while those who have received the spirit of adoption are begotten of Sarah, the free woman: the freedom with which we have been endowed by Christ. The Lord speaks to the Jews, who still preferred to be sons of the bondwoman: "If you remain in my word, you will truly be my disciples, and you will know the truth, and the truth will make you free" (John 8:31, 32). Hence they too, not knowing that what was said was mystical, say: "We are the seed of Abraham, and we have never been slaves to anyone: how do you say, You will be free? Jesus answered them: Amen, amen I say to you, that everyone who commits sin is the slave of sin. But the slave does not remain in the house forever; but the son remains forever". If we are slaves of sin, Hagar the Egyptian has begotten us; if sin does not reign in our mortal body, we are truly sons of God.
Homily on Galatians 4

What is the meaning of "after the flesh?" Having said that Faith united us to Abraham, and it having seemed incredible to his hearers, that those who were not begotten by Abraham should be called his sons, he proves that this paradox had actually happened long ago; for that Isaac, born not according to the order of nature, nor the law of marriage, nor the power of the flesh, was yet truly his own son. He was the issue of bodies that were dead, and of a womb that was dead; his conception was not by the flesh, nor his birth by the seed, but the Word of God fashioned Him. Not so in the case of the bondman; He came by virtue of the laws of nature, and after the manner of marriage. Nevertheless, he that was not according to the flesh was more honorable than he that was born after the flesh. Therefore let it not disturb you that ye are not born after the flesh; for from the very reason that ye are not so born, are ye most of all Abraham's kindred. The being born after the flesh renders one not more honorable, but less so, for a birth not after the flesh is more marvellous and more spiritual. And this is plain from the case of those who were born of old time; Ishmael, for instance, who was born according to the flesh, was not only a bondman, but was cast out of his father's house; but Isaac, who was born according to the promise, being a true son and free, was lord of all.
Against Heresies Book IV

Thus, after their simplicity and innocence, did these daughters [of Lot] so speak, imagining that all mankind had perished, even as the Sodomites had done, and that the anger of God had come down upon the whole earth. Wherefore also they are to be held excusable, since they supposed that they only, along with their father, were left for the preservation of the human race; and for this reason it was that they deceived their father. Moreover, by the words they used this fact was pointed out-that there is no other one who can confer upon the elder and younger church the [power of] giving birth to children, besides our Father. Now the father of the human race is the Word of God, as Moses points out when he says, "Is not He thy father who hath obtained thee [by generation], and formed thee, and created thee?" At what time, then, did He pour out upon the human race the life-giving seed-that is, the Spirit of the remission of sins, through means of whom we are quickened? Was it not then, when He was eating with men, and drinking wine upon the earth? For it is said, "The Son of man came eating and drinking;" and when He had lain down, He fell asleep, and took repose. As He does Himself say in David, "I slept, and took repose." And because He used thus to act while He dwelt and lived among us, He says again, "And my sleep became sweet unto me." Now this whole matter was indicated through Lot, that the seed of the Father of all-that is, of the Spirit of God, by whom all things were made-was commingled and united with flesh-that is, with His own workmanship; by which commixture and unity the two synagogues-that is, the two churches-produced from their own father living sons to the living God.
Homily on Galatians 4

Contrary to usage, he calls a type an allegory; his meaning is as follows; this history not only declares that which appears on the face of it, but announces somewhat farther, whence it is called an allegory. And what hath it announced? no less than all the things now present.

For these women are two covenants; one from mount Sinai, bearing children unto bondage, which is Hagar. "These:" who? the mothers of those children, Sarah and Hagar; and what are they? Two covenants, two laws. As the names of the women were given in the history, he abides by this designation of the two races, showing how much follows from the very names. How from the names?
Commentary on Galatians

For these are the two testaments, one indeed from Mount Sinai, bearing children into slavery, which is Hagar. For Sinai is a mountain in Arabia, which borders on that which is now Jerusalem, and is in slavery with her sons. But that Jerusalem which is above is free, which is the mother of us all.

The explanation of nearly everyone on this passage is this: they interpret Hagar, the slave woman, as the Law and the people of the Jews, but Sarah, the free woman, as the Church, which has been gathered from the Gentiles and which is the mother of the saints, as Paul says: Which is the mother of us all. She did not give birth for a long time, before Christ was born of the Virgin, and she was barren, since Isaac, the laughter of the world, was not yet resounding from the chosen father with the voice of sublime doctrines; for indeed Abraham too is rendered in our language "chosen father with sound." But Hagar, which means παροικία, that is, "sojourning," or "pilgrimage," or "tarrying," begets Ishmael, who only hears the precepts of God and does not do them, a rustic man, bloodthirsty, haunting the deserts, who is an enemy to all his brothers born of the free woman and resists them with a hostile front. Nor is it any wonder that the Old Testament, which was established and written down on Mount Sinai, which is in Arabia and borders on that which is now Jerusalem, is not perpetual: since sojourning, too, is different from perpetual possession, and the name of Mount Sinai sounds "temptation," and Arabia signifies "setting"; and, on the contrary, that Jerusalem which is above, which is free and the mother of the saints, shows that this Jerusalem which exists at present is below, and sunk in what is low and lowest. There are some who understand the two Testaments in another way as well: so that they interpret divine Scripture, the old as well as the new, either as the slave woman or as the free woman, according to the diversity of understanding and the judgment of those who read it; and they would have those who still serve the letter and have the spirit of fear unto slavery be begotten of Hagar the Egyptian, but those who ascend to higher things and are willing to understand allegorically what is written be the sons of Sarah, whose name in our language means ἄρχουσα, that is, "princess," in the feminine gender. And they assert that they adopt this view out of the following necessity: because it would be unjust to understand Moses and all the prophets as born of the slave woman, but any of the Gentiles whatever as born of the free woman. Hence, they say, it is better that we should judge not only, concerning those who are in the Church, some to be slaves and others free according to the diversity of their understandings (as we said above), but also, concerning one and the same man, that as long as he follows the history he is the son of the slave woman; but when, as Jesus opens the Scriptures, his heart has been set on fire, and in the breaking of the bread he has looked upon him whom before he did not see (Luke 24), then he too is called a son of Sarah. Marcion and Manichaeus were unwilling to remove from their codex this passage in which the Apostle said: "Which things indeed are allegorical", and the rest that follows, thinking that it was left there against us: namely, that the Law is to be understood otherwise than it is written; whereas, certainly, even if it is to be taken allegorically (which we too confess, and Paul teaches), it was so composed not at the will of the reader, but by the authority of the writer; and by the very thing which they seemed to keep against us they are crushed: that Moses, the servant of God the Creator, wrote spiritual things, their Apostle too teaching that very thing, he whom they themselves assert to be the preacher of another Christ and of a better God.
Commentary on Galatians

Which things are said through allegory.

Allegory belongs properly to the art of grammar, and how it differs from metaphor or the other tropes, we learn as little children in the schools. It puts forward one thing in the words and signifies another in the sense. The books of the orators (supply: of allegories) and of the poets are full of it. Divine Scripture too is woven together through it in no small part. Understanding this, Paul the apostle (since he had touched secular letters to some extent) used the very word of the figure, so as to call it allegory, as it is called among his own people: namely, so that by this sense he might show more fully the loose use (abusionem) of the Greek word in this place. That Paul knew secular letters, though not to perfection, his own words testify: "One of them, a prophet of their own, said: Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, idle bellies" (Titus 1:12). This heroic verse is by the poet Epimenides, whom both Plato and the other ancient writers recall. Among the Athenians also, when he was making his defense in the Areopagus, he added this: "As also certain of your poets have said: For we are also his offspring" (Acts 17:28). This half-line is found in Aratus, who wrote about the heaven and the stars. And also this: "Very evil conversations corrupt good morals" (1 Cor. 15:33); it is an iambic trimeter taken from a comedy of Menander. From these and other passages it is evident that Paul was not ignorant of secular letters, and that what he here called allegory he elsewhere called spiritual understanding. As there: "For we know that the Law is spiritual" (Rom. 7:14), in place of saying allegory, or figured allegorically. And elsewhere: "All ate the same spiritual food, and drank the same spiritual drink. And they drank of the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ" (1 Cor. 10:3-4). There is no one who doubts that the manna here, and the eruption of the sudden spring, and the rock itself that follows, are to be taken allegorically. I know what can be objected on the contrary: "Brothers, if a man has been overtaken in some fault, you who are spiritual instruct such a one in the spirit of gentleness" (below, 6:1). And in another place: "But the spiritual man judges all things, yet he himself is judged by no one" (1 Cor. 2:15): namely, that the word spiritual sounds something other than what we said above. But we call that man spiritual, in that he judges all things and is himself judged by no one, who, knowing all the mysteries of the Scriptures, understands them in a lofty way, and, seeing Christ in the divine books, admits in them nothing of Jewish tradition.
Homily on Galatians 4

The bond-woman was called Hagar, and "Hagar" is the word for Mount Sinai in the language of that country. So that it is necessary that all who are born of the Old Covenant should be bondmen, for that mountain where the Old Covenant was delivered hath a name in common with the bondwoman. And it includes Jerusalem, for this is the meaning of, "And answereth to Jerusalem that now is." That is, it borders on, and is contiguous to it. "For she is in bondage with her children." What follows from hence? Not only that she was in bondage and brought forth bondmen, but that this Covenant is so too, whereof the bondwoman was a type. For Jerusalem is adjacent to the mountain of the same name with the bondwoman, and in this mountain the Covenant was delivered. Now where is the type of Sarah?
Epistle to the Philippians 3

These things, brethren, I write to you concerning righteousness, not because I take anything upon myself, but because ye have invited me to do so. For neither I, nor any other such one, can come up to the wisdom of the blessed and glorified Paul. He, when among you, accurately and stedfastly taught the word of truth in the presence of those who were then alive. And when absent from you, he wrote you a letter, which, if you carefully study, you will find to be the means of building you up in that faith which has been given you, and which, being followed by hope, and preceded by love towards God, and Christ, and our neighbour, "is the mother of us all." For if any one be inwardly possessed of these graces, he hath fulfilled the command of righteousness, since he that hath love is far from all sin.
Against Heresies Book V

Now all these things being such as they are, cannot be understood in reference to super-celestial matters; "for God," it is said, "will show to the whole earth that is under heaven thy glory." But in the times of the kingdom, the earth has been called again by Christ [to its pristine condition], and Jerusalem rebuilt after the pattern of the Jerusalem above, of which the prophet Isaiah says, "Behold, I have depicted thy walls upon my hands, and thou art always in my sight," And the apostle, too, writing to the Galatians, says in like manner, "But the Jerusalem which is above is free, which is the mother of us all." He does not say this with any thought of an erratic Aeon, or of any other power which departed from the Pleroma, or of Prunicus, but of the Jerusalem which has been delineated on [God's] hands. And in the Apocalypse John saw this new [Jerusalem] descending upon the new earth.
Against Marcion, Book III, Chapter 25

But we do confess that a kingdom is promised to us upon the earth, although before heaven, only in another state of existence; inasmuch as it will be after the resurrection for a thousand years in the divinely-built city of Jerusalem, "let down from heaven," [Revelation 21:2] which the apostle also calls "our mother from above;" [Galatians 4:26] and, while declaring that our πολίτευμα, or citizenship, is in heaven, he predicates of it that it is really a city in heaven. This both Ezekiel had knowledge of [Ezekiel 48:30-35] and the Apostle John beheld. [Revelation 21:10-23] And the word of the new prophecy which is a part of our belief, attests how it foretold that there would be for a sign a picture of this very city exhibited to view previous to its manifestation. This prophecy, indeed, has been very lately fulfilled in an expedition to the East. For it is evident from the testimony of even heathen witnesses, that in Judæa there was suspended in the sky a city early every morning for forty days. As the day advanced, the entire figure of its walls would wane gradually, and sometimes it would vanish instantly. We say that this city has been provided by God for receiving the saints on their resurrection, and refreshing them with the abundance of all really spiritual blessings, as a recompense for those which in the world we have either despised or lost; since it is both just and God-worthy that His servants should have their joy in the place where they have also suffered affliction for His name's sake. Of the heavenly kingdom this is the process. After its thousand years are over, within which period is completed the resurrection of the saints, who rise sooner or later according to their deserts there will ensue the destruction of the world and the conflagration of all things at the judgment: we shall then be changed in a moment into the substance of angels, even by the investiture of an incorruptible nature, and so be removed to that kingdom in heaven of which we have now been treating, just as if it had not been predicted by the Creator, and as if it were proving Christ to belong to the other god and as if he were the first and sole revealer of it.
Against Marcion Book III

But we do confess that a kingdom is promised to us upon the earth, although before heaven, only in another state of existence; inasmuch as it will be after the resurrection for a thousand years in the divinely-built city of Jerusalem, "let down from heaven," which the apostle also calls "our mother from above; " and, while declaring that our poli/teuma, or citizenship, is in heaven, he predicates of it that it is really a city in heaven.
Against Marcion Book V

I find it was in their foresight of all this, that the heavenly intelligences gazed with admiration on "the Jerusalem which is above," and by the mouth of Isaiah said long ago: "Who are these that fly as clouds, and as doves with their young ones, unto me? " Now, as Christ has prepared for us this ascension into heaven, He must be the Christ of whom Amos spoke: "It is He who builds His ascent up to the heavens," even for Himself and His people.
Hippolytus Refutation of All Heresies Book V

"If ye hasten to fly out of Egypt, and repair beyond the Red Sea into the wilderness," that is, from earthly intercourse to the Jerusalem above, which is the mother of the living; "If, moreover, again you return into Egypt," that is, into earthly intercourse, "ye shall die as men." For mortal, he says, is every generation below, but immortal that which is begotten above, for it is born of water only, and of spirit, being spiritual, not carnal. But what (is born) below is carnal, that is, he says, what is written. "That which is born of the flesh is flesh, and that which is born of the spirit is spirit." This, according to them, is the spiritual generation.
HOMILIES ON EXODUS 8

Hear also the Apostle proclaiming concerning these things "according to the wisdom which had been given to him in his ministry": "but the Jerusalem" he says "which is above is free, which is the mother of us all". Just as, therefore, Egypt, that earthly region, is called for the children of Israel a "house of bondage" in comparison with Judaea and Jerusalem, which are made for them a house of liberty, so in comparison with the heavenly Jerusalem, which is, so to speak, the mother of liberty, this whole world and all things that are in this world are a "house of bondage".
QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 40: ON “REJOICE, O BARREN ONE”

WHAT DOES THE PROPHET MEAN WHEN HE SAYS, “REJOICE, O BARREN ONE WHO DOES NOT BEAR; BREAK FORTH AND CRY ALOUD, YOU WHO DO NOT LABOR, BECAUSE THE CHILDREN OF THE DESOLATE ARE MORE THAN THOSE OF HER WHO HAS A HUSBAND." — Since the children of earthly Jerusalem have fallen away from God, joy cannot be ascribed to her, but rather sorrow. Therefore, as a criticism to this Jerusalem, the prophet says that that higher Jerusalem should rejoice, the one the Apostle calls “our mother” (Gal. 4:26): because without groaning and pains she has far more children than this Jerusalem, which in tears gives birth carnally, namely, the Jews, whereas the other gives birth to Christians spiritually through faith. He calls her “desolate” because she is the life that Adam, the first man, abandoned when he followed death. So when people are reborn, they return to the life they had deserted. This life is Christ, because he says, “I am the life” (Jn. 14:6). And God the Father is also life, because the Lord says, “As the Father has life, so he has given the Son to have life” (Jn. 5:26). Without doubt the Holy Spirit is life as well, since the Lord says, “He will receive from what is mine” (Jn. 16:15). Whoever receives from life is necessarily life. Therefore the three are one life. This is the life by faith in whom we are reborn. She is our mother, as we read in Genesis, because she, namely, Life, is the mother of all the living (Gen. 3:20). And who are the living, if not those who believe?
QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 15: ON “REJOICE, O BARREN ONE”

WHAT IS IT THAT THE PROPHET SAYS: REJOICE, BARREN WOMAN, YOU WHO DO NOT GIVE BIRTH; BREAK FORTH AND CRY OUT, YOU WHO DO NOT LABOR IN CHILDBIRTH, BECAUSE THE CHILDREN OF THE DESOLATE ARE MORE NUMEROUS THAN THOSE OF HER WHO HAS A HUSBAND? — In this passage we understand two mothers: the heavenly and the earthly, that is, the free Jerusalem, of which the Apostle says that she is our mother, and this Jerusalem which he says is in slavery with her children, that is, the Jews. For the prophet, proclaiming the coming of the Lord and seriously calling out in joyful voice for the time of grace, exhorts the heavenly Jerusalem, called “desolate” because she did not yet have dwelling in her the children generated through faith, to rejoice. For the time had come when she should have the children foretold long ago, and many more than those of this Jerusalem, because Christians have surpassed the number of Jews. She is therefore called barren because she is a virgin, who does not bring forth a son through physical union and embrace, but spiritually through faith alone. Therefore she is not said to be in labor; for one who is in labor suffers pains. This one cries out instead in the joy of human salvation. But earthly Jerusalem is said to have a husband because she gave birth carnally. For the city is presented as a kind of mother, just as that heavenly dwelling to which we are called is called our mother.
Homily on Galatians 4

Those therefore, who are born of her are not bondmen. Thus the type of the Jerusalem below was Hagar, as is plain from the mountain being so called; but of that which is above is the Church. Nevertheless he is not content with these types, but adds the testimony of Isaiah to what he has spoken...
The Proof of the Apostolic Preaching

Wherefore the Church beareth much fruit of the redeemed: because no longer Moses (as) mediator nor Elijah (as) messenger, but the Lord Himself has redeemed us, granting many more children to the Church than to the first Synagogue; as Isaiah declared, saying: "Rejoice thou barren, that didst not bear." The barren is the Church, which never at all in former times presented sons to God. "Cry out and call, thou that didst not travail: for the children of the desolate are more than of her which hath an husband." Now the first Synagogue had as husband the Law.
The Refutation of All Heresies - Book 5

He is not undone, he says, but revolves as it were, and goes round himself. Moreover, also, cities in which we dwell, because we turn and go round in them, are denominated "Poleis." In this manner, he says, the Phrygians call this one "Aipolis," inasmuch as he everywhere ceaselessly turns all things, and changes them into their own peculiar (functions). And the Phrygians style him, he says, "very fruitful" likewise, "because," says he, "more numerous are the children of the desolate one, than those of her which hath an husband; " that is, things by being born again become immortal and abide for ever in great numbers, even though the things that are produced may be few; whereas things carnal, he says, are all corruptible, even though very many things (of this type) are produced. For this reason, he says, "Rachel wept for her children, and would not," says (the prophet), "be comforted; sorrowing for them, for she knew," says he, "that they are not." But Jeremiah likewise utters lamentation for Jerusalem below, not the city in Phoenicia, but the corruptible generation below. For Jeremiah likewise, he says, was aware of the Perfect Man, of him that is born again-of water and the Spirit not carnal. At least Jeremiah himself remarked: "He is a man, and who shall know him? " In this manner, (the Naassene) says, the knowledge of the Perfect Man is exceedingly profound, and difficult of comprehension. For, he says, the beginning of perfection is a knowledge of man, whereas knowledge of God is absolute perfection.
Homily on Galatians 4

Who is this who before was "barren," and "desolate?" Clearly it is the Church of the Gentiles, that was before deprived of the knowledge of God? Who, "she which hath the husband?" plainly the Synagogue. Yet the barren woman surpassed her in the number of her children, for the other embraces one nation, but the children of the Church have filled the country of the Greeks and of the Barbarians, the earth and sea, the whole habitable world. Observe how Sarah by acts, and the Prophet by words, have described the events about to befal us. Observe too, that he whom Isaiah called barren, Paul hath proved to have many children, which also happened typically in the case of Sarah. For she too, although barren, became the mother of a numerous progeny. This however does not suffice Paul, but he carefully follows out the mode whereby the barren woman became a mother, that in this particular likewise the type might harmonize with the truth. ...
Commentary on Galatians

For it is written: Rejoice, barren one, you who do not bear; break forth and cry out, you who do not travail: for many more are the children of the desolate than of her who has a husband (Isa. 54:1.)

The synagogue had the Law as her husband; and, according also to the prophecy of Hannah, she was once fruitful in children (1 Sam. 1). But the barren Church, without Christ as husband, without any address of the Bridegroom's word, lay long in the desert. But after the synagogue received the bill of divorce into her hands, and turned all her husband's ornaments into the ornament of an idol, then the husband, his former girdle rotting, wove another belt for his loins, another loincloth out of the Gentiles; and she, as soon as she was joined to her husband, conceived and gave birth. And in Isaac the Lord cries out through the prophet: "Is a nation born all at once?" (Isa. 66:8): when in a single day, in the Acts of the Apostles, three thousand and five thousand men believed (Acts 3 ff.). Nor do I think it necessary for us to speak of the Christian multitude and of the fewness of the Jews, since the banners of the cross shine forth in the whole world, and a Jew scarcely appears in the cities, rare and conspicuous.
Against Heresies Book IV

For not alone upon Abraham's account did He say these things, but also that He might point out how all who have known God from the beginning, and have foretold the advent of Christ, have received the revelation from the Son Himself; who also in the last times was made visible and passable, and spake with the human race, that He might from the stones raise up children unto Abraham, and fulfil the promise which God had given him, and that He might make his seed as the stars of heaven, as John the Baptist says: "For God is able from these stones to raise up children unto Abraham." Now, this Jesus did by drawing us off from the religion of stones, and bringing us over from hard and fruitless cogitations, and establishing in us a faith like to Abraham. As Paul does also testify, saying that we are children of Abraham because of the similarity of our faith, and the promise of inheritance.
Against Heresies Book V

If, then, God promised him the inheritance of the land, yet he did not receive it during all the time of his sojourn there, it must be, that together with his seed, that is, those who fear God and believe in Him, he shall receive it at the resurrection of the just. For his seed is the Church, which receives the adoption to God through the Lord, as John the Baptist said: "For God is able from the stones to raise up children to Abraham." Thus also the apostle says in the Epistle to the Galatians: "But ye, brethren, as Isaac was, are the children of the promise." And again, in the same Epistle, he plainly declares that they who have believed in Christ do receive Christ, the promise to Abraham thus saying, "The promises were spoken to Abraham, and to his seed. Now He does not say, And of seeds, as if [He spake] of many, but as of one, And to thy seed, which is Christ." And again, confirming his former words, he says, "Even as Abraham believed God, and it was accounted to him for righteousness. Know ye therefore, that they which are of faith are the children of Abraham. But the Scripture, fore-seeing that God would justify the heathen through faith, declared to Abraham beforehand, That in thee shall all nations be blessed. So then they which are of faith shall be blessed with faithful Abraham." Thus, then, they who are of faith shall be blessed with faithful Abraham, and these are the children of Abraham. Now God made promise of the earth to Abraham and his seed; yet neither Abraham nor his seed, that is, those who are justified by faith, do now receive any inheritance in it; but they shall receive it at the resurrection of the just. For God is true and faithful; and on this account He said, "Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth."
Homily on Galatians 4

It is not merely that the Church was barren like Sarah, or became a mother of many children like her, but she bore them in the way Sarah did. As it was not nature but the promise of God which rendered Sarah a mother, [for the word of God which said, "At the time appointed I will return unto thee, and Sarah shall have a son," (Gen. 18:14.) this entered into the womb and formed the babe,] so also in our regeneration it is not nature, but the Words of God spoken by the Priest, (the faithful know them,) which in the Bath of water as in a sort of womb, form and regenerate him who is baptized.

Wherefore if we are sons of the barren woman, then are we free. But what kind of freedom, it might be objected, is this, when the Jews seize and scourge the believers, and those who have this pretence of liberty are persecuted? for these things then occurred, in the persecution of the faithful. Neither let this disturb you, he replies, this also is anticipated in the type, for Isaac, who was free, was persecuted by Ishmael the bondman. ...
Commentary on Galatians

But we, brothers, are children of promise according to Isaac.

That the Apostle and those like him are children of promise according to Isaac presents no difficulty of understanding. But since Origen, in expounding this passage, set down the Apostle's text thus: "But you, brothers, are children of promise according to Isaac", the question is raised how he now calls the Galatians, whom he had called senseless, and of whom he had said that they had begun in the spirit and were finishing in the flesh, children of the promise according to Isaac. We say, therefore, that the Apostle calls them children of the promise according to Isaac for this reason: because he does not utterly despair of their salvation, and he reckons that they will once more return to the spirit in which they had begun, and become children of the free woman. But if they are brought to completion in the flesh, they are children of the slave woman.
Homily on Galatians 4

What! does all this consolation consist in showing that freemen are persecuted by bond-men? By no means, he says, I do not stop here, listen to what follows, and then, if you be not pusillanimous under persecution, you will be sufficiently comforted. And what is it that follows? "Cast out the son of the handmaid, for he shall not inherit with the son of the freewoman." Behold the reward of tyranny for a season, and of recklessness out of season! the son is cast out of his father's house, and becomes, together with his mother, an exile and a wanderer. And consider too the wisdom of the remark; for he says not that he was cast forth merely because he persecuted, but that he should not be heir. For this punishment was not exacted from him on account of his temporary persecution, (for that would have been of little moment, and nothing to the point,) but he was not suffered to participate in the inheritance provided for the son. And this proves that, putting the persecution aside, this very thing had been typified from the beginning, and did not originate in the persecution, but in the purpose of God. Nor does he say, "the son of Abraham shall not be heir," but, "the son of the handmaid," distinguishing him by his inferior descent. Now Sarah was barren, and so is the Gentile Church; observe how the type is preserved in every particular, as the former, through all the by-gone years, conceived not, and in extreme old age became a mother, so the latter, when the fulness of time is come, brings forth. And this the prophets have proclaimed, saying, "Rejoice, thou barren that bearest not; break forth and cry, thou that travailest not; for more are the children of the desolate than of her which hath the husband." And hereby they intend the Church; for she knew not God, but as soon as she knew Him, she surpassed the fruitful synagogue.
Commentary on Galatians

But as then the one who had been born according to the flesh persecuted the one according to the spirit, so it is now also. But what does the Scripture say? Cast out the bondwoman and her son: for the son of the bondwoman shall not be heir with my son Isaac. Therefore, brothers, we are not sons of the bondwoman, but of the free woman. With which freedom Christ has made us free.

I do not think that we can find where Ishmael persecuted Isaac, but only this: that when the son of the Egyptian woman, who was the elder by birth, was playing with Isaac, Sarah was indignant and said to Abraham: "Cast out the bondwoman and her son: For the son of the bondwoman shall not inherit with my son Isaac" (Gen. 21:10). And surely simple play among infants does not deserve expulsion and disinheritance. But the Apostle, as a Hebrew of the Hebrews, and taught at the feet of the master Gamaliel (who once restrained in council the Pharisees raging against the Lord), understood from the words of Sarah, who said: "for the son of the bondwoman shall not inherit with my son Isaac", that that play had not been simple. But because perhaps Ishmael, as the elder by birth, and circumcised at a time when he could already understand and feel what he suffered, was claiming the birthright for himself, Scripture called the quarrel of the little ones play. Hence Sarah too, not bearing these words, and not enduring the habit of the bondwoman's son, who from an early age claimed the birthright for himself, broke out in speech: "Cast out the bondwoman with her son: For the son of the bondwoman shall not inherit with my son Isaac". And when it seemed hard to Abraham (for more is always owed to the firstborn) that Ishmael should not only cease to be the first, but should not even receive an equal portion with his younger brother, God, who willed that the free woman be within and the bondwoman be driven out of doors, confirms Sarah's words and speaks to Abraham: "Let it not be hard in your sight concerning the boy and the bondwoman. In all that Sarah shall say to you, hear her voice: for in Isaac shall your seed be called". As then, therefore, the elder brother Ishmael persecuted Isaac, who was still nursing and little, claiming for himself the prerogative of circumcision, claiming for himself the birthright: so now also Israel according to the flesh is raised up, is puffed up, is exalted against the younger brother, the Christian people from the Gentiles. Let us consider the madness of the Jews, who killed both the Lord and the prophets, and persecuted the apostles, and oppose the will of God: and we shall see that far greater persecutions, as histories also teach us, have been stirred up by the Jews against the Christians than by the Gentiles. Do we wonder at the Jews? Today also those who are little ones in Christ and live carnally persecute those who have been born of water and the spirit, and who, rising with Christ, seek the things that are above, not below. Let them do what they will: let them with Ishmael persecute Isaac: they will be cast out of doors with their mother, the Egyptian bondwoman, nor will they receive the inheritance, which he alone who was born of the promise shall obtain. And elegant too is this, that he who was born according to the flesh persecutes the spiritual one. For the spiritual man never persecutes the carnal, but pardons him as a rustic brother: he knows that he can make progress in time. And if ever he sees the son of the Egyptian woman angry, he remembers the one father, who created light, oxen and the gnat, and that in a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and earthenware.
The Stromata Book 1

"Since, when we were children," says the same apostle, "we were kept in bondage under the rudiments of the world. And the child, though heir, differeth nothing from a servant, till the time appointed of the father." Philosophers, then, are children, unless they have been made men by Christ. "For if the son of the bond woman shall not be heir with the son of the free," at least he is the seed of Abraham, though not of promise, receiving what belongs to him by free gift. "But strong meat belongeth to those that are of full age, even those who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern both good and evil." "For every one that useth milk is unskilful in the word of righteousness; for he is a babe," and not yet acquainted with the word, according to which he has believed and works, and not able to give a reason in himself.
On the Apparel of Women Book II
Nay, rather banish quite away from your "free" head all this slavery of ornamentation.
Homily on Galatians 4

He turns and discusses this on all sides, desiring to prove that what had taken place was no novelty, but had been before typified many ages ago. How then can it be otherwise than absurd for those who had been set apart so long and who had obtained freedom, willingly to subject themselves to the yoke of bondage?
Commentary on Galatians

Therefore let us say with the apostle Paul: We are not sons of the bondwoman, but of the free woman (2 Tim. 2); and, renewed in Christ, let us hear the words of the Lord speaking to the Jews: "If you abide in my word, you shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free" (John 8:31, 32). Made free by this freedom, the Apostle too said: For though I am free from all. "He who commits sin is the slave of sin" (1 Cor. 9:19). He, because he knew himself free from all vices and a stranger to all concupiscence and error, rightly rejoiced in the freedom of Christ, saying: We are not sons of the bondwoman, but of the free woman: with which freedom Christ has made us free (John 8:34).
AGAINST TWO LETTERS OF PELAGIUS 3.12

Let us, therefore, choose whether to call the righteous men of old the children of the bondwoman or of the free. Be it far from us to say, of the bondwoman; therefore if of the free, they pertain to the new testament in the Holy Spirit, whom, as making alive, the apostle opposes to the killing letter. For on what ground do they not belong to the grace of the new testament, from whose words and looks we convict and rebut such most frantic and ungrateful enemies of the same grace as these?

n: Be not held again under the yoke of bondage, of the old law. (Witham) --- This verse must be understood in the same manner as the 9th verse of the preceding chapter. See the annotations upon it.

If you converted from heathenism be circumcised, it must be by believing and professing it necessary, which is false doctrine, and then Christ will profit you nothing: not that the practice of those ceremonies was at the time sinful, especially for those that had been Jews, but it was an error to judge them necessary for converted Gentiles. Besides, he that judges circumcision necessary, must also judge himself bound to keep all the other ceremonies and precepts of the law. (Witham)

The false teachers had insisted on the observance of circumcision and a few other rites only, as necessary for salvation; but St. Paul assures them, that the receiving of circumcision is an open profession of Judaism, and that he that makes this profession, binds himself to the observance of every part of the law, since a curse is pronounced against those that do not keep it in all its parts. If then circumcision be necessary for salvation, the whole law is necessary also. (Calmet)
If you think that justice cannot be obtained but under the law, you make a renunciation of the justice of Christ: his mediation becomes of no avail to you. (Calmet)

We in spirit hope for true justice by faith in Christ; yet not by faith only, but by faith working by charity. (Witham) --- Here note with St. Augustine, that faith is not to be idle, but working or doing good works in charity: wherefore not faith alone. (De opere et fide. chap. xiv.)

, &c. This persuasion of yours is not from him who calleth you; is not from God: and I hope you will be shortly again of no other mind than what I taught you. (Witham) --- This was a Jewish proverb, and alluded to the time of the Pasch, when it was not permitted to eat of any but unleavened bread; during which time the least leaven made the whole mass unclean to a Jew....Some Greek copies read, mikra zume olon to phurama zumoi, when the sense will be, "a little leaven causes the whole mass to rise." (Calmet) --- Hence the introduction of any, however small, share of the ceremonial and Jewish rites, will greatly disfigure the purity and simplicity of the Christian institute. --- As for me, my adversaries misrepresent me, when they say I preach circumcision; which if I did, I should not be persecuted as I am by the Jews. I never preach it necessary for Gentiles converted, though I have not condemned the use of it in the Jewish converts, provided they do not oblige other converts to it. --- The scandal of the cross is therefore made void. The sense is, according to St. Jerome, that the Jews' greatest objection against St. Paul used to be, because he preached that circumcision and the law of Moses need not be observed: another objection against him was, that he preached Jesus, who was crucified on an infamous cross, to be their great Messias. He reasons then in this manner, that if the Jews think he again preacheth the necessity of circumcision and the precepts of the old law, they will no longer be offended that he preacheth Christ crucified, because they were not so much offended with the latter as with the first. Thus also St. Chrysostom on this verse. Others expound it thus: If I preach circumcision and the ceremonies of the law, therefore according to my doctrine, the cross of Christ, and justification by the merits of Christ crucified, is abolished, because justification is still to be sought for by the works of the law. --- I would they were even cut off: separated from your communion by excommunication. This seems the true sense; so that I need not mention any other exposition. See Cornelius a Lapide. (Witham)
An occasion to the flesh; i.e. that you abuse not, by a vicious life, that Christian liberty which Christ hath purchased for you, but be united in the spirit of charity. (Witham)

All the law, as far as it regards our duty to our neighbour, is contained in this text of the apostle; he says the same in his epistle to the Romans, Chap. xiii. He that loves his neighbour has fulfilled the law.

So that you[1] do not the things that you would. He does not say, so that you cannot do, as others falsely translate; as if men were under an absolute necessity of sinning, or doing ill; which is also contradictory to the foregoing words, walk by the spirit, and you will not accomplish the works of the flesh. (Witham) --- Here some suppose, says St. Augustine, that the apostle denieth that we have free liberty of will: not understanding that this is said to them, if they will not hold fast the grace of faith conceived, by which only they can walk in the spirit, and not accomplish the lusts of the flesh. (St. Augustine, in chap. v. Gal.)

Uncleanness, immodesty, luxury. In the Greek there are but two vices named; luxury is not mentioned; and, perhaps, the Latin interpreter put two words to explain one Greek word. (Witham) --- St. Augustine here sheweth that there are other damnable sins besides infidelity.

The fruit of the Spirit is charity, &c. There are numbered twelve of these fruits in the Latin, though but nine in the Greek text, in St. Chrysostom; St. Jerome; St. Augustine, tract. lxxxvii. in Joan. p. 756. The difference may again happen by the Latin interpreter using two words to express one Greek word. It is observed, that longanimity and patience are in a manner the same; so are benignity and goodness; and so may be here continency and chastity. (Witham) ____________________ [1] Ver. 17. Ita ut non quæcunque vultis, illa faciatis; ina me a an thelete tauta poiete. Dr. Wells, in his correction to the Protestant translation, leaves out cannot.

f: An Answer to the Jews

For the Jews say, that from the beginning God sanctified the seventh day, by resting on it from all His works which He made; and that thence it was, likewise, that Moses said to the People: "Remember the day of the sabbaths, to sanctify it: every servile work ye shall not do therein, except what pertaineth unto life." Whence we (Christians) understand that we still more ought to observe a sabbath from all "servile work" always, and not only every seventh day, but through all time.
Against Marcion Book V

Both dispensations, therefore, emanate from that same God by whom, as we have found, they were both sketched out beforehand. When he speaks of "the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free," does not the very phrase indicate that He is the Liberator who was once the Master? For Galba himself never liberated slaves which were not his own, even when about to restore free men to their liberty.
Against Marcion Book V

It was not meet that those who had received liberty should be "entangled again with the yoke of bondage" -that is, of the law; now that the Psalm had its prophecy accomplished: "Let us break their bands asunder, and cast away their cords from us, since the rulers have gathered themselves together against the Lord and against His Christ.
On Modesty
"Liberty in Christ" has done no injury to innocence.
On Fasting

Xerophagies, however, (they consider) the novel name of a studied duty, and very much akin to heathenish superstition, like the abstemious rigours which purify an Apis, an Isis, and a Magna Mater, by a restriction laid upon certain kinds of food; whereas faith, free in Christ, owes no abstinence from particular meats to the Jewish Law even, admitted as it has been by the apostle once for all to the whole range of the meat-market -(the apostle, I say), that detester of such as, in like manner as they prohibit marrying, so bid us abstain from meats created by God.
Homily on Galatians 5

Have ye wrought your own deliverance, that ye run back again to the dominion ye were under before? It is Another who hath redeemed you, it is Another who hath paid the ransom for you. Observe in how many ways he leads them away from the error of Judaism; by showing, first, that it was the extreme of folly for those, who had become free instead of slaves, to desire to become slaves instead of free; secondly, that they would be convicted of neglect and ingratitude to their Benefactor, in despising Him who had delivered, and loving him who had enslaved them; thirdly, that it was impossible. For Another having once for all redeemed all of us from it, the Law ceases to have any sway. By the word, "stand fast," he indicates their vacillation.

By the word "yoke" he signifies to them the burdensomeness of such a course, and by the word "again" he points out their utter senselessness. Had ye never experienced this burden, ye would not have deserved so severe a censure, but for you who by trial have learnt how irksome this yoke is, again to subject yourself to it, is justly unpardonable.
Commentary on Galatians

Stand, and do not be held again by the yoke of slavery.

From this too it is shown that he who clings to the yoke of slavery does not stand; and also that he who has been granted freedom by Christ was under the yoke for as long as he had the spirit of slavery in fear and followed the beginnings of the Law. When he says, stand, he urges a firm and stable faith in Christ, so that the churches of Galatia may remain with foot fixed upon the Savior. Of this the righteous man also speaks in another place: "He set my feet upon the rock" (Ps. 39:3), in place of what is, "upon Christ": namely, that they may not be carried about by every wind of doctrine and swept off in different directions (Eph. 4). Hence it is also said to those who stand: "And he who stands, let him see that he does not fall" (1 Cor. 10:12). And in another place: "Stand, act manfully, be strengthened" (ibid. 16:13), so that they may stand with him whom Stephen, persevering in martyrdom, saw standing at the right hand of the Father (Acts 7), and who spoke to Moses: "But you, stand with me" (Exod. 34:2). Now by the yoke of slavery he means the Law, hard, difficult, laborious, which day and night wears out its worshippers with heavy toil. As Peter too says in the Acts of the Apostles: "Why do you try", he says, "to put a heavy yoke upon the neck of the brothers, which neither we nor our fathers have been able to bear" (Acts 15:10)? And when he added, not again, it is not that the Galatians had kept the Law before; but that the yoke of idolatry too is heavy, the yoke by which the people of the Egyptians was oppressed and sank like lead in the Red Sea (Exod. 15). In this sense he had also said above: "How are you turning again to the weak and needy elements, which you wish to serve once more, observing days, and months, and times, and years?" For the Galatians, who at the preaching of the apostle Paul had abandoned idols and at once risen to the grace of the Gospel, were not returning to the slavery of the Jewish Law, which they had never known before; but in wishing to observe times, to be circumcised in the flesh and to offer bodily sacrifices, they were in a manner returning to the same rites which they had served before in idolatry. For they say that the priests of Egypt, and the Ishmaelites, and the Midianites have no foreskin. And that the nations observe days, months and years, would that we did not know, so that there might never be a festivity shared by us with them.
The Prescription Against Heretics
Writing also to the Galatians, he inveighs against such men as observed and defend circumcision and the (Mosaic) law. Thus runs Hebion's heresy.
On Modesty

Even if, for certain, the apostle had granted pardon of fornication to that Corinthian, it would be another instance of his once for all contravening his own practice to meet the requirement of the time. He circumcised Timotheus alone, and yet did away with circumcision.
Homily on Galatians 5

Lo, what a threat! reasonably then did he anathematize even angels. How then shall Christ profit them nothing? for he has not supported this by argument, but only declared it, the credence due to his authority, compensating, as it were, for all subsequent proof. Wherefore he sets out by saying, "Behold, I Paul say unto you," which is the expression of one who has confidence in what he asserts. We will subjoin what we can ourselves as to how Christ shall profit nothing them who are circumcised.

He that is circumcised is circumcised for fear of the Law, and he who fears the Law, distrusts the power of grace, and he who distrusts can receive no benefit from that which is distrusted. Or again thus, he that is circumcised makes the Law of force; but thus considering it to be of force and yet transgressing it in the greater part while keeping it in the lesser, he puts himself again under the curse. But how can he be saved who submits himself to the curse, and repels the liberty which is of Faith? If one may say what seems a paradox, such an one believes neither Christ nor the Law, but stands between them, desiring to benefit both by one and the other, whereas he will reap fruit from neither. Having said that Christ shall profit them nothing, he lays down the proof of it shortly and sententiously.
Commentary on Galatians

Behold, I Paul say to you that if you be circumcised, Christ profits you nothing.

In the Gospel the Savior speaks to the disciples: "He who hears you hears me; he who receives you receives me" (Luke 10:16). And the Apostle testifies, saying: "And I live, now not I; but Christ lives in me" (above, 2:20); and elsewhere: "Or do you seek a proof of him who speaks in me, Christ" (2 Cor. 13:3)? From this it is clearly proved that what he now says, Behold, I Paul say to you, is to be received not as the words of Paul only, but of the Lord. For when in the first Epistle to the Corinthians he had first set down: "But to those who are married I give charge, not I, but the Lord" (1 Cor. 7:10); and had at once added: "but to the rest I command" (ibid., 12), then, lest his authority be thought cheap, "I think," he says, "that I too have the spirit of God": so that, with the spirit and Christ speaking in him, he who, imitating the prophets, might say, "Thus says the Lord almighty", would not be held in contempt. But what has been said, Behold, I Paul say to you that if you be circumcised, Christ profits you nothing, will become greater if it is joined with the beginning, where he says: "Paul an apostle, not from men, nor through man, but through Jesus Christ", and the rest: so that the hearers may be moved not so much by the authority of the one sent as by that of the one sending. Someone may say: Contrary to this passage is what is written to the Romans: "Circumcision indeed profits, if you keep the Law" (Rom. 2:25); and below: "What then has the Jew more, or what is the profit of circumcision? Much in every way. First indeed, because the oracles of God were entrusted to them" (Rom. 3:1-2). For if Christ profits nothing to those who have been circumcised, how does circumcision profit those who keep the Law? This indeed will be resolved by this answer, that we say that the Epistle written to the Romans was dictated to those who had believed from among the Jews and the Gentiles, and that Paul acted so that neither people would be offended: namely, so that each people might possess its own privilege, so that neither would the Gentiles be circumcised, nor would the circumcised draw forward a foreskin. But writing to the Galatians he used another argument. For they were not of the circumcision, but of the Gentiles who had believed. Nor could circumcision profit those who, after the grace of the Gospel, were turning back again to the elements of the Law. And in the Acts of the Apostles the history relates (Acts 15) that, when certain men of the circumcision had risen up and asserted that those who had believed from among the Gentiles ought to be circumcised and to keep the law of Moses, the elders who were at Jerusalem, and the apostles gathered together with them, decreed by letter that the yoke of the Law should not be laid upon them, and that they should observe nothing further, except only to keep themselves from things sacrificed to idols, and from blood, and from fornication, or, as is written in some copies, "and from things strangled". And lest any doubt remain that circumcision profits nothing, but that it was on account of those who had believed from among the Jews that he tempered his judgment on circumcision to the Romans, coming down little by little to the later parts of the same Epistle he showed that neither circumcision nor uncircumcision avails anything, saying: "Circumcision therefore is nothing, and uncircumcision is nothing, but the keeping of the commandments of God" (1 Cor. 7:19). For circumcision is nothing to such a degree that it profited nothing even the house of Israel, which boasted of circumcision, as the prophet records: "All the nations are uncircumcised in flesh, but the house of Israel is uncircumcised in heart" (Ezek. 44:9); and the uncircumcised Melchizedek blessed the circumcised Abraham. For what he says, If you be circumcised (Gen. 14), is as if he had meant to say: if you be circumcised in the flesh. This in another place he calls not circumcision but mutilation, saying: "See the mutilation. For we are the circumcision, who serve by the spirit of God, and glory in Christ, and do not trust in the flesh" (Phil. 3:2-3). He does not trust in the flesh who expects every benefit from Christ, and does not sow in the flesh, so as to reap corruption from the flesh, but in the spirit, from which eternal life is brought forth. The sentence must be examined more closely: If you be circumcised, Christ profits you nothing. That is, not only that, if they are circumcised, circumcision itself does not profit them; but that, even if they seem to have the other virtues in Christ apart from circumcision, all of them perish once they have been circumcised after faith in Christ. What then? Did circumcision profit Timothy nothing? Much in every way. For he was circumcised not so much in order that he might think he could gain some advantage from circumcision itself, as that he might win the rest (1 Cor. 9). He became a Jew to the Jews, so that by his circumcision he might bring the Jews over to the faith of Christ. For circumcision does not profit precisely when it is thought to bring some benefit of itself.
Hippolytus Refutation of All Heresies Book VIII

And certain other (heretics), contentious by nature, (and) wholly uniformed as regards knowledge, as well as in their manner more (than usually) quarrelsome, combine (in maintaining) that Easter should be kept on the fourteenth day of the first month, according to the commandment of the law, on whatever day (of the week) it should occur. (But in this) they only regard what has been written in the law, that he will be accursed who does not so keep (the commandment) as it is enjoined. They do not, however, attend to this (fact), that the legal enactment was made for Jews, who in times to come should kill the real Passover. And this (paschal sacrifice, in its efficacy,) has spread unto the Gentiles, and is discerned by faith, and not now observed in letter (merely). They attend to this one commandment, and do not look unto what has been spoken by the apostle: "For I testify to every man that is circumcised, that he is a debtor to keep the whole law." In other respects, however, these consent to all the traditions delivered to the Church by the Apostles.
Homily on Galatians 5

That you may not suppose that this is spoken from ill-will, I say not to you alone, he says, but to every one who receiveth circumcision, that he is a debtor to do the whole Law. The parts of the Law are linked one to the other. As he who from being free has enrolled himself as a slave, no longer does what he pleases, but is bound by all the laws of slavery, so in the case of the Law, if you take upon you a small portion of it, and submit to the yoke, you draw down upon yourself its whole domination. And so it is in a worldly inheritance: he who touches no part of it, is free from all matters which are consequent on the heirship to the deceased, but if he takes a small portion, though not the whole, yet by that part he has rendered himself liable for every thing. And this occurs in the Law, not only in the way I have mentioned, but in another also, for Legal observances are linked together. For example; Circumcision has sacrifice connected with it, and the observance of days; sacrifice again has the observance both of day and of place; place has the details of endless purifications; purifications involve a perfect swarm of manifold observances. For it is unlawful for the unclean to sacrifice, to enter the holy shrines, to do any other such act. Thus the Law introduces many things even by the one commandment. If then thou art circumcised, but not on the eighth day, or on the eighth day, but no sacrifice is offered, or a sacrifice is offered, but not in the prescribed place, or in the prescribed place, but not the accustomed objects, or if the accustomed objects, but thou be unclean, or if clean yet not purified by proper rules, every thing is frustrated. Wherefore he says, "that he is a debtor to the whole Law." Fulfil not a part, but the whole, if the Law is of force; but if it be not of force, not even a part.
Commentary on Galatians

And I solemnly testify to every man who circumcises himself, that he is a debtor to do the whole Law.

God, who commanded circumcision first to Abraham and then through Moses in the Law, appointed not circumcision alone but many other things as well to be observed: feast days to be attended at Jerusalem; whole burnt offerings of victims, always morning and evening; the sacrifice of the lamb in one place only; rest for the land in its seventh season; the fiftieth year of release; and the rest, which it is easy for every reader to gather for himself from the Scriptures. We shall therefore hem in Ebion and his followers, who think that those who believe in Christ after the Gospel must be circumcised, so that either they practice circumcision together with the other things that are commanded in the Law, or else, if it is impossible for all of them to be done, circumcision too should cease, since it has been passed over along with the rest as useless. But if they answer that they are bound to do only what is possible (for God, they say, does not demand of us the things we cannot fulfill, but those we can), we shall tell them that it does not belong to the same God both to wish the Law to be kept and to abandon those who keep the Law. Or how could he make them guilty for leaving the Law undone, when, even if they wish it, they cannot fulfill it all? We, for our part, follow the spiritual law, which says: "You shall not bridle the mouth of the ox that treads out the grain" (Deut. 25:4), and with the Apostle we understand: "Does God care about oxen" (1 Tim. 5:18; 1 Cor. 9:9)? Surely he says it for our sake; and we keep delightful sabbaths (Isa. 58:13), not so that our ox and ass and our worthless cattle may rejoice on the sabbath, but those men and beasts of whom it is written: "Men and beasts you will save, O Lord" (Ps. 35:7). By men we mean all who are rational and spiritual; by beasts, those who are of slower wit and are taught by the spiritual to keep the sabbaths of the Lord. Nor is what was said above, "If you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing", and what follows, "I testify to every man who circumcises himself, that he is a debtor to do the whole Law", contrary to what we are now bringing forward. For it is not the hearers of the Law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the Law will be justified. For the doer of the Law is the one who can say: "We are not the circumcision"; and, "A Jew in secret"; and, "We know that the Law is spiritual". But whoever follows the mutilation and the letter that kills is not a doer of the Law, but truly an enemy of the law, above all after the coming of the Savior, who takes away the veil from the heart of those who turn to him, so that all of us, beholding the glory of the Lord with unveiled face, may be transfigured from the oldness of the letter into the newness of the spirit.
Homily on Galatians 5

Having established his point, he at length declares their danger of the severest punishment. When a man recurs to the Law, which cannot save him, and falls from grace, what remains but an inexorable retribution, the Law being powerless, and grace rejecting him?

Thus having aggravated their alarm, and disquieted their mind, and shown them all the shipwreck they were about to suffer, he opens to them the haven of grace which was near at hand. This is ever his wont, and he shows that in this quarter salvation is easy and secure.
Commentary on Galatians

You have been made void from Christ: you who are justified in the Law have fallen away from grace.

Just as no one can serve two masters (Matt. 6), so it is difficult to fulfil at one and the same time both the shadow and the truth of the Law. The shadow is in the old Law, until the day breathes and the shadows are removed; the truth is in the Gospel of Christ: "For grace and truth were made through Jesus Christ" (John 1:17). Therefore he who thinks that he is justified in some observance of the Law loses the grace of Christ, and lets go the Gospel which he had held; and when he has lost grace, he is deprived of faith in Christ, and ceases in His work. For κατηργήθητε ἀπὸ τοῦ Χριστοῦ is rather to be understood, not as it has been badly translated in the Latin, You have been made void from Christ (Evacuati estis a Christo), but as "you have ceased in the work of Christ" (in Christi opere cessastis), so that what he had commanded above specifically about circumcision, saying, "if you are circumcised, Christ profits you nothing", he now applies generally to the whole Law: that those make no progress in the work of Christ who have believed that they are to be justified in any observance whatever of the Law.
LETTERS 82.19.3

He is refuting those who believed that they were justified in the law, not those who observed its legitimate provisions in honor of him by whom they were commanded, understanding both that they were commanded as a foreshadowing of the truth and that they belonged to a particular time.

Concerning this expectation and hope Paul writes to the Galatians: "For we through the Spirit wait for the hope of righteousness by faith." He says "we wait for it," not we are in possession of it.

We need none of those legal observances, he says; faith suffices to obtain for us the Spirit, and by Him righteousness, and many and great benefits.
Commentary on Galatians

For we through the spirit, by faith, wait for the hope of righteousness.

He put "spirit" to distinguish it from the letter. But by the hope of righteousness Christ is to be understood, because He Himself is truth, patience, hope, righteousness and all the virtues; whose second coming we await, since He is to judge all things, and will then be present no longer in patience but in righteousness, to render to each one according to his works. Awaiting the presence of this God, the apostle, and those who are like him, say: "Thy kingdom come" (Matt. 6:10), so that when the Son has delivered the kingdom to God and the Father, and He Himself also has been subjected in all who are subjected, then the head may be subjected in the body, and God may be all in all (1 Cor. 15). For He who now is in part, through individuals, will then begin to be wholly through all.
AGAINST MARCION 5.4.11

Since circumcision and uncircumcision belonged to the one God, both therefore were annulled in Christ because of the priority given to faith, this being the faith of which it was written "the Gentiles shall believe in his name."
Against Marcion Book V

If, now, he were for excluding circumcision, as the messenger of a new god, why does he say that "in Christ neither circumcision availeth anything, nor uncircumcision? For it was his duty to prefer the rival principle of that which he was abolishing, if he had a mission from the god who was the enemy of circumcision.
Against Marcion Book V

Furthermore, since both circumcision and uncircumcision were attributed to the same Deity, both lost their power in Christ, by reason of the excellency of faith-of that faith concerning which it had been written, "And in His name shall the Gentiles trust? " -of that faith "which," he says "worketh by love." By this saying he also shows that the Creator is the source of that grace.
Homily on Galatians 5

Observe the great boldness with which he now encounters them; Let him that hath put on Christ, he says, no longer be careful about such matters. Having before said that Circumcision was hurtful, how is it that he now considers it indifferent? It is indifferent as to those who had it previously to the Faith, but not as to those who are circumcised after the Faith was given. Observe too the view in which he places it, by setting it by the side of Uncircumcision; it is Faith that makes the difference. As in the selection of wrestlers, whether they be hook-nosed or flat-nosed, black or white, is of no importance in their trial, it is only necessary to seek that they be strong and skilful; so all these bodily accidents do not injure one who is to be enrolled under the New Covenant, nor does their presence assist him.

What is the meaning of "working through love?" Here he gives them a hard blow, by showing that this error had crept in because the love of Christ had not been rooted within them. For to believe is not all that is required, but also to abide in love. It is as if he had said, Had ye loved Christ as ye ought, ye would not have deserted to bondage, nor abandoned Him who redeemed you, nor treated with contumely Him who gave you freedom. Here he also hints at those who have plotted against them, implying that they would not have dared to do so, had they felt affection towards them. He wishes too by these words to correct their course of life.
Commentary on Galatians

For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision avails anything, nor uncircumcision, but faith which works through love.

For those who wish to live in Christ Jesus, virtues are to be sought, vices to be shunned; but the intermediate things, which lie between virtues and vices, are neither to be shunned nor to be sought, such as circumcision and uncircumcision and other things like them. Circumcision indeed profits, if you keep the Law. It was useful for this reason to those who lived under the Law: not because they were circumcised, but because the oracles of God were entrusted to them, and turning these into works they were not strangers to salvation. Nor should it trouble us that it was Zipporah who, taking a stone, circumcised her son and kept the strangling angel away from her husband (Exod. 4), or however else it is reported to be written in the Hebrew; for he has now testified not so much that circumcision profits nothing at all, as that it does not avail in Christ Jesus, since indeed from the time when the Gospel shone out over the whole world, the injury of circumcision is superfluous. It availed then, as did the other things of the Law as well, when carnal blessings too were promised to those who kept the Law: namely, that if they fulfilled it, they would be blessed in the city, blessed in the field, would have full barns, and many other things that are contained in the promises (Deut. 28). We, however, wish to avail and be strengthened in Christ Jesus, that is, in the true circumcision, and not in the Jewish mutilation. "For he is not a Jew who is one openly, nor is circumcision that which is manifest in the flesh; but he is a Jew who is one in secret, and circumcision is of the heart, in the spirit, not the letter" (Rom. 2:28, 29). Circumcision of the flesh, therefore, profits nothing in Christ, but circumcision of the heart and of the ears does, which takes away that reproach of the Jews: "Behold, your ears are uncircumcised, and you cannot hear" (Exod. 6:12). Circumcision of the lips profits, which Moses, in his humility, pleaded that he did not yet have, as is written in the Hebrew: "But I am one having uncircumcision in my lips". Circumcision also affords much benefit in matters of sex, when unchastity is cut away through chastity. Therefore in Christ Jesus neither circumcision avails nor bodily uncircumcision, because they are placed in the middle, that is, between vices and virtues; but faith, which works through love, so that both the faith which was reckoned to Abraham for righteousness may be approved, and every work of faith may be set in love, since the whole Law and the Prophets hang on love. For in these two commandments, "You shall love your God, and you shall love your neighbor", the Savior declared that the Law and the Prophets consist. And Paul in another place: "For you shall not commit adultery, you shall not steal, you shall not covet, and if there is any other commandment, it is summed up in this word: You shall love your neighbor as yourself" (Rom. 13:9). If, then, every commandment is summed up in what was said, "You shall love your neighbor as yourself", and faith working through love avails very much, it is manifest that the working of faith through love contains the fullness of all the commandments. But just as, according to the apostle James, faith without works is dead (Jas. 2:17, 20), so without faith, even though works be good, they are reckoned dead. Those, therefore, who do not believe in Christ and are of upright morals, what more do they have than works of virtue? Let that harlot from the Gospel supply an example of the faith which works through love: when, in the house of the Pharisee, she had washed with her tears the feet of the Lord as he reclined at table, wiped them with her hair, and anointed them with ointment, and the Lord had put to the murmuring Pharisee the parable of the debtors of fifty and five hundred denarii, he added: "Wherefore I say to you: Her many sins are forgiven her, because she loved much" (Luke 7:47 and 50). And turning to the woman herself, he said: "Your faith has made you safe: go in peace". For in this place it is openly shown that this woman had faith working through love, which availed much in Christ. Suppose someone should say: He rightly showed that circumcision avails nothing in Christ, since he knew that it had once availed; but was anyone in doubt about uncircumcision too, that he should say, nor uncircumcision? But if we consider that very many Christians, that is, of our own number, who from the wild olive have been grafted into the root of the good olive (Rom. 11), exult against the broken branches of the Jewish people and say that uncircumcision, in which Abraham pleased God and faith was reckoned to him for righteousness, avails more than circumcision, which was given as a sign of faith and did not profit Israel who had it: we shall see that this presumption of certain people too is now most carefully excluded.

They bear in mind how the churches were rebuked by the apostle: "O foolish Galatians, who hath bewitched you? " and, "Ye did run so well; who hath hindered you? " and how the epistle actually begins: "I marvel that ye are so soon removed from Him, who hath called you as His own in grace, to another gospel.
Homily on Galatians 5

This is not an interrogation, but an expression of doubt and sorrow. How hath such a course been cut short? who hath been able to do this? ye who were superior to all and in the rank of teachers, have not even continued in the position of disciples. What has happened? who could do this? these are rather the words of one who is exclaiming and lamenting, as he said before, "Who did bewitch you?" (Gal. iii: 1.)
Commentary on Galatians

You were running well; who hindered you from obeying the truth?

What the Latin translator has now set down, not to obey the truth (veritati non obedire), which in the Greek is written τῇ ἀληθείᾳ μὴ πείθεσθαι, he rendered in an earlier passage thus: "not to believe the truth" (non credere veritati). This, indeed, we noted in its proper place is not found in the old manuscripts, although the Greek copies too have been confused by this error. But the sense is this: You were worshiping the Father in spirit and truth, and, receiving of the fullness of Christ, you knew that the Law was only given to the people through Moses, and not also made; but grace and truth were not only given but also made through Jesus Christ. Since, therefore, you were running so well, serving the truth rather than images, by what perverse teacher have you been hindered, that you follow the shadow of the Law and abandon the truth of the Gospel?
