Consent to no one. But since we have found this written neither in the Greek books nor in those who have commented on the Apostle, it seems it should be passed over.
Homily on Galatians 5

He who called you, called you not to such fluctuations, he did not lay down a Law, that you should judaize. Then, that no one might object, "Why do you thus magnify and aggravate the matter by your words; one commandment only of the Law have we kept, and yet you make this great outcry?" hear how he terrifies them, not by things present but future.
Commentary on Galatians

Your persuasion is not from him who called you.

In the Latin manuscripts I have found it written thus: "Your persuasion is from God, who called you." I think, indeed, that this was originally from him (ex eo), and that, not being understood, "from God" (ex Deo) gradually became common because of the similarity, in place of what is from him (ex eo). But not even so can the sense stand, namely that he should now, on the contrary, assert that the persuasion and obedience of those whom he had just accused of not obeying the truth, showing that it lay in their own choice either to obey or not to obey, is not so much from those who are called as from him who calls. It is therefore better and more truly read thus: Your persuasion is not from him who called you. For the work of God is one thing, the work of men another. It is the work of God to call; it is the work of men either to believe or not to believe. And if anywhere in the Scriptures the free will of man is affirmed, as there: "If you will be willing and will hear me" (Exod. 19:5); and again: "And now, Israel, what does the Lord your God ask of you?" (Deut. 10:12), it is also proved most of all from this passage. But certain of the simpler sort, thinking that they were deferring to God by making our persuasion also lie in his power, have taken away the part of speech not and rendered a sense contrary to the Apostle. Whether, therefore, in the good sense or in the bad, neither God nor the devil is the cause, because our persuasion is not from him who called us, but from ourselves, who either consent or do not consent to the one who calls. Otherwise: This persuasion which you now follow is not from God, who called you in the beginning, but from those who afterwards troubled you.
Homily on Galatians 5
And thus this slight error, he says, if not corrected, will have power (as the leaven has with the lump) to lead you into complete Judaism.
Commentary on Galatians

A little leaven leavens the whole lump.

It is badly rendered in our codices: "A little leaven corrupts the whole mass", and the translator has rendered his own sense rather than the words of the Apostle. Now Paul uses this very same saying to the Corinthians as well, where he commanded that the man who had his father's wife should be taken away from their midst and handed over to penance, for the destruction and affliction of the flesh through fasts and sicknesses, so that the spirit might be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus Christ. For he says: "Your glorying is not good. Do you not know that a little leaven corrupts the whole mass" (1 Cor. 5:5, 6 ff.)? or (as we have already corrected it) leavens the whole lump? And at once he added: "Purge out the old leaven, that you may be a new lump, as you are unleavened; for Christ our pasch has been sacrificed. Therefore let us feast, not in the old leaven, nor in the leaven of malice and wickedness, but in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth." But now, by this same saying, he teaches that the spiritual bread of the Church, which came down from heaven, ought not to be violated by a Jewish interpretation; and the Lord commanded the very same thing to the disciples, that they should beware of the leaven of the Pharisees (John 6). The evangelist, making this plainer, added: "Now he had spoken to them of the doctrine of the Pharisees" (Matt. 16:12). And what is this other doctrine of the Pharisees, if not the observance of the Law according to the flesh? So this is the sense: Do not think that the snares of a few men, who come from Judea and teach something different, are to be despised. A spark is a small thing, and while it is being looked at it is almost not seen; but if it catches hold of tinder, and the fire, however small, finds what feeds it, it consumes walls, cities, the widest forests and whole regions. Leaven too, whose parable in the Gospel is turned to the other side (Luke 13), seems a small thing and of no account; but when it has been mixed into flour and has corrupted the whole mass by its strength, everything that has been mixed with it passes over into its power. So too a perverse doctrine, beginning from one man, at first, in its beginning, scarcely finds two or three hearers; but little by little it creeps through the body like a cancer, and, as the common proverb has it, the scab of one beast befouls the whole flock. Therefore the spark must be put out as soon as it appears, and the leaven removed from the neighborhood of the mass, the rotting flesh cut away, and the scabby animal driven from the sheepfolds, lest the whole house, mass, body and flock burn, be corrupted, rot and perish. Arius in Alexandria was a single spark; but because it was not put out at once, its flame laid waste the whole world.
Commentary on Matthew

This is the leaven of which the Apostle too speaks: A little leaven corrupts the whole lump. Leaven of this kind, which must be shunned by every means, Marcion had, and Valentinus, and all the heretics. Leaven has this power: if it is mixed with flour, what seemed small grows into something greater and draws the whole mass of dough to its own taste. So too heretical doctrine: if it has cast even a tiny spark into your breast, in a short time it grows up into a huge flame and draws the whole of a man's possession to itself.
Against Marcion Book V
"But he that troubleth you shall have to bear judgment." From what God? From (Marcion's) most excellent god? But he does not execute judgment.
Commentary on Galatians

He says he trusts in this hope concerning them, because they had entered the path of error not willingly, but being deceived. Therefore, having shown them the true way, he believes that they can easily return. But whoever troubles you will bear judgment, whoever he may be. Just as the one who turns a wandering person back is to be rewarded, as James the Apostle says in his letter: Whoever turns a sinner back will save his soul from death and cover a multitude of sins (James 5:20); so too the one who forces the one walking in the right path to turn aside onto a way of error will obtain condemnation, whoever he may be. For this reason, he subjects these; so that they would not defend themselves based on their merit, because they were descendants of Abraham according to the flesh. Finally, exalting themselves, they say to Jesus: We are children of Abraham (John 8:33).
Homily on Galatians 5

He does not say, "ye are not minded," but, "ye will not be minded;" that is, you will be set right. And how does he know this? he says not "I know," but "I trust in God, and invoking His aid in order to your correction, I am in hopes;" and he says, not merely, "I have confidence in the Lord," but, "I have confidence towards you in the Lord." Every where he connects complaint with his praises; here it is as if he had said, I know my disciples, I know your readiness to be set right. I have good hopes, partly because of the Lord who suffers nothing, however trivial, to perish, partly because of you who are quickly to recover yourselves. At the same time he exhorts them to use diligence on their own parts, it not being possible to obtain aid from God, if our own efforts are not contributed.

Not only by words of encouragement, but by uttering a curse or a prophecy against their teachers, he applies to them an incentive. And observe that he never mentions the name of these plotters, that they might not become more shameless. His meaning is as follows. Not because "ye will be none otherwise minded," are the authors of your seduction relieved from punishment. They shall be punished; for it is not proper that the good conduct of the one should become an encouragement to the evil disposition of the other. This is said that they might not make a second attempt upon others. And he says not merely, "he that troubleth," but, "whosoever he be," in the way of aggravation.
Commentary on Galatians

I have confidence in you in the Lord that you will think nothing else.

Not by conjecture, as some would have it, but by the prophetic spirit Paul declares that the Galatians will return to the way of truth which they had lost (1 Cor. 12). For he who exhorted others to be zealous for spiritual gifts, but rather that they might prophesy, himself also, full of the same grace, said: "We know in part, and we prophesy in part" (ibid., 13:9). Foreseeing therefore in the spirit that they would believe nothing else than what they were being taught through the Epistle, he says: I have confidence in you in the Lord that you will think nothing else. For the addition of the Lord's name too signifies this very thing. For if he had been reckoning this by conjecture, he could have said: I have confidence in you. But now, by adding in the Lord, trusting in a certain divine spirit, he prophesied what he had known would come to pass.
Commentary on Galatians

But he who troubles you shall bear judgment, whoever he is.

He is covertly tearing at Peter, they say, whom he writes above that he withstood to his face because he did not walk with a straight foot toward the truth of the Gospel. But neither would Paul speak with so insolent a curse about the prince of the Church (Gal. 2), nor did Peter deserve to be made guilty of troubling the Church. From this it must be judged that it is said of some other person, who either had been with the apostles, or had come from Judea, or had believed from among the Pharisees, or at any rate was esteemed great among the Galatians, so that he bears the judgment for the troubled Church, whoever he is. Now "to bear judgment" is what he said in other words in what follows: "Each one shall bear his own burden." And I think that in the Scriptures "burden" can be taken both in a good and in a bad sense, that is, both of those who are weighed down by grave sins, and of those who sustain the light burdens of the virtues. Of sins the penitent speaks in the psalm: "My iniquities are lifted up over my head; like a heavy burden they have weighed heavily upon me" (Ps. 37:5). Of the virtues, and of the teaching of the virtues, the Savior says: "For my yoke is sweet, and my burden is light" (Matt. 11:30). And that teaching too is taken for a burden is made plain in the Gospel. For the Pharisees bind heavy burdens, and such as cannot be borne, and lay them upon the shoulders of men, but they themselves are unwilling to touch them with one finger (ibid. 23). How grave a thing it is to disturb someone out of tranquility, and to stir up the calm hearts of men as if with waves, the words of the Savior to the apostles testify, when he says: "Let not your heart be troubled, nor be afraid" (John 14). For it is better for him who troubles anyone in the Church and causes him to stumble that a millstone be put around his neck and he be cast with it into the sea, than that he cause to stumble one of these least ones who are pointed out by the Savior (Luke 17). The Galatians, then, had been troubled between spirit and letter, circumcision and mutilation, hidden and manifest Judaism, not knowing what to do. It can also be taken more briefly in this way: Whoever he is who draws you back to the teaching of the Pharisees and desires to be circumcised in the flesh; though he be eloquent and boast of his learning in the Law, I say nothing more except this (which even you cannot deny): that he shall bear judgment for this work, and shall receive the reward for his labor.
An Answer to the Jews

And, of course, it had been meet that the mystery of the passion itself should be figuratively set forth in predictions; and the more incredible (that mystery), the more likely to be "a stumbling-stone," if it had been nakedly predicted; and the more magnificent, the more to be adumbrated, that the difficulty of its intelligence might seek (help from) the grace of God.
Homily on Galatians 5

Observe how clearly he exonerates himself from the charge, that in every place he judaized and played the hypocrite in his preaching. Of this he calls them as witnesses; for ye know, he says, that my command to abandon the Law was made the pretext for persecuting me. "If I still preach circumcision, why am I still persecuted? for this is the only charge which they of the Jewish descent have to bring against me. Had I permitted them to receive the Faith, still retaining the customs of their fathers, neither believers nor unbelievers would have laid snares for me, seeing that none of their own usages were disturbed. What then! did he not preach circumcision? did he not circumcise Timothy? Truly he did. How then can he say, "I preach it not?" Here observe his accuracy; he says not, "I do not perform circumcision," but, "I preach it not," that is, I do not bid men so to believe. Do not therefore consider it any confirmation of your doctrine, for though I circumcised, I did not preach circumcision.

That is, if this which ye assert be true, the obstacle, the hindrance, is removed; for not even the Cross was so great an offence to the Jews, as the doctrine that their father's customs ought not to be obeyed. When they brought Stephen before the council, they said not that this man adores the Crucified, but that he speaks "against this holy place and the Law." (Acts vi: 13.) And it was of this they accused Jesus, that He broke the Law. Wherefore Paul says, If Circumcision be conceded, the strife you are involved in is appeased; hereafter no enmity to the Cross and our preaching remains. But why do they bring this charge against us, while waiting day after day to murder us? it is because I brought an uncircumcised man into the Temple (Acts xxi: 29.) that they fell upon me. Am I then, he says, so senseless, after giving up the point of Circumcision, vainly and idly to expose myself to such injuries, and to place such a stumbling-block before the Cross? For ye observe, that they attack us for nothing with such vehemence as about Circumcision. Am I then so senseless as to suffer affliction for nothing at all, and to give offence to others? He calls it the offence of the Cross, because it was enjoined by the doctrine of the Cross; and it was this which principally offended the Jews, and hindered their reception of the Cross, namely, the command to abandon the usages of their fathers.
Commentary on Galatians

But I, brothers, if I preach circumcision, why do I still suffer persecution? Then has been made void (or, as the Greek has it better, has ceased) the stumbling block of the cross.

We read in the Acts of the Apostles, and the apostle Paul himself also often mentions in his Epistles, that he endured very frequent persecutions from the Jews, because he taught that those from among the Gentiles who had believed in Christ ought not to be circumcised. These, then, of whom he said above: "But he who troubles you shall bear judgment, whoever he is", in order to deceive the Galatians, added this too: Not only do Peter and James and John and the other apostles in Judea observe circumcision and the other precepts of the Law, but Paul himself as well, who taught you otherwise than the truth of the matter stands, circumcised Timothy, and frequently became a Jew to the Jews, the truth compelling him. Wishing now to remove this opinion from the minds of the Galatians, Paul says: But I, brothers, if I preach circumcision, why do I still suffer persecution? All the hatred of the Jews against me, he says, and the madness with which they rage against me, is on account of nothing else than that I teach the Gentiles that they ought not to be circumcised and to keep the burdens of the Law, which are superfluous and already abolished. But since I suffer persecution, it is manifest that I do not preach circumcision, which I destroy. For I do not suffer persecution from the Jews so much because I preach the Crucified, and say that Jesus is the Christ whom the Law and the prophets foretold, as because I teach that the Law has been fulfilled. And that the cross is a stumbling block to the Jews and foolishness to the Gentiles, our Lord himself shows, who is called a stone of offense and a rock of stumbling (Matt. 21; Luke 20): for no other reason, I think, than that preaching, when it has advanced toward its hearers under full sail, strikes against the cross as soon as it comes to it, and can by no means proceed further on a free course. But this cross, which among the Jews is a stumbling block and among the Gentiles foolishness, is to us who believe power and wisdom. "For Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God" (1 Cor. 1:24), so that, because of that which was called foolishness, the foolishness of God might become wiser than men; and because of that which was called weakness and a stumbling block, the weakness of God might become stronger than men. But since, he says, the stumbling block of the cross of Christ remains, and I suffer persecution, which I would not suffer if the stumbling block did not remain, in vain do certain people keep boasting that I preach circumcision, by attacking which I endure persecution.
A Treatise on the Soul

How should he not, when he himself experiences the same? "I would," says he, "that they were even cut off which trouble you." In perfect agreement with reason was that indignation which resulted from his desire to maintain discipline and order.
On Modesty

"When I was a child," he says, "as a child I spake, as a child I understood; but when I became a man, those (things) which had been the child's I abandoned: " so truly did he turn away from his early opinions: nor did he sin by becoming an emulator not of ancestral but of Christian traditions, wishing even the precision of them who advised the retention of circumcision. And would that the same fate might befall those, too, who obtruncate the pure and true integrity of the flesh; amputating not the extremest superficies, but the inmost image of modesty itself, while they promise pardon to adulterers and fornicators, in the teeth of the primary discipline of the Christian Name; a discipline to which heathendom itself bears such emphatic witness, that it strives to punish that discipline in the persons of our females rather by defilements of the flesh than tortures; wishing to wrest from them that which they hold dearer than life! But now this glory is being extinguished, and that by means of those who ought with all the more constancy to refuse concession of any pardon to defilements of this kind, that they make the fear of succumbing to adultery and fornication their reason for marrying as often as they please-since "better it is to marry than to burn.
Homily on Galatians 5

Observe how bitterly he speaks here against their deceivers. At the outset he directed his charge against those who were deceived, and called them foolish, once and again. Now, having sufficiently corrected and instructed them, he turns to their deceivers. And you should remark his wisdom in the manner in which he admonishes and chastens the former as his own children, and as capable of receiving correction, but their deceivers he cuts off, as aliens and incurably depraved. And this he does, partly, when he says, "he shall bear his judgment whosoever he be;" partly when he utters the imprecation against them, "I would that they which unsettle you would even cut themselves off." And he says well "that unsettle you." For they had compelled them to abandon their own fatherland, their liberty, and their heavenly kindred, and to seek an alien and foreign one; they had cast them out of Jerusalem which is above and free, and compelled them to wander forth as captives and emigrants. On this account he curses them; and his meaning is as follows, For them I have no concern, "A man that is heretical after the first and second admonition refuse." (Tit. iii: 10) If they will, let them not only be circumcised, but mutilated. Where then are those who dare to mutilate themselves; seeing that they draw down the Apostolic curse, and accuse the workmanship of God, and take part with the Manichees? For the latter call the body a treacherous thing, and from the evil principle; and the former by their acts give countenance to these wretched doctrines, cutting off the member as being hostile and treacherous. Ought they not much rather to put out the eyes, for it is through the eyes that desire enters the soul? But in truth neither the eye nor any other part of us is to blame, but the depraved will only. But if you will not allow this, why do you not mutilate the tongue for blasphemy, the hands for rapine, the feet for their evil courses, in short, the whole body? For the ear enchanted by the sound of a flute hath often enervated the soul; and the perception of a sweet perfume by the nostrils hath bewitched the mind, and made it frantic for pleasure. Yet this would be extreme wickedness and satanic madness. The evil spirit, ever delighting in slaughter, hath seduced them to crush the instrument, as if its Maker had erred, whereas it was only necessary to correct the unruly passion of the soul. How then does it happen, one may say, that when the body is pampered, lust is inflamed? Observe here too that it is the sin of the soul, for to pamper the flesh is not an act of the flesh but of the soul, for if the soul choose to mortify it, it would possess absolute power over it. But what you do is just the same as if one seeing a man lighting a fire, and heaping on fuel, and setting fire to a house, were to blame the fire, instead of him who kindled it, because it had caught this heap of fuel, and risen to a great height. Yet the blame would attach not to the fire but to the one who kindled it; for it was given for the purpose of dressing food, affording light, and other like ministries, not for burning houses. In like manner desire is implanted for the rearing of families and the ensuring of life, not for adultery, or fornication, or lasciviousness; that a man may become a father, not an adulterer; a lawful husband, not a seducer; leaving heirs after him, not doing damage to another man's. For adultery arises not from nature, but from wantonness against nature, which prescribes the use not the misuse. These remarks I have not made at random, but as a prelude to a dispute, as skirmishing against those who assert that the workmanship of God is evil, and who neglecting the sloth of the soul, madly inveigh against the body, and traduce our flesh, whereof Paul afterwards discourses, accusing not the flesh, but devilish thoughts.
Commentary on Galatians

Would that they were even cut off who trouble you.

It is asked how Paul, the disciple of him who says: "Bless those who curse you," and who himself says: "Bless, and do not curse" (Rom. 12:14), and in another place: "Nor shall cursers possess the kingdom of God" (1 Cor. 6:10), has now both cursed those who trouble the churches of Galatia, and cursed them with the prayer of one who wishes it: Would that they were even cut off who trouble you. For the suffering of castration is so detestable that both he who has inflicted it on the unwilling is punished by the public laws, and he who has castrated himself is held infamous. For granted, they say, that this is true: "Christ lives in me"; and this: "Or do you seek a proof of Christ who speaks in me?" (2 Cor. 13:3), certainly a word of cursing cannot be understood as coming from him who says: "Learn from me, because I am humble, and meek, and gentle of heart" (Matt. 11:29). And it is thought rather that he was unable to restrain himself out of Jewish fury and a kind of unbridled madness than that he imitated him who, like a lamb before its shearer, did not open his mouth, and did not curse in return those who cursed him (Isa. 53). But, condemned, he handed himself over to death. To this, whoever answers on Paul's behalf will say the following: that the words he spoke were not so much of fury against his adversaries as of love for the churches of God. For he saw that the whole province, which he himself, with his own blood and his perils, had brought over from idolatry to the faith of Christ, was thrown into confusion by a sudden persuasion, and with an apostle's grief, a father's grief, he could not contain himself: he changed his voice, and was angry with those whom he had coaxed, so that those whom he had been unable to hold by gentleness he might at least hold by rebuke. Nor is it to be wondered at if the Apostle, as a man, and one still shut up in a weak little vessel, and seeing another law in his body taking him captive and leading him in the law of sin, said this once, a thing into which we see that holy men frequently fall. But this too can be said (although to some it may seem superfluous): that Paul did not so much curse them as pray for them, that they might lose those parts of the body through which they were driven to sin. And just as it was said in the Gospel that it is better for someone to enter the kingdom of heaven without an eye, and without a hand, and without a foot, and without any other part of the members, than to go whole into Gehenna (Matt. 18), so now too he wishes them rather to lose one part of the body than, by occasion of the whole body, to be condemned to everlasting fire. If ever this passage is censured by the heathen, we have shown how they can be answered. Now let it be brought forward by us against the heretics, namely Marcion and Valentinus and all who bark against the Old Testament: by what reasoning can those who accuse the Creator of being bloodthirsty, a stern warrior and only a judge, excuse this in the Apostle of the good God? And certainly I think there is no sentence anywhere in the old Law so savage, so bloody, as would that they were cut off who trouble you. Nor can they say that the Apostle prayed for the enemies of Christ, who were troubling his churches. Nor that it was uttered out of love, since the very weight of the words shows it to be full of swelling anger and indignation. Whatever excuse, therefore, they bring forward for the Apostle, this we shall not plead in defense of the old Law.

He who indulges his pleasures gratifies his body; but he who is controlled liberates from its passions his soul which is master of the body. And if they tell us that we are called to freedom, only let us not use our freedom as an opportunity for the flesh, as the apostle says.

Nay, rather banish quite away from your "free" head all this slavery of ornamentation.
Homily on Galatians 5

Henceforward he appears to digress into a moral discourse, but in a new manner, which does not occur in any other of his Epistles. For all of them are divided into two parts, and in the first he discusses doctrine, in the last the rule of life, but here, after having entered upon the moral discourse, he again unites with it the doctrinal part. For this passage has reference to doctrine in the controversy with the Manichees. What is the meaning of, "Use not your freedom for an occasion to the flesh?" Christ hath delivered us, he says, from the yoke of bondage, He hath left us free to act as we will, not that we may use our liberty for evil, but that we may have ground for receiving a higher reward, advancing to a higher philosophy. Lest any one should suspect, from his calling the Law over and over again a yoke of bondage, and a bringing on of the curse, that his object in enjoining an abandonment of the Law, was that one might live lawlessly, he corrects this notion, and states his object to be, not that our course of life might be lawless, but that our philosophy might surpass the Law. For the bonds of the Law are broken, and I say this not that our standard may be lowered, but that it may be exalted. For both he who commits fornication, and he who leads a virgin life, pass the bounds of the Law, but not in the same direction; the one is led away to the worse, the other is elevated to the better; the one transgresses the Law, the other transcends it. Thus Paul says that Christ hath removed the yoke from you, not that ye may prance and kick, but that though without the yoke ye may proceed at a well-measured pace. And next he shows the mode whereby this may be readily effected; and what is this mode? ...

Here again he hints that strife and party-spirit, love of rule and presumptousness, had been the causes of their error, for the desire of rule is the mother of heresies. By saying, "Be servants one to another," he shows that the evil had arisen from this presumptuous and arrogant spirit, and therefore he applies a corresponding remedy. As your divisions arose from your desire to domineer over each other, "serve one another;" thus will ye be reconciled again. However, he does not openly express their fault, but he openly tells them its corrective, that through this they may become aware of that; as if one were not to tell an immodest person of his immodesty, but were continually to exhort him to chastity. He that loves his neighbor as he ought, declines not to be servant to him more humbly than any servant. As fire, brought into contact with wax, easily softens it, so does the warmth of love dissolve all arrogance and presumption more powerfully than fire. Wherefore he says not, "love one another," merely, but, "be servants one to another," thus signifying the intensity of the affection. When the yoke of the Law was taken off them that they might not caper off and away another was laid on, that of love, stronger than the former, yet far lighter and pleasanter; and, to point out the way to obey it, ...
Commentary on Galatians

But through love serve one another, for the whole law is fulfilled in one word: You shall love your neighbor as yourself.

He who, though he was free from all, made himself the slave of all for love's sake, that he might win the more (1 Cor. 9:19), rightly exhorts the others too to serve one another through love, which seeks not what is its own but what is its neighbor's. For he who wishes to become first shall be the slave of all (Mark 10:44); so that, just as the Savior, being in the form of God, did not think it robbery to be equal with God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a slave, and being found in fashion as a man, he humbled himself, becoming obedient even unto death, and the death of the cross (Phil. 2), so we too should now know that whatever things we formerly seemed to do under the compulsion of the Law, we, being free, must do rather through love.
Commentary on Galatians

For you have been called to freedom, brothers: only do not (it is understood) give freedom as an occasion to the flesh:

because this is not found in the Greek, the Latin translator put it in. Since this passage is very obscure, I have decided to translate it word for word from the tenth book of the Stromata. Not that the individual parts cannot be explained in their own places and senses; but because, separated from the preceding subject matter, they form a single difficult body: and if they are understood just as they sound, they seem to clash with one another inconsequently and abruptly, and to be all in a ferment. These, then, are Origen's words: "The passage is difficult, and it seems to us that it should be discussed thus. He who is free, and in a higher sense follows the spirit and the truth, despises both the preceding types and the letter: he ought not on that account to look down on the lesser, and give those who cannot perceive more sublimely an occasion to despair of themselves utterly. For although they are weak and are called flesh in comparison with the spirit, yet they are the flesh of Christ. For if he understands the mystery of love that serves the weaker, let him do something for the sake of the weak, lest in his knowledge a brother perish, for whom Christ died. Pay careful attention, therefore, whether this sense is woven together from what follows. You, he says, brothers, have been called to freedom: perhaps for this reason, that not all were able to grasp the calling of freedom. That is why you now hear: Only do not give freedom as an occasion to the flesh. For through love the greater ought to serve the lesser: because he who wishes to be greater will be the slave of all (Matt. 20; Mark 10). So let the spiritual man neither tear the flesh of Christ, nor give them an occasion to bite back at him when he provokes them, lest they be consumed by one another. He, then, who walks by the spirit, and pursues the words of the Scriptures by the spirit, must not fulfill the desire of their flesh. But if we understand what is said, 'Walk by the spirit, and you will not fulfill the desire of the flesh', in the simple way (as most people think), Paul will suddenly break out into these things against the argument and the hypothesis of the whole Epistle; for immediately there follows: 'But if you are led by the spirit, you are not under the Law.' And although up to this point the discourse holds together in some measure, again, if we follow the simple understanding, it suddenly carries us over to disordered precepts, discussing flesh and spirit, that is: 'Now the works of the flesh are manifest, this one and that one.' And on the other hand: 'But the fruit of the spirit is love', and the rest. But neither in these should we despair of the sequence; for the history of the divine volumes contains the works of the flesh, and it does not greatly help those who understand it just as it is written. For who will not be taught to serve licentiousness and to count fornication as nothing, when he has read of Judah going in to a harlot (Gen. 38), and that the patriarchs had many wives at the same time? How will he not be provoked to idolatry who supposes that the blood of bulls and the other victims of Leviticus signify nothing more than what sounds in the letter? And that the word of Scripture, set out in the open, teaches enmities is proved also from this passage: 'O wretched daughter of Babylon, blessed is he who will repay you your repayment with which you repaid us. Blessed is he who will seize and dash your little ones against the rock' (Ps. 136:8, 9). And from that one: 'In the morning I killed all the sinners of the land' (Ps. 100:8), and other things like these: namely, concerning strifes, jealousy, anger, quarrels, dissensions. To these things (unless we perceive something higher) the examples of the history provoke us more than they forbid them. Heresies too have arisen more from the carnal understanding of Scripture than from the work of our flesh, as very many suppose. Envy and drunkenness, moreover, we learn through the letter of the Law. Noah gets drunk after the flood, and the patriarchs with their brother Joseph in Egypt (Gen. 9 and 43). And carousings too are written in the book of Kingdoms, with David dancing and beating the timbrels before the Ark of the covenant of God (1 Sam. 6), and things like these. It is asked how the simple word of divine Scripture, which is called flesh, provokes us to sorceries and to evil arts, unless we cross over to the spirit of that same Scripture. I think this is what is signified by Daniel and the three youths being found ten times wiser than the magi, the enchanters, the Gazarenes and the Chaldeans, and by Moses being learned in all the wisdom and teaching of the Egyptians. It is therefore the occasion of many evils if anyone remains in the flesh of Scripture. Those who do such things will not obtain the kingdom of God. Wherefore let us seek the spirit of Scripture and its fruits, which are not said to be manifest. For it is with much labor and sweat, and with fitting cultivation, that the fruit of the spirit is found in the Scriptures. Hence I judge that Paul spoke carefully and cautiously when he said of the carnal senses of Scripture: 'Now the works of the flesh are manifest' (Gal. 5:19). But of the spiritual he did not set down, as there, 'the fruit of the spirit is manifest'; but thus: 'But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace', and the rest (ibid., 22). But if, leaving the types behind, we pass over to the truth and the spirit of Scripture, at once love is first opened to us, and stepping on from there to joy, we arrive at peace, through which we attain patience. And who would not be instructed in mercy and goodness, when he has understood that even those things in the Law which some think grim (I mean punishments and battles, and the overthrow of nations, and the threats against peoples through the prophets) are remedies rather than penalties? For the Lord will not be angry forever (Isa. 57). When these things, then, have been opened to us, we shall have a more reasonable faith, and temperance will accompany our corrected morals, and self-control and chastity will follow it: and after all these things the Law will begin to be for us." Thus far Origen.
Commentary on Galatians

To which we can add, saying that those called from the slavery of the Law to the freedom of the Gospel (to whom it was said above: "Stand, and do not cling again to the yoke of slavery") are even now admonished that, following the light yoke of Christ and the delightful precepts of the Gospel, they should by no means think it permitted to them to use this very freedom of living as an occasion of the flesh: that is, to live according to the flesh, to be circumcised according to the flesh; but rather to stand in the spirit, to cut off the foreskin of the flesh in the spirit, and, stretching toward the higher things of the spirit, to leave behind the lowliness of the letter. It can also be understood otherwise. Let someone learn: If I have ceased, O Paul, to be under the Law, and I have been called from slavery to freedom, then I ought to live as befits freedom, and not be bound by any precepts, but whatever has pleased me and my will has suggested, this I should do, fulfill, pursue. To this the Apostle replied: that we have indeed been called into the freedom of the spirit, but in such a way that freedom itself does not serve the flesh. Nor let us think that, because all things are lawful for us, all things are expedient: rather, because we have ceased to be slaves of the Law, having been made free, let us all the more serve one another through love, so that the precepts of the sprawling Law may be summed up in the single heading of love.
Commentary on Galatians

This passage can be better explained thus, and become as it were one sequence and one body, linking itself together and not disagreeing with itself. Brothers, you have been called from the slavery of the Law into the freedom of the Gospel. But I beseech you not to abuse freedom as license, and think that all things which are lawful are expedient for you, and give occasion to the flesh and to licentiousness. Rather, learn that this freedom is a greater slavery, so that the obedience which formerly the Law extorted from the unwilling, you now render by serving one another through love. For indeed all that burden of the Law, and its manifold precepts, have not so much been shut out by the grace of the Gospel as abridged in the one word of love, that we love our neighbor as ourselves. For he who loves his neighbor fulfills the whole law (Matt. 22), bestowing good things on him and not inflicting evils. But if affection ceases, and there is no love, through which the whole law is fulfilled, there will be a kind of public brigandage among men, so that, raging against one another and biting one another, they are consumed by one another. But you, brothers, ought for this reason to live according to the spiritual law, so that you do not accomplish the desires that belong to the flesh. For the flesh fears cold, spurns hunger, is wasted by vigils, burns with lusts, desires whatever is soft and pleasant. The spirit, on the contrary, seeks the things that are contrary to the flesh and that can weaken it. And so it comes about that you should not think yourselves free just because you have ceased to be under the slavery of the Law, but should rather know that you are held fast by the law of nature; because it does not follow at once that, if the law does not command, nature too has ceased, so that, namely, works should not follow your will; but you are often compelled, the flesh fighting against the spirit, to do the things you do not will to do. Therefore, brothers, I beseech you not to give your freedom as an occasion for the flesh, but rather to serve the spirit, so that you may begin to do the things you will, and to owe nothing to the law, that is, not to be under the flesh. For you will truly be able to have in the Gospel the freedom of the abolished law when the flesh in no way compels you to do what you do not will, but, serving the spirit, you have shown that you are not under the Law.

Now, if none other but the Creator shall be found to execute judgment, it follows that only He, who has determined on the cessation of the law, shall be able to condemn the defenders of the law; and what, if he also affirms the law in that portion of it where it ought (to be permanent)? "For," says he, "all the law is fulfilled in you by this: `Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself.' " If, indeed, he will have it that by the words "it is fulfilled" it is implied that the law no longer has to be fulfilled, then of course he does not mean that I should any more love my neighbour as myself, since this precept must have ceased together with the law.

That charity and brotherly affection are to be religiously and stedfastly practised. In Malachi: "Hath not one God created us? Is there not one Father of us all? Also in the same place: "Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called the sons of God." Also in the same place: "Verily I say unto you, That if two of you shall agree on earth concerning everything, whatever you shall ask it shall be given you from my Father which is in heaven. " Likewise in the same place: "And if I should have all faith, so that I can remove mountains, but have not charity, I am nothing. It loveth all things, believeth all things, hopeth all things, beareth all things. Charity shall never fail." Of this same thing to the Galatians: "Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself. But if ye bite and accuse one another, see that ye be not consumed one of another." Of this same thing in the Epistle of John: "In this appear the children of God and the children of the devil. Seeing that they made so much of the Law, he says, "If you wish to fulfill it, do not be circumcised, for it is fulfilled not in circumcision but in love." Observe how he cannot forget his grief, but constantly touches upon what troubled him, even when launched into his moral discourse.
Commentary on Galatians

And love is so great a good that the whole law is summed up in it. In another place also the Apostle enumerates the good things of love, saying: "It is not jealous, it does not act wrongly" (1 Cor. 13:4). And having unfolded many things in between, at the end he concludes: "It hopes all things, it endures all things, love never fails." And the Savior in the Gospel says that this is the sign of his disciple: if he loves his neighbor (Matt. 22). This indeed, I think, applies not only to men but also to angels. The same thing is said in other words: "What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to others; and whatever you wish that men should do to you, do you also likewise the same to them" (ibid. 7:12). I do not wish my wife to be defiled by adultery, I do not wish my property to be plundered, I do not wish to be crushed by false testimony, and, to comprise everything in a brief word, I take it ill that anything unjust should be done to me. If, through love working in me, I either do or wish these same things for another, the whole law is fulfilled. Nor is it difficult to show how all the precepts, you shall not kill, you shall not commit adultery, you shall not steal, you shall not bear false witness, and the rest like these, are held together by the single observance of love. What is hard to show is how the sacrifices too that are prescribed in Leviticus, and the abstinence from foods or the permission of them, since some are called clean and others unclean, and also the continual recurrence of the solemn feasts through the years, are summed up in the one precept of love. Unless perhaps one should go over to this position, so as to affirm that the Law is spiritual, and that we served the images and patterns of heavenly things before the true High Priest came; and that after he, offering himself once as a victim, redeemed us by his own blood, all that variety and difficulty of the ancient Law was fulfilled in his love toward men. For the Father so loved the world that he gave his most dear and only-begotten Son for us. But for him who, once living by the spirit, has put to death the works of the flesh, and, being loved by the Savior, is called no longer a slave but a friend, the Law is no longer laid down, which was established for the ungodly and sinners, and for the insubordinate and the wicked. But now, while we do all the things that are more difficult, if only in small part, this one thing alone we do not do, which is both easier to do and without which all that we do is void. The body feels the injury of fasting; vigils waste the flesh; alms are sought by labor; blood in martyrdom, however much faith burns, is still not shed without pain and fear. There are those who do all these things: love alone is without labor. And because it alone makes the heart clean, it is assailed in us by the devil, so that we may not see God with a pure mind. For when I sit and speak against my brother, and lay a stumbling block against my mother's son (Ps. 49:20), when I am tormented by another's happiness and make another's good my evil, is not what follows fulfilled in me: "If you bite and devour one another, see that you are not consumed by one another"? The possession of love is rare. Who, following the Apostle, is willing himself to be anathema from Christ for his brothers? Who, mourning with those who mourn and rejoicing with those who rejoice, is wounded by another's wound? Who is slain by a brother's death? We are all lovers of ourselves rather than lovers of God. See how great is the good of love. If we undergo martyrdom in such a way that we wish our relics to be honored by men; if, pursuing the good opinion of the crowd, we fearlessly shed our blood and give away our substance even to the point of our own beggary, to this work is owed not so much a reward as a penalty, and these are the torments of faithlessness rather than a crown of victory.

What, then, is that-how execrable should it appear to you-which I have learnt with extreme anguish and grief of mind, to wit, that there are not wanting those who defile the temples of God, and the members sanctified after confession and made glorious, with a disgraceful and infamous concubinage, associating their beds promiscuously with women's! In which, even if there be no pollution of their conscience, there is a great guilt in this very thing, that by their offence originate examples for the ruin of Others. "But if ye bite and find fault with one another, take heed that ye be not consumed one of another." From abuse and revilings also I entreat you to abstain, for "revilers do not attain the kingdom of God; " and the tongue which has confessed Christ should be preserved sound and pure with its honour. For he who, according to Christ's precept, speaks things peaceable and good and just, daily confesses Christ. We had renounced the world when we were baptized; but we have now indeed renounced the world when tried and approved by God, we leave all that we have, and have followed the Lord, and stand and live in His faith and fear.
Homily on Galatians 5

That he may not distress them, he does not assert this, though he knew it was the case, but mentions it ambiguously. For he does not say, "Inasmuch as ye bite one another," nor again does he assert, in the clause following, that they shall be consumed by each other; but "take heed that ye be not consumed one of another," and this is the language of apprehension and warning, not of condemnation. And the words which he uses are expressly significant; he says not merely, "ye bite," which one might do in a passion, but also "ye devour," which implies a bearing of malice. To bite is to satisfy the feeling of anger, but to devour is a proof of the most savage ferocity. The biting and devouring he speaks of are not bodily, but of a much more cruel kind; for it is not such an injury to taste the flesh of man, as to fix one's fangs in his soul. In proportion as the soul is more precious than the body, is damage to it more serious. "Take heed that ye be not consumed one of another." For those who commit injury and lay plots, do so in order to destroy others; therefore he says, Take heed that this evil fall not on your own heads. For strife and dissensions are the ruin and destruction as well of those who admit as of those who introduce them, and eats out every thing worse than a moth does.
Commentary on Galatians

But if you bite and devour one another, see that you are not consumed by one another.

This can also be taken simply: that we should not disparage one another, nor think to avenge ourselves with a curse, nor, when grieved, desire to grieve in return, and, like beasts, bite and likewise be bitten back, so that after the bites there follow destruction and consumption. But it is better, lest Paul, against reason and the sequence of the whole Epistle, should suddenly break out into extraneous precepts, to understand it in such a way that we refer everything to circumcision and the observance of the Law. HOW ARE WE FREE IN CHOICE AND WILL, WHEN THE APOSTLE SAYS, “THE FLESH DESIRES AGAINST THE SPIRIT, AND THE SPIRIT AGAINST THE FLESH, SO THAT YOU DO NOT DO THE THINGS THAT YOU WOULD” (Gal. 5:17)? AND IF THE FLESH DESIRES AGAINST THE SPIRIT, IT IS EVIL. FOR THE SPIRIT SUGGESTS WHAT IS GOOD. — Do not understand “flesh” here as the substance of flesh, but as evil deeds and unbelief signified under the name of flesh. For since all error comes from visible and worldly things, and the flesh is akin to them, because it is composed of elements, he calls every error “flesh.” He calls not only adulteries, fornications, and lusts the works of the flesh, but also idolatry, sorcery, blasphemies, and such things. Does the flesh compel to blasphemy or to idolatry? Are not these vices of the soul, when it consents to error? Yet he rightly says to those who act correctly that they are not in the flesh, but in the spirit. And yet they are in the body for this very purpose. Therefore, whoever walks well and does not despair of the hope of the faithful, though placed in the flesh, is said not to be in the flesh; but one who lives badly and is blasphemous is said to be in the flesh and to be flesh. For just as those who act well are spiritual even with the flesh, so those who live badly are carnal even with the soul itself. This is what he calls it. This error, then, which he calls flesh, desires against the spirit, that is, it suggests evil things against that same spirit, which is the law of God. For he introduces two laws, that of God and that of the Devil. Therefore he says “spirit” because the law of God is spiritual, to resist the flesh, that is, to resist the vices, so as to preserve a person for God; but the law of the Devil, which is error, opposes through the allurements of lust and the sweetness of worldly things. With these in conflict, the human being is in the middle: when he consents to the spirit, the flesh does not want it; but when he gives his hand to the flesh, he spurns the spirit, that is, he despises the law of God. Therefore, when he consents to the flesh, the spirit calls him back so that he does not do what he wishes; but when he agrees to the spirit, the flesh urges him not to do what he thinks beneficial. Yet the spirit rightly and sensibly resists and calls him back, so that it may snatch the person away from the counsels of Satan. But the flesh, which is the opposing law, therefore urges and resists the spirit of the law in order to deceive through trickery. The Apostle therefore proclaims this so as to show to human choice to which side it should commit its will, not to empty the freedom of choice, but to teach the will to which it should join itself. If, however, there were no freedom of will, neither the law of the Devil, which is the flesh, nor the law of God, which is the spirit, by opposing one another, would press a person with their counsels. For whoever entices, persuades; and whoever persuades does not use force, but ensnares; and the one who is ensnared has his will changed by certain deceits. But if there were no free will, a person would, against his will, be dragged to those things which he does not want.

Not that he has taken away from us our own free choice, by which we assent either to the flesh or to the spirit; but because what we do is not properly ours, but the work itself is reckoned either to the flesh or to the spirit. It is a matter of great labor and of excessive disputation, once the works of the flesh and of the spirit have been set out, to find some middle things which seem to belong neither to the flesh nor to the spirit. We are called carnal when we give ourselves wholly to pleasures; spiritual, when we follow the Holy Spirit going before us, that is, when we are wise with Him instructing us, and are taught with Him as our authority. The animal men (animales), I think, are the philosophers, who suppose their own thoughts to be wisdom, of whom it is rightly said: "But the animal man does not receive the things that are of the spirit. For it is foolishness to him". To make this clearer, let us take an example: let the flesh be called earth, the soul gold, the spirit fire. As long as the gold is in the earth, it loses its own name, and is called after the earth with which it is mixed. But when, separated from the soil, it has received both the appearance and the name of gold, it is indeed called gold, but not yet tested. If, however, it has been smelted and purged through fire, then it receives the splendor of gold and the dignity of its own adornment. So too the soul, standing between soil and fire, that is, between flesh and spirit, when it has handed itself over to the flesh, is called flesh; when to the spirit, it is called spirit. But if it has trusted its own thought, and has supposed that it finds the truth without the grace of the Holy Spirit, it is marked, like impure gold, with the name of the animal man.

To this we shall answer briefly: it is not the same thing to be under the Law and to be as if under the Law, just as it is not the very same thing to be in the likeness of the flesh of sin and to be in the flesh of sin. So, therefore, the holy prophets too, and Moses, walking by the spirit and living by the spirit, lived not under the Law but as if under the Law, so that they themselves seemed indeed to be under the Law, but might gain those who were under the Law and call them forth from the lowliness of the letter to the height of the spirit.
