There is one body, and one Spirit, as ye have been called in one hope of your calling; one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God." All these things speaks the Catholic Church. And again, in the Gospel the Lord says: "That which is born of the flesh is flesh, and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit; because God is a Spirit, and he is born of God." Therefore, whatsoever things all heretics and schismatics do are carnal, as the apostle says: "For the works of the flesh are manifest, which are, fornications, uncleannesses, incest, idolatries, witchcrafts, hatreds, contentions, jealousy, anger, divisions, heresies, and the like to these; concerning which have told you before, as I also foretell you now, that whoever do such things shall not inherit the kingdom of God." And thus the apostle condemns, with all the wicked, those also who cause division, that is, schismatics and heretics. Unless therefore they receive saving baptism in the Catholic Church, which is one, they cannot be saved, but will be condemned with the carnal in the judgment of the Lord Christ.
Homily on Galatians 5

Answer me now, thou that accusest thine own flesh, and supposest that this is said of it as of an enemy and adversary. Let it be allowed that adultery and fornication proceed, as you assert, from the flesh; yet hatred, variance, emulations, strife, heresies, and witchcraft, these arise merely from a depraved moral choice. And so it is with the others also, for how can they belong to the flesh? you observe that he is not here speaking of the flesh, but of earthly thoughts, which trail upon the ground. Wherefore also he alarms them by saying, that "they which practice such things shall not inherit the kingdom of God." If these things belonged to nature and not to a bad moral choice, his expression, "they practice," is inappropriate, it should be, "they suffer." And why should they be cast out of the kingdom, for rewards and punishments relate not to what proceeds from nature but from choice?
Commentary on Titus

And to the Galatians it is numbered among the works of the flesh: "Now the works of the flesh are manifest, which are fornication, uncleanness, licentiousness, idolatry, sorceries, enmities, contentions, rivalries, angers, quarrels, dissensions, heresies, envyings, drunkennesses, revellings, and other things like these, which I foretell to you as I have foretold: that those who do such things will not possess the kingdom of God" (Gal. 5:19 ff.). In these it must be carefully observed that, just as the other vices which are numbered among the works of the flesh exclude us from the kingdom of God, so heresies too take the kingdom of God away from us; and it makes no difference in what way anyone is excluded from the kingdom, so long as he is excluded.
Commentary on Galatians

Now the works of the flesh are manifest, which are: fornication, impurity, licentiousness, idolatry, sorceries, enmities, strifes, jealousies, angers, quarrels, dissensions, heresies, envyings, drunkenness, carousings, and things like these, which I foretell to you, as I have also foretold: that those who do these things shall not possess the kingdom of God.

Above, when we were expounding about the flesh and the spirit, we had spoken of a threefold understanding: either that those are fleshly who, being little ones and bodily, could not take solid food in Christ and the nourishment of full age; or that those are carnal who, in the Jewish manner, follow only the history and the letter; or certainly, according to the simple sense, that flesh and spirit subsist in the fashioning of man, and that according to the difference of substance there are works either of the flesh or of the spirit. Now therefore the works of the flesh which are named here, namely fornication, impurity, licentiousness and the rest that follow, seem to me to refer rather to the simple understanding of flesh and spirit than to the flesh of the Law and to the little ones in Christ, although in that place above, where we translated word for word from the tenth book of Origen's Stromata, what may also be thought about these things has been set out. And when he says: Now the works of the flesh are manifest, he shows either that they are known to all, because they are plainly evil of themselves and to be shunned, so much so that even those who do them wish to hide what they do; or certainly that they are manifest only to those who have believed in Christ. For very many of the Gentiles glory in their shames, and think that if they have satisfied their pleasure, they have won a kind of victory of disgraceful deeds. But this too is elegantly done, that he placed works in the flesh and fruits in the spirit: because vices come to an end in themselves and perish, while virtues sprout with fruits and overflow. Nor let us think that the soul has no work, if vices are assigned to the flesh and virtues to the spirit. For the soul (as we said above), placed in a kind of middle ground, is either joined to the flesh, and it is said of it: "My spirit shall not remain in these men, because they are flesh" (Gen. 6:3); or it is united to the spirit and passes into the name of spirit. "For he who cleaves to the Lord is one spirit" (1 Cor. 6:17). So the first work of the flesh is fornication. He put the manifest ones at the beginning, so that we should not be in doubt about those in the middle. For whatever a man does is outside the body, but he who commits fornication sins against his own body. And we are not our own: for we have been bought with a price; let us glorify and carry God in our body. In this the fornicator is of greater guilt: because he takes the members of Christ and makes them the members of a harlot. For the two shall be in one flesh. He who is not a believer and does not believe in Christ makes his own members the members of a harlot; he who believes and commits fornication makes the members of Christ the members of a harlot. On the other hand, whether the unbeliever in his fornication violates a temple or builds a temple to an idol, I do not know. For demons are worshiped above all through vices. This one thing I know: that he who commits fornication after faith in Christ violates the temple of God. The second work of the flesh is called impurity, and licentiousness follows it as its companion. For just as in the old Law Scripture embraced in general terms the abominable crimes which are done in secret, and which it is most shameful even to name (lest both the mouth of the speaker and the ears of the hearers be defiled), saying: "Modest", or "reverent, make the sons of Israel, away from all impurity" (Lev. 15:31): so in this place he has named as impurity and licentiousness the other extraordinary pleasures, and even the works of marriage itself, if they are not done modestly and with decency, as under the eyes of God, so that only the begetting of children is served.
The Stromata Book 6

Now it is adultery, if one, abandoning the ecclesiastical and true knowledge, and the persuasion respecting God, accedes to false and incongruous opinion, either by deifying any created object, or by making an idol of anything that exists not, so as to overstep, or rather step from, knowledge. And to the Gnostic false opinion is foreign, as the true belongs to him, and is allied with him. Wherefore the noble apostle calls one of the kinds of fornication, idolatry, in following the prophet, who says: "[My people] hath committed fornication with stock and stone. They have said to the stock, Thou art my father; and to the stone, Thou hast begotten me."
The Prescription Against Heretics

On this point, however, we dwell no longer, since it is the same Paul who, in his Epistle to the Galatians, counts "heresies" among "the sins of the flesh," who also intimates to Titus, that "a man who is a heretic" must be "rejected after the first admonition," on the ground that "he that is such is perverted, and committeth sin, as a self-condemned man.
Commentary on Galatians

Fourth in the catalogue of the works of the flesh, idolatry holds its place. For he who has once given himself over to licentiousness and pleasure does not look back to the Creator. Besides, all idolatry delights in festivity, gluttony, the belly, and the things that are below the belly. And lest sorceries and the arts of witchcraft should perhaps seem not to be forbidden in the New Testament, they too are named among the works of the flesh. For it often happens to the wretched through magic arts both to love and to be loved. Enmity too, which is placed after sorceries: what guilt it carries is declared by its being placed right after a manifest crime. For as far as lies in us, we ought to be no one's enemy, but to have peace with all. But if, by speaking the truth, we earn some enemies, it is not so much we who are their enemies as they who are enemies of the truth. For what is also said to Abraham in Genesis: "I will be an enemy to your enemies, and I will oppose those who oppose you", is to be understood as above: not so much that Abraham was an enemy to them, as that they were enemies to the virtues and religion of Abraham, by which, having trampled on idols, he worshiped the God he had come to know. That too which is commanded to the people of Israel, that with everlasting hatred and a discord handed down to their descendants they should be enemies to the Midianites (Num. 31), is said as to those who were under the pedagogue, and who in another place deserved to hear: "You shall hate your enemy" (Matt. 5:43). Or certainly the dissension was made not so much between persons as between ways of life: so that, just as God usefully put enmities between the serpent and the woman, lest their friendship, through which man was cast out of paradise, should be harmful to man, so also in the Israelites and the Midianites it was rather a dissimilar way of life than one nation that was condemned. The seventh place among the works of the flesh is held by strife, set as it were in a sacred and eminent number among the vices. "But the slave of the Lord ought not to quarrel, but to be gentle toward all, a teacher, long-suffering, instructing with gentleness even those who argue against him" (2 Tim. 2:24, 25). After strife there follows, eighth, jealousy, which in the Greek language is called more expressively and more familiarly ζῆλος. From this evil, indeed, I do not know which of us is free. For both the patriarchs were jealous of their brother Joseph, and Miriam and Aaron, the prophetess of God and the priest, were deceived by such a passion against Moses (Gen. 37; Num. 12): so much so that she of whom Scripture had told, saying: "And Miriam the prophetess, taking a timbrel" (Exod. 15:20), and the rest, was afterwards cast out of the camp, defiled with the disease of leprosy, and marked a longer penance by a separation of seven days (Num. 12). Then anger follows, which does not work the righteousness of God (Jas. 1), and is a species of fury. Between irascibility and anger, however, there is this difference: that the irascible man is always angry, while the angry man is roused for a time. And I do not know who could possess the kingdom of God, when he who is angry is separated from the kingdom (Matt. 5). Quarrels too, which the Greeks, signifying something else, call ἐριθείας (since a quarrel is called μάχη), keep men from the kingdom of God. Now ἐριθεία is when someone, always ready to contradict, delights in another's vexation, and contends with womanish wrangling, and provokes the one who contends with him. Among the Greeks this is called by another name, φιλονεικία (love of contention). Dissensions too are works of the flesh: when someone, being by no means perfect in the same mind and the same judgment, says: "I am of Paul, and I of Apollos, and I of Cephas, and I of Christ" (1 Cor. 1:12). But this same dissension is also found within households among themselves: namely of husband against wife, father against son, brother against brother, fellow slave against fellow slave, soldier against tent-mate, craftsman against craftsman of the same trade. Sometimes it happens that dissension arises even in the expositions of the Scriptures: from which the heresies too, which are now placed among the works of the flesh, bubble up. For if the wisdom of the flesh is hostile to God (Rom. 8) (and all doctrines of falsehood that fight against God are hostile to him), consequently heresies also, being hostile to God, are referred to the works of the flesh. Now Αἵρεσις in Greek is named from choice: because, namely, each one chooses for himself that discipline which he thinks is better. Whoever, therefore, understands Scripture otherwise than the sense of the Holy Spirit, by which it was written, demands, although he has not withdrawn from the Church, can nevertheless be called a heretic, and is of the works of the flesh, choosing the things that are worse.
Against Heresies Book I

But as to themselves, they hold that they shall be entirely and undoubtedly saved, not by means of conduct, but because they are spiritual by nature. For, just as it is impossible that material substance should partake of salvation (since, indeed, they maintain that it is incapable of receiving it), so again it is impossible that spiritual substance (by which they mean themselves) should ever come under the power of corruption, whatever the sort of actions in which they indulged. For even as gold, when submersed in filth, loses not on that account its beauty, but retains its own native qualities, the filth having no power to injure the gold, so they affirm that they cannot in any measure suffer hurt, or lose their spiritual substance, whatever the material actions in which they may be involved. Wherefore also it comes to pass, that the "most perfect" among them addict themselves without fear to all those kinds of forbidden deeds of which the Scriptures assure us that "they who do such things shall not inherit the kingdom of God." For instance, they make no scruple about eating meats offered in sacrifice to idols, imagining that they can in this way contract no defilement. Then, again, at every heathen festival celebrated in honour of the idols, these men are the first to assemble; and to such a pitch do they go, that some of them do not even keep away from that bloody spectacle hateful both to God and men, in which gladiators either fight with wild beasts, or singly encounter one another. Others of them yield themselves up to the lusts of the flesh with the utmost greediness, maintaining that carnal things should be allowed to the carnal nature, while spiritual things are provided for the spiritual.
On the Resurrection of the Flesh

It is after displaying to the Galatians these pernicious works that he professes to warn them beforehand, even as he had "told them in time past, that they which do such things should not inherit the kingdom of God," even because they bore not the image of the heavenly, as they had borne the image of the earthy; and so, in consequence of their old conversation, they were to be regarded as nothing else than flesh and blood.
Decretals, Epistles of Pope Fabian, To All the Bishops of the East, Of the right of bishops not to be accused or hurt by detraction

Those, furthermore, who commit those sins whereof the apostle says, "They who do such things shall not inherit the kingdom of God," are by all means to be guarded against, and are to be compelled to seek amendment if they do not choose it voluntarily, because they are marked with the stains of infamy, and go down into the pit, unless assistance is brought them by sacerdotal authority.
Commentary on Galatians

Envy follows heresies, which let us not think to be the same as zeal. For zeal can also be taken in a good sense, when someone strives to emulate the things that are better. But envy is tormented by another's happiness, and is split into a twofold passion: when either one is something oneself in that in which one does not wish another to be, or, seeing another to be better, one grieves that one is not like him. One of the moderns, translating a Greek verse, played finely in elegiac meter on envy, saying: Nothing is more just than envy, which straightway gnaws its own author and tortures his mind. The blessed Cyprian also wrote a very excellent book On Zeal and Envy, and whoever reads it will not hesitate to number envy among the works of the flesh. Between the envious man and the envied man there is this difference: that the envious man envies one more fortunate, while the envied man is he who suffers envy from another. The fourteenth place among the works of the flesh is held by drunkenness. For drunkards shall not possess the kingdom of God. And the Lord to the disciples: "Take heed", he says, "lest perhaps your hearts be weighed down with wine and debauchery" (Luke 21:34). By wine a man's senses are overturned, his feet stumble, his mind wavers, lust is kindled. Hence the Apostle cries out: "And wine, in which is licentiousness" (Eph. 5:18). Each one has the power of his own opinion. I follow the Apostle: that in wine there is licentiousness, in wine drunkenness. And that drunkenness and licentiousness are numbered among the works of the flesh, not even he who is overcome by these same passions can deny. And although some think I deserve blame in that book which I wrote on preserving virginity, because I said that young girls ought to flee wine like poison, I shall not repent of the opinion. For there it was rather the work of wine than a creature of God that was condemned by us; and we took away license from a virgin glowing with the natural heat of her age, lest under the pretext of drinking a little she should drink more and perish. Otherwise, we knew both that wine is consecrated into the blood of Christ and that Timothy was commanded to drink wine. Drunkenness, moreover, can come about as much from wine as from the other kinds of drink that are prepared in various ways; whence it is also said of the saint: "He shall not drink wine and strong drink (siceram)" (Luke 1:15). Sicera means "drunkenness". And lest anyone who does not drink wine should think that something else might be drunk by him, the pretext is excluded, since everything that can make drunk is taken away together with wine. The fifteenth, which is also the last among the works of the flesh, is carousing. "For the people ate and drank, and rose up to play" (Exod. 32:6). Licentiousness is always joined to drunkenness. A certain not undistinguished orator, describing a drunken man roused from sleep, said finely: "Once roused, he could not sleep, and being drunk, he could not stay awake." By this saying he expressed that in a certain way he was neither dead nor alive. It would be long to unfold all the works of the flesh and make a catalogue of the vices. So he included them all in one word, saying: and things like these. Would that we could avoid them as easily as we understand them! "I foretell", he says, "to you, as I foretold: that those who do such things shall not attain the kingdom of God". Where he had foretold it before: "Let not sin reign", he says, "in your mortal body, so as to obey its desires" (Rom. 6:12). Sin has all these species, on distinguishing which we have perhaps lingered now longer than was fitting. Therefore in a soul in which sin has reigned, the kingdom of God cannot reign. "For what partnership has righteousness with iniquity? What communion has light with darkness? What agreement has Christ with Belial?" (2 Cor. 6:14, 15). And we think that we attain the kingdom of God if we are free from fornication, idolatry and sorceries. Behold, enmities, strife, anger, quarrel, dissension, drunkenness too, and the rest which we consider small, exclude us from the kingdom of God. Nor does it matter whether one is excluded from blessedness by one or by several, since all alike exclude. In the Latin codices adultery also, and unchastity, and murders are reported as written in this catalogue of vices. But it must be known that no more than fifteen works of the flesh are named, and these we have also discussed.
Irenaeus Against Heresies Book 5

And then, again, he proceeds to tell us the spiritual actions which vivify a man, that is, the engrafting of the Spirit; thus saying, "But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, long-suffering, goodness, benignity, faith, meekness, continence, chastity: against these there is no law." As, therefore, he who has gone forward to the better things, and has brought forth the fruit of the Spirit, is saved altogether because of the communion of the Spirit; so also he who has continued in the aforesaid works of the flesh, being truly reckoned as carnal, because he did not receive the Spirit of God, shall not have power to inherit the kingdom of heaven.
The Stromata Book 4

"But I say, Walk in the Spirit, and ye shall not fulfil the lusts of the flesh," counsels the apostolic command; "for the flesh lusteth against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh. These, then, are contrary" (not as good to evil, but as fighting advantageously), he adds therefore, so that ye cannot do the things that ye would. Now the works of the flesh are manifest, which are, fornication uncleanness, profligacy, idolatry, witchcrafts, enmities, strifes, jealousies, wrath, contentions, dissensions, heresies, envyings, drunkenness, revellings, and such like; of which I tell you before, as I have also said before, that they which do such things shall not inherit the kingdom of God. But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, long-suffering, gentleness, temperance, goodness, faith, meekness." He calls sinners, as I think, "flesh," and the righteous "spirit."
Hippolytus Exegetical Fragments
And the fruits of Egypt are wasted, that is, the works of the flesh, but not the fruit of the Spirit, love, joy, and peace.
Methodius Discourse X. Domnina

The vine, and that not in a few places, refers to the Lord Himself, and the fig-tree to the Holy Spirit, as the Lord "maketh glad the hearts of men," and the Spirit healeth them. And therefore Hezekiah is commanded first to make a plaster with a lump of figs—that is, the fruit of the Spirit—that he may be healed—that is, according to the apostle—by love; for he says, "The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, long-suffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, meekness, temperance;" which, on account of their great pleasantness, the prophet calls figs.
Homily on Galatians 5

He says not, "the work of the Spirit," but, "the fruit of the Spirit." Is the soul, however, superfluous? the flesh and the Spirit are mentioned, but where is the soul? is he discoursing of beings without a soul? for if the things of the flesh be evil, and those of the Spirit good, the soul must be superfluous. By no means, for the mastery of the passions belongs to her, and concerns her; and being placed amid vice and virtue, if she has used the body fitly, she has wrought it to be spiritual, but if she separate from the Spirit and give herself up to evil desires, she makes herself more earthly. You observe throughout that his discourse does not relate to the substance of the flesh, but to the moral choice, which is or is not vicious. And why does he say, "the fruit of the Spirit?" it is because evil works originate in ourselves alone, and therefore he calls them "works," but good works require not only our diligence but God's loving kindness. He places first the root of these good things, and then proceeds to recount them, in these words, "Love, joy, peace, long-suffering, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, meekness, temperance; against such there is no law." For who would lay any command on him who hath all things within himself, and who hath love for the finished mistress of philosophy? As horses, who are docile and do every thing of their own accord, need not the lash, so neither does the soul, which by the Spirit hath attained to excellence, need the admonitions of the Law. Here too he completely and strikingly casts out the Law, not as bad, but as inferior to the philosophy given by the Spirit.
Commentary on Galatians

But the fruit of the spirit is love, joy, peace, long-suffering, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, self-control; against such there is no Law.

And what other among the fruits of the spirit ought to hold the first place, if not love, without which the other virtues are not reckoned to be virtues, and from which are born all things that are good? Indeed, both in the Law and in the Gospel it holds the chief place: "You shall love the Lord your God from your whole heart, and from your whole soul, and from your whole strength; and you shall love your neighbor as yourself" (Deut. 6:5; Matt. 22:37). With how many good things love is filled we have both touched on briefly above, and now let it suffice to have said even a little: that love does not seek the things that are its own, but those of another (1 Cor. 13). And although someone, by his own fault, is an enemy to the one who loves, and strives to stir up his tranquillity into the waves of hatred, yet he is never disturbed; never does he judge a creature of God worthy of hatred. For love covers a multitude of sins (1 Pet. 4:8). That saying too which is spoken by the Savior, "A good tree cannot bring forth evil fruits, nor an evil tree bring forth good fruits" (Matt. 7:18), I think was pronounced not so much about men as about the fruits of the flesh and of the spirit: because neither can the spirit ever commit those vices which have been enumerated among the works of the flesh, nor can the flesh abound in these fruits which arise from the spirit. It can happen, however, through the negligence of the one who possesses it, that the spirit which dwells in a man does not have its fruits; and, on the contrary, that the flesh, its works having been put to death, ceases to sin. Yet they do not go so far that the tree of the spirit, when neglected, bears the works of the flesh, and the tree of the flesh, when cultivated, puts forth spiritual fruits. In the second place among the spiritual fruits joy has been set, which the Stoics too, who distinguish between words rather subtly, judge to be something other than gladness. For joy, they say, is the elation of a mind exulting over things that are worthy; but gladness is an unbridled elation of the mind, which knows no measure, and rejoices even in things that are mixed with vice. Others set pleasure over against joy: not that pleasure which stirs the body to lust, tickles the senses, and flatters with a sweet feeling, but another bearing the same name as this (ὁμώνυμον), which without moderation and without any seemliness of gladness lifts up its voice in laughter. But if this is true, and their distinction between words neither deceives nor is deceived, let us consider whether perhaps it was for this reason that it was said: "There is no rejoicing for the ungodly, says the Lord" (Isa. 57:21). At the same time this too must be noted, that joy follows after love. For he who loves anyone always rejoices in his happiness. And if he sees him deceived by some error and fallen on the slippery ground of sins, he will grieve indeed, and will hasten to rescue him; but sadness will not be able to change his joy, since he knows that none of the rational creatures perishes forever before God. The third fruit of the spirit is peace, from which Solomon too, who went before as a type of Christ, received his name. And concerning the Church the Psalmist sings: "His place has been made in peace" (Ps. 75:2). And among the eight blessings of the Gospel it is written: "Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God" (Matt. 5:9). In the first psalm of the steps, too, it is sung: "With those who hated peace I was peaceable" (Ps. 119:6). And let us not think that peace is to be sought only in this, that we do not quarrel with another; rather, the peace of Christ, that is, our inheritance, is with us then, if a tranquil mind is disturbed by no passions. After peace follows long-suffering (longanimitas), or patience (patientia), because we can render μακροθυμίαν in either way. Contrary to this is faint-heartedness, of which it is written: "The faint-hearted man is exceedingly foolish; but he who is patient and bears all things is a wise man" (Sir. 7). And with intensification (ἐπιτάσει) he is called "very wise", as is also written in Proverbs: "A long-suffering man is great in prudence" (Prov. 14:29). Kindness (benignitas) also, or sweetness (suavitas) (since among the Greeks χρηστότης sounds as both), is a mild virtue, winning, tranquil, and fitted for the fellowship of all good men, inviting to familiarity with itself, sweet in speech, temperate in manners. Finally the Stoics too define it thus: Kindness is a virtue disposed of its own accord to doing good. Goodness is not much different from kindness, because it too seems disposed to doing good. But it differs in this, that goodness can be rather sombre, and with a brow furrowed by severe manners it can indeed do good and grant what is asked, yet not be sweet in fellowship and invite all by its own sweetness. This too the followers of Zeno define thus: Goodness is a virtue that profits; or, a virtue from which usefulness arises; or, a virtue for its own sake; or, a disposition which is the fountain of usefulnesses.

Among the fruits of the spirit, faith possesses the seventh and more sacred place, which elsewhere too is set among three: hope, faith, love. Nor is it any wonder if hope is not mentioned in this catalogue, since what is hoped for is in faith, and the Apostle, writing to the Hebrews, defines it thus: "Now faith is the substance of things to be hoped for, the proof of things not yet appearing" (Heb. 11:1). For that which we hope will come, and which is not yet in the present, we possess by faith, hoping that we hold what we believe. It is asked also how faith has been set in love. He who loves never judges himself to be wronged; he never suspects anything except that he loves and is loved. But when love has gone far away, faith departs along with it.
Commentary on Galatians

After faith gentleness is counted, which is opposed to anger, quarrels and dissensions, and is never provoked to its contraries, truly sprouting forth good fruits from the good tree of the spirit. Through this Moses, the servant of God, deserved to receive the testimony of Scripture, which says: "Moses was gentle, beyond all men upon the earth" (Num. 12:3). Upon the earth, he says. For he could not be beyond those who saw God face to face, because we are often compelled to do many things through the weakness of the flesh. Concerning David too (although many judge that it was prophesied of our Lord, which we also do not deny), the Holy Spirit sings, as a type of the one to come: "Remember, O Lord, David, and all his gentleness" (Ps. 131:1). Whose gentleness shone forth more than all toward Saul, Absalom and Shimei (1 Sam. 24; 2 Sam. 15)? When the one wished to kill him; the other, plotting a revolution, strove to cheat him of his rule; the other, throwing stones at him and tossing up dust, shouted and said: "Go out, go out, you wicked man" (ibid., 16:7). Self-control is placed last among the fruits of the spirit. This we ought to understand not only of chastity, but also of food and drink, of anger too and agitation of mind, and of the lust for disparaging others. Between modesty and self-control, however, there is this difference: that modesty is found in perfect men and those of consummate virtue, of whom the Savior says: "Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth" (Matt. 5:4); and of himself: "Learn from me, for I am meek, and humble, and gentle of heart" (Matt. 11:29). Self-control, on the other hand, is indeed on the road of virtue, but has not yet reached the goal, because desires still arise in the thought of the one who controls himself and pollute the ruling part of the mind, although they do not overcome him nor drag the one who thinks them into the deed. And self-control is necessary not only in desires and cupidity, but also in the three remaining passions, namely grief, gladness and fear. Against such fruits of the spirit there is no Law. "For the Law is not laid down for the righteous man, but for the wicked and the insubordinate, for the ungodly and sinners" (1 Tim. 1:9). The Law says to me: "You shall not commit adultery; you shall not kill; you shall not speak false testimony; you shall not defraud; you shall not desire what belongs to others; you shall not swear falsely; you shall not steal" (Exod. 20:12 ff.). If I do none of these things, because love, the fruit of the spirit, reigns in me, the precepts of the Law are superfluous to me. Finally, the wise men of the world too held this opinion about philosophy: that what the public laws compel men to do by necessity, philosophy persuades them to do by will.

Origen, linking this passage with the preceding ones, reads it thus: "Against such there is no Law, who have crucified the flesh of Christ with vices and lusts": so that he is not saying, as it sounds in the Latin, that those who are Christ's have crucified their own flesh with vices and lusts, but that the flesh of Christ has been crucified by them with vices and lusts. And he asks how, in the case of those who have the fruits of the spirit, and against whom the Law has ceased to be, the crucifixion of the Lord's flesh is set down as praise, when in Hebrews it is set down as reproach: "Crucifying again in themselves the Son of God, and holding him up to display" (Heb. 6:6). For "crucifying again" there is in the Greek, better, a single compound word, ἀνασταυροῦντες, which we can render "re-crucifying" (recrucifigentes). First, then, it must be noted that to crucify is one thing, to re-crucify another. Next, that to re-crucify the Son of God is not the same thing as to crucify the flesh of Christ with vices and lusts. For the flesh of Christ is not principally and properly the Son of God, but Jesus Christ, who, though he was in the beginning with the Father, God the Word, was made flesh and emptied himself, taking the form of a slave, so that he might crucify the flesh and despoil the principalities and powers, triumphing over them on the tree (Phil. 2), so that that saying of the Apostle might be fulfilled: "For in that he died, he died to sin once" (Rom. 6:10). Therefore, if our bodies are members of Christ, it follows that our flesh too is the flesh of Christ, which we crucify, mortifying through it, upon the earth, fornication, impurity, passion, evil desire and avarice; and it is now set down in praise of us, who have crucified the flesh of Christ Jesus with vices and lusts, and always carry about the mortification of Jesus in our body, so that his life also may be made manifest in our flesh. Yet it is no small labor so to live in the present age that even now the life of Jesus is made manifest in our flesh. For thus will our mortal bodies also be quickened through the spirit dwelling in us. Where the Latin translator put "vices", in the Greek παθήματα, that is, "passions", is read. And since passion can signify both pain and the other necessities of the poor body, the Apostle cautiously added "desires", so that he might not seem to deny the nature of the body in spiritual men, but the vices. And let this warning be given thus if we follow the common edition (Vulgatam editionem), reading: But those who are Christ's have crucified the flesh with vices and lusts: so that we say they have crucified not the flesh of Christ but their own. I had almost forgotten the second interpretation. For I had said beforehand that all that follows is to be referred to the Law and to circumcision. The sense, therefore, is this: those in whom is the fruit of the spirit, love, joy and the rest, have crucified the bodily understanding of Scripture, which is now called the flesh of Christ, with its passions and desires, which breed fuel for vices in little ones and sucklings. He has crucified the flesh of Christ who does not wage war according to the flesh of history, but follows the spirit of allegory going before him.

Let us not become desirous of empty glory, provoking one another, envying one another.

The single word κενόδοξοι (vainglorious) among the Greeks the Latin translator has expressed by a circumlocution of three words. How many definitions and meanings glory has, both the innumerable books of the philosophers and the two volumes that Cicero wrote on glory give evidence. But since we are attempting to discuss not the etymologies of words but the sense of Scripture, we will connect this passage with what precedes in this way: If we live by the spirit, let us obey the spirit, serving one another not at all through the Law but through love. We ought not to contend about the interpretation of the Scriptures and say: "Circumcision is better"; "No, rather uncircumcision"; "History is to be despised and allegory followed"; "Nay, allegory is empty and shadowy, and fixed by no roots of truth." From this it comes about that envyings arise against one another. "For they wish", he says, "to shut you out, that you may emulate them": wishing not so much to teach the truth of the Law as to win. But so that we may not pass over the word glory entirely untouched, leaving the philosophers their trifles, let us go over some points from the Scriptures. The name of glory denotes the opinion of the crowd and praise sought through the favor of men, where it is said: "But they do all things that they may be glorified by men" (Matt. 23:5). And elsewhere: "How can you believe, seeking glory from one another" (John 5:44)? Further, in a good sense, in the same place: "And not seeking the glory that is from him who alone is". From this we understand that the same word signifies now a virtue, now a vice. If I seek glory from men, it is a vice; if from God, it is a virtue, for he also exhorts us to true glory, saying: "But those who glorify me I will glorify". Glory also signifies something else in the divine Scriptures, when something more august and more divine presents itself to the gaze of men. The glory of the Lord was seen in the tabernacle (Exod. 40), and in the temple that was built by Solomon there was glory (1 Kings 8:10-11), and in the face of Moses, when he did not know that his countenance had been glorified; and of this glory of the countenance I think the Apostle too speaks: "But we all, contemplating the glory of the Lord with unveiled face, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the spirit of God" (2 Cor. 3:18). And the Savior himself has been called the splendor of glory and the figure of the substance of God (Heb. 1). Stephen too saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing at his right hand (Acts 7). Now, that we too may take upon ourselves the license of coining names (for new things, as someone says, new names must be coined): since here it is said, Let us not become desirous of empty, or of vacant glory, let us assert that those are desirous of full glory who desire the glory of God, and the praise worthy of virtue, and a sight showing forth something more divine. Hence too in very many places our translators have rendered "majesty" in place of glory. For a long time now I have been longing to burst out into words, but I am held back by fear of speaking. Yet I will speak, and I will not keep silent about my own passion, a passion almost common to all: not about riches, not about power, not about beauty and comeliness of body, for these are plainly named among the works of the flesh. Almsgiving, if it is done for the sake of praise, is empty glory; so is long prayer, and the pallor that follows from fasting. These are not my words, but those of the Savior thundering in the Gospel (Matt. 6). Chastity itself too, in marriage, in widowhood, in virgins, often seeks human applause; and, what I have long been afraid to say, yet it must be said, martyrdom itself, if it is undergone so that we may be held in admiration and praise by the brothers: the blood has been shed in vain. Let the Apostle speak, let the vessel of election speak: "If I hand over my body that I may glory, but have not love, it profits me nothing" (1 Cor. 13:3). To him who had said: "I know a man in Christ fourteen years ago, whether in the body, I do not know, or out of the body, I do not know, God knows, caught up as far as the third heaven" (2 Cor. 12:2); and a little after: "Caught up into paradise, he heard secret words which it is not lawful for a man to speak": to him, I say, who labored more than all, lest the greatness of the revelations should exalt him, there was given a goad of his flesh, an angel of Satan, to buffet him, so that he might not be lifted up. And indeed three times he asked the Lord that it might depart from him; but it was said to him: "My grace is sufficient for you: for power is perfected in weakness". What is so much the work of God as to read the Scriptures, to preach in the Church, to desire the priesthood, to minister before the altar of the Lord? Yet even these, unless one guards his heart with all diligence, spring from the desire for praise. You may see very many (as Tully too says) inscribing their books "On despising glory", and, for the sake of glory, setting the titles of their own name at the head. We interpret the Scriptures; we often turn the stylus; we write things worthy to be read; and unless these are done for the sake of Christ, but for remembrance among posterity and fame among the peoples, the whole labor will be made void, and we shall be like a sounding drum and a clanging cymbal (1 Cor. 13). You may see very many contending among themselves about the Scriptures and making the word of God an athletic arena: they provoke one another, and if they are beaten, they envy; for they are desirous of empty glory. I know that in the Latin codices, in the testimony we set down above, "If I hand over my body that I may glory", they have "that I may burn" (ardeam) in place of "that I may glory" (glorier); but because of the similarity of the word, by which among the Greeks "I may burn" and "I may glory", that is, καυθήσομαι and καυχήσομαι, are distinguished by part of a single letter, the error has grown up among our people. But among the Greeks themselves, too, the copies differ.

He says not, "in meekness," but, "in a spirit of meekness," signifying thereby that this is acceptable to the Spirit, and that to be able to administer correction with mildness is a spiritual gift. Brothers, and if a man has been overtaken in some fault, you who are spiritual, instruct such a one in the spirit of gentleness, considering yourself, lest you too be tempted.

Paul knew that he was a worshiper of that God who does not want the death of the sinner, but his repentance (Ezek. 18, 33), and that, the Trinity excepted, every creature, even if it does not sin, nevertheless can sin; so he exhorts even the one who is spiritual, through fear for himself lest he sin, to stretch out his hand to one who is falling. And he fittingly calls the one overtaken in a fault a "man," one who can die, showing by the very name the frailty of his condition, so that he who, as a man deceived by error and plunged into a whirlpool, cannot raise himself up without help and a helper may be worthy of pardon. But to the spiritual one "man" is not added; rather, it is commanded as though to God, that he should instruct the man overtaken in a fault, or (as the Greek has it better) perfect him, in the spirit of mildness. Now he who is being perfected does not lack everything, but some things. In short, if he has gone astray overtaken not by many sins but by some vice, let the spiritual man apply the spirit of mildness and gentleness in correcting the sinner, lest he wish to correct the one who errs while rigid, while angry and severe; but let him call him forth, pledging salvation, promising pardon; let him bring forward the testimony of Christ, that he invites those weighed down by the heavy burden of the law and of sins to his sweet yoke and light burden, that they may learn that he is humble and meek and gentle of heart (Matt. 11), and may find rest for their souls. Let us use this testimony against the heretics who, inventing fables of diverse natures, say that the spiritual is a good tree and never bears bad fruit. Behold, the Apostle, whose authority they themselves also follow, says that those who are spiritual can sin, if through the loftiness of their heart they are puffed up and fall. This we too likewise confess; and also that the χοϊκοὺς ("earthly") become spiritual, if they turn back to better things. There may be set against us what is written to the Corinthians: "What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod, or in love and the spirit of gentleness" (1 Cor. 4:21)? For if there he says that he comes to sinners not in the spirit of gentleness but with a rod, how is it that here, to those who have been overtaken in some sin, he applies not the rod but the spirit of gentleness? But there it is said to those who, after their sin, not perceiving their error, were unwilling to be subject to their superiors and to be corrected by repentance. Where, however, the sinner, understanding his wound, hands himself over to the physician to be cured, there the rod is not necessary, but the spirit of mildness. But perhaps this too may be asked: if someone ought to instruct a sinner in the spirit of mildness for this reason, that he considers himself lest he too be tempted, then the righteous man, who is certain of his own mind, who knows that he cannot fall, ought not to instruct the sinner in the spirit of mildness? To this we shall say that even if the righteous man has conquered, knowing with how much labor he overcame, he will all the more grant pardon to the one who sins. For the Savior too was tempted for this reason, in all things like us, without sin, so that he might be able to suffer with us and to grieve with our infirmities, taught by his own example how difficult victory is in the flesh. If anyone has remained a virgin right up to old age, let him pardon the one who was once deceived by the heat of youth, knowing with what difficulties he passed through that age. If anyone, tortured for confessing the name of Christ, sees another, in torments, deny, let him have compassion on the wounds of the denier, and let him marvel not so much that the other was conquered as that he himself conquered. Notice also the caution of the writer, in that he did not say: Considering yourself, lest you fall; but, lest you too be tempted. For to be conquered or to conquer is sometimes in our power; but to be tempted is in the power of the tempter. For if the Savior was tempted, who can be secure that he will cross the seas of this life untempted? Let those who think that Paul said out of humility, and not truly, "Even if I am unskilled in speech, yet not in knowledge", defend the coherence of this passage. For according to proper order he ought to have said: "You who are spiritual, instruct such a one in the spirit of mildness, considering yourselves, lest you too be tempted"; and not to bring in the singular number after the plural. A Hebrew of the Hebrews, then, and one who was most learned in his native tongue, was not able to express deep meanings in a foreign language; nor did he care greatly about words, since he had the sense safe. These things according to the simple understanding. But, so that we may also pursue the order of the second exposition, this passage is to be opened up from the end of the Epistle to the Romans. For there, when he was likewise writing about the foods and observances of the Jews, and was describing those who despised the precepts of the Law according to the letter as strong and perfect, but those who were still led by the ancient custom as weak and little ones, and saw that there was a quarrel between the spiritual and the fleshly, he admonished the spiritual not to despise the fleshly, and said: "But take up the one who is weak in faith, not in disputes over thoughts. For one believes he may eat all things; but he who is weak, let him eat vegetables. Let him who eats not despise him who does not eat; and let him who does not eat not judge him who eats, for God has taken him up. Who are you to judge another's slave? To his own master he stands or falls. But he will stand: for God is able to make him stand" (Rom. 14:1 ff.). And after discussing much in between on this sense, he added at the end: "Do not, for the sake of food, destroy the work of God". And again: "But we who are stronger ought to bear the weaknesses of the weak, and not to please ourselves. Let each of you please his neighbor for good edification" (Rom. 15:1, 2).

Commentary on Galatians

Bear one another's burdens, and so you will fulfil the law of Christ.

That sin is a burden, the Psalmist too testifies, saying: "My iniquities are lifted up over my head; like a heavy burden they have weighed heavily upon me" (Ps. 37:5). And Zechariah saw iniquity, in the form of a woman, sitting upon a talent of lead (Zech. 5). This burden the Savior bore for us, teaching us by his own example what we ought to do. For he himself carries our iniquities and grieves for us (Isa. 53), and those who are weighed down by the burden of sins and of the Law he invites to the light burden of virtue, saying: "My yoke is sweet, and my burden light" (Matt. 11:30). Whoever, therefore, does not despair of a brother's salvation, but stretches out his hand to him as he pleads, and, as far as lies in him, weeps with the one who weeps, is weak with the weak, and judges the sins of others to be his own, he through love fulfils the law of Christ. What is the law of Christ? "This is my commandment, that you love one another" (John 13:34). What is the law of the Son of God? "Love one another, as I also have loved you". How did the Son of God love us? "There is no greater love than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends" (John 15:13). Whoever has no clemency, and has not put on the bowels of mercy and of tears, though he be spiritual, will not fulfil the law of Christ. But let us also join this passage with what went before. For we follow a twofold understanding. If anyone is weak in the faith, and is still nourished on the milk of infancy, and cannot so quickly pass from the observance of the Law to the spiritual mysteries, you who are stronger, bear his burdens, so that the brother for whom Christ died may not perish through your knowledge. He also bears a brother's need who helps a poor man weighed down by the burden of want, and makes himself friends of the mammon of iniquity (Luke 16); and him Christ addresses after the resurrection: "Come to me, you blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. For I was hungry, and you gave me to eat; I was thirsty, and you gave me to drink" (Matt. 25:34, 35). In accordance with this sense Paul also, teaching Timothy in another Epistle, added: "Command the rich of this age not to be high-minded" (that is to say, "not to be proud"), "nor to hope in the uncertainty of riches, but in God, who furnishes all things abundantly for enjoyment; to do good, to be rich in good works, to give readily, to share, to lay up for themselves a good foundation for the future, that they may lay hold of the true life" (1 Tim. 6:17-19). Whoever has laid hold of the true life, that is, of him who says: "I am the life" (John 14:6), has fulfilled the law of Christ, which tends toward life.
Homily on Galatians 6

"For if a man thinketh himself to be something, when he is nothing, he deceiveth himself."

Here again he reflects on their arrogance. He that thinks himself to be something is nothing, and exhibits at the outset a proof of his worthlessness by such a disposition.
Commentary on Galatians

For if anyone thinks himself to be something, when he is nothing, he leads himself astray.

If anyone will not carry the burdens of others, and, without mercy, is content with his own work and virtue alone, seeking not the things that are another's but the things that are his own, that is, a lover of himself alone and not also of God, he himself leads himself astray. Now this can be read and punctuated in two ways: either, "if anyone thinks himself to be something, when he is nothing"; or thus: "If anyone thinks himself to be something", so that we afterwards add, "when he is nothing, he leads himself astray". And this difference resounds more in the Greek than in the Latin. The sense of the first punctuation is this: He who thinks himself to be something, and is nothing, deceives himself. The second sense is loftier, and is the one that pleases us more: If anyone thinks himself to be something, in that he supposes himself to be something, and judges himself not by clemency toward his neighbor but by his own work and labor, content with his own virtue alone, that man by this very arrogance becomes nothing, and he himself deceives himself: which is better said in the Greek, φρεναπατᾷ, that is, he deceives his own mind; for which the Latin translator put "he leads himself astray" (se ipse seducit). And he deceives his own mind who supposes himself to be wise, and, according to Isaiah, is wise in himself and understanding in his own sight (Isa. 5). With reference to circumcision and the Law, the understanding of this passage is connected thus: He who is spiritual, and has no mercy toward his neighbor, despising the lowly because he himself is loftier, he himself deceives himself, not knowing that this is the law of the spirit, that we love one another.
Sermons on the Song of Songs, Sermon 69

For the foolish woman believed him who promised, but who was deceiving: "You shall be as gods, knowing good and evil." Had he not already first deceived himself, he who had persuaded himself that he would be like the Most High? For he who thinks himself to be something, when he is nothing, deceives himself.
Homily on Galatians 6

"But let each man prove his own work."

Here he shows that we ought to be scrutinizers of our lives, and this not lightly, but carefully to weigh our actions; as for example, if thou hast performed a good deed, consider whether it was not from vain glory, or through necessity, or malevolence, or with hypocrisy, or from some other human motive. For as gold appears to be bright before it is placed in the furnace, but when committed to the fire, is closely proved, and all that is spurious is separated from what is genuine, so too our works, if closely examined, will be distinctly made manifest, and we shall perceive that we have exposed ourselves to much censure.

"And then shall he have his glorying in regard of himself alone and not of his neighbor."

This he says, not as laying down a rule, but in the way of concession; and his meaning is this: Boasting is senseless, but if thou wilt boast, boast not against thy neighbor, as the Pharisee did. For he that is so instructed will speedily give up boasting altogether; and therefore he concedes a part that he may gradually extirpate the whole. He that is wont to boast with reference to himself only, and not against others, will soon reform this failing also. For he that does not consider himself better than others, for this is the meaning of "not in regard of his neighbor," but becomes elated by examining himself by himself, will afterwards cease to be so. And that you may be sure this is what he desires to establish, observe how he checks him by fear, saying above, "let every man prove his own work," ...
Commentary on Galatians

But let every man prove his own work: and so he shall have glory in himself only, and not in another.

This is the sense: You who reckon yourself spiritual, and are stronger by reason of another's weakness, ought not to consider the feebleness of the one who lies fallen, but your own strength. For if another cannot pass perfectly from Judaism to Christianity, it does not follow that you are therefore a perfect Christian; but if your own conscience does not reproach you, you have glory in yourself and not in another. An athlete is not strong because he has defeated a weak man and overcome the feeble limbs of his opponent; but if he is sturdy, and glories in his own strength, not in the weakness of another. It can also be understood in another way: he who has the consciousness of a good work, and, considering himself, finds no fault with his own work, ought not to glory about this before another, and pour out his praise abroad, and share it with everyone, and seek a boast from the favor of men; but let him have glory in himself, and say: "But far be it from me to glory, except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world is crucified to me, and I to the world". He who seeks glory from another, to him the world has not been crucified, nor has he himself been crucified with Christ. For he has received his reward, what he was seeking from men.
Homily on Galatians 6

"For each man shall bear his own burden."

He appears to state a reason prohibitory of boasting against another; but at the same time he corrects the boaster, so that he may no more entertain high thoughts of himself by bringing to his remembrance his own errors, and pressing upon his conscience the idea of a burden, and of being heavily laden.
Commentary on Galatians

For each one shall bear his own burden.

This seems to contradict what went before, where he says: "Bear one another's burdens": for if each one shall bear his own burden, one will not be able to bear another's burdens. But we must see that there he commanded that in this life we should support one another when we sin, and be a help to each other in the present age; here, however, he speaks of the Lord's judgment upon us: that it is not by another's sin and by comparison with someone worse, but according to our own work, that we are judged by him either sinners or saints, each one receiving according to his own work. Though obscurely, we are taught through this little saying a new doctrine that lies hidden: that while we are in the present age we can help one another, whether by prayers or by counsels; but when we have come before the judgment seat of Christ, neither Job nor Daniel nor Noah can intercede for anyone, but each one bears his own work (Ezek. 14).
Homily on Galatians 6

"But let him that is taught in the word communicate unto him that teacheth in all good things."

Here he proceeds to discourse concerning Teachers, to the effect that they ought to be tended with great assiduity by their disciples. Now what is the reason that Christ so commanded? For this law, "that they which preach the Gospel should live of the Gospel," (1 Cor. ix: 14.) is laid down in the New Testament; and likewise in the Old, (Num. xxxi: 47; xxxv; 1-8.) many revenues accrued to the Levites from the people; what is the reason, I say, that He so ordained? Was it not for the sake of laying a foundation beforehand of lowliness and love? For inasmuch as the dignity of a teacher oftentimes elates him who possesses it, He, in order to repress his spirit, hath imposed on him the necessity of requiring aid at the hands of his disciples. And to these in turn he hath given means of cultivating kindly feelings, by training them, through the kindness required of them to their Teacher, in gentleness towards others also. By this means no slight affection is generated on both sides. Were not the cause of this what I have stated it to be, why should He, who fed the dull-minded Jews with manna, have reduced the Apostles to the necessity of asking for aid? Is it not manifest He aimed at the great benefits of humility and love, and that those who were under teaching might not be ashamed of Teachers who were in appearance despicable? To ask for aid bears the semblance of disgrace, but it ceased to be so, when their Teachers with all boldness urged their claim, so that their disciples derived from hence no small benefit, taught hereby to despise all appearances. Wherefore he says, "But let him that is taught in the word communicate unto him that teacheth in all good things," that is, let him show to him all generosity; this he implies by the words, "in all good things." Let the disciple, says he, keep nothing to himself, but have every thing in common, for what he receives is better than what he gives - as much better as heavenly are better than earthly things. This he expresses in another place, "If we sowed unto you spiritual things, is it a great matter if we shall reap your carnal things?" (1 Cor. ix: 11.) Wherefore he gives the procedure the name of a "communication," showing that an interchange takes place. Hereby too love is greatly fostered and confirmed. If the teacher asks merely for competency, he does not by receiving it derogate from his own dignity. For this is praiseworthy, so assiduously to apply to the Word, as to require the aid of others, and to be in manifold poverty, and to be regardless of all the means of subsistence. But if he exceed the due measure, he injures his dignity, not by mere receiving, but by receiving too much. Then, lest the vice of the Teacher should render the disciple more remiss in this matter, and he should frequently pass him by, though poor, on account of his conduct, ...
Commentary on Galatians

But let him who is catechized in the word share with him who catechizes him in all good things.

Marcion interpreted this passage in such a way as to think that the faithful and the catechumens ought to pray together, and that the teacher ought to share in prayer with his disciples; he was especially carried away by the fact that there follows in all good things. Yet surely, if the discourse had been about prayer, the command ought not to have been given to him who is catechized, but to him who catechizes him, that is, not to the disciple, but to the teacher. Then, too, the other things that follow do not agree with his exposition: "Whatever a man has sown, that he will also reap". And: "But in doing good let us not fail: for in its own time we shall reap, not failing". This, therefore, is the sense: since above he had commanded the spiritual to instruct in a spirit of gentleness those who had been overtaken in some fault, and to bear one another's burdens, fulfilling the law of Christ, now, on the contrary, he commands those who were still weaker, and disciples, and carnal, that, just as they themselves reap spiritual things from their teachers, so they should furnish carnal things to their teachers, who, giving themselves wholly to divine learning and study, are in need of the necessities of this life; and so that may come to pass which is written of the manna: "He who had much did not have too much; and he who had little did not have too little" (2 Cor. 8:15). Now in the present passage he has called good things, according to the custom of the crowd and common usage, food and clothing and the other things that men count among good things. "For having food and clothing, with these we are content" (1 Tim. 6:8). Nor is it surprising if Paul designated the things that were necessary to the body by the name of good, since even our Savior, to those who had not yet ascended to the summit of the virtues but were still walking on a lower level, and who were asking that faith be added to them, said: "If therefore you, though you are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your heavenly Father give good things to those who ask him" (Matt. 7:11)! I think that Job too, when he was speaking to his wife as to one of the foolish women, spoke of bodily riches with regard to her, who thought so: "If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord" (Job 2:10); and again, of the straits and afflictions and temptation, which bring victory: "Why should we not endure evil?" Whereas, surely, evil and good are placed not in riches and afflictions, but in virtues and vices, as the righteous man says in the psalm: "Who is the man who wants life, desires to see good days? Keep your tongue from evil, and let your lips not speak deceit. Turn away from evil, and do good" (Ps. 33:13 ff., and 36:27). Properly, evil is called that which must be avoided; good, that which we ought to do. That rich man too in the Gospel, who did not have the knowledge of evil and good, rightly reckoned the fruitfulness of his fields to be good things, saying: "Soul, you have good things laid up for many years: rest, eat, drink, and be merry" (Luke 12:19). And the other, who lay in purple and abounded in delights, hears from Abraham in the underworld: "You received good things in your life" (Luke 16:25). This also must be considered, whether perhaps it may also be understood that a command is given to the disciples to share the word with those who instruct them, to obey them, and to show themselves teachable and compliant; yet in those things that are good, that are spiritual, and not perverted by heretical or Jewish depravity.

Something of the kind the Apostle too, as we have said already, commands the Galatians: Let him who is catechized share with him who catechizes him in all good things, and he exhorts disciples to the refreshment of their teachers; and since anyone could plead poverty and evade the command, before such a one could put it forward he resolves the impending question, saying: Do not be deceived; God is not mocked; for what a man sows, that he will also reap; and the sense is: in vain do you plead want when your conscience holds something else; you can deceive me as I exhort you, but know that however much you sow, so much you will also reap.

For which reason you must diligently observe and keep the practice delivered from divine tradition and apostolic observance, which is also maintained among us, and almost throughout all the provinces; that for the proper celebration of ordinations all the neighbouring bishops of the same province should assemble with that people for which a prelate is ordained. And the bishop should be chosen in the presence of the people, who have most fully known the life of each one, and have looked into the doings of each one as respects his habitual conduct. And this also, we see, was done by you in the ordination of our colleague Sabinus; so that, by the suffrage of the whole brotherhood, and by the sentence of the bishops who had assembled in their presence, and who had written letters to you concerning him, the episcopate was conferred upon him, and hands were imposed on him in the place of Basilides. Neither can it rescind an ordination rightly perfected, that Basilides, after the detection of his crimes, and the baring of his conscience even by his own confession, went to Rome and deceived Stephen our colleague, placed at a distance, and ignorant of what had been done, and of the truth, to canvass that he might be replaced unjustly in the episcopate from which he had been righteously deposed. The result of this is, that the sins of Basilides are not so much abolished as enhanced, inasmuch as to his former sins he has also added the crime of deceit and circumvention. For he is not so much to be blamed who has been through heedlessness surprised by fraud, as he is to be execrated who has fraudulently taken him by surprise. But if Basilides could deceive men, he cannot deceive God, since it is written, "God is not mocked." But neither can deceit advantage Martialis, in such a way as that he who also is involved in great crimes should hold his bishopric, since the apostle also warns, and says, "A bishop must be blameless, as the steward of God."

And here he points out the difference between ambition of this kind, and in temporal affairs, by saying, "Be not deceived; God is not mocked; for whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap. For he that soweth unto his own flesh shall of the flesh reap corruption; but he that soweth unto the Spirit shall of the Spirit reap eternal life." As in the case of seeds, one who sows pulse cannot reap corn, for what is sown and what is reaped must both be of one kind, so is it in actions, he that plants in the flesh, wantonness, drunkenness, or inordinate desire, shall reap the fruits of these things. And what are these fruits? Punishment, retribution, shame, derision, destruction. For of sumptuous tables and viands the end is no other than destruction; for they both perish themselves, and destroy the body too. But the fruit of the Spirit is of a nature not similar but contrary in all respects to these. For consider; hast thou sown alms-giving? the treasures of heaven and eternal glory await thee: hast thou sown temperance? honor and reward, and the applause of Angels, and a crown from the Judge await thee.
Commentary on Galatians

Be not deceived, God is not mocked: for what things a man sows, these he shall also reap.

Foreseeing in the spirit that those who are taught, and who ought to supply their teachers with expenses and the necessities of life, could plead poverty and say: My field has dried up this year with drought; hail has crushed my vineyard; the taxes have carried off the revenues that there could have been; I have nothing from which to give what is commanded, he added: Be not deceived, God is not mocked. He knows, he says, your hearts; he is not ignorant of your means. A plausible excuse can somehow placate a man; it cannot deceive God. And at the same time he exhorts them to render what has been commanded, calling it seed, so that one should not think lost what he is going to receive back with multiplied interest. To the Corinthians too he taught the reckoning of what is given and received by a similar example: "He who sows sparingly shall also reap sparingly: and he who sows in blessing shall also reap of blessing. Each one as he has purposed in his heart, not out of sadness or of necessity: for God loves a cheerful giver" (2 Cor. 9:6-7).

But there is that species of knowledge which is characteristic of the herald, and that which is, as it were, characteristic of a messenger, and it is serviceable in whatever way it operates, both by the hand and tongue. There is a time when we sow and the enemies cannot corrupt the seeds that we sow, they cannot lie in wait for our husbandry; but there is also a time when we sow and what we sow is corrupted. Let Paul the Apostle teach us about this difference in sowing. Hear, then, what he himself says: "he who sows," he says, "in the flesh, of the flesh shall reap corruption, and he who sows in the spirit, of the spirit shall reap life eternal." These, then, are they whose seeds the Midianites corrupt, who "sow in the flesh." These are they whose "fruits are destroyed" and perish. But those seeds which "are sown in the spirit" the Midianites cannot corrupt. For the adversary powers cannot ascend to the spiritual fields and defile the fresh-broken ground of the spirit belonging to those who "do not sow upon thorns, but break up for themselves fresh ground." But this too must be added; for I wish to admonish both myself along with you concerning wariness over the seeds and diligence over the spiritual fruits. It frequently happens that someone, toiling much in spiritual work, has produced very many fruits and filled his barns with the crops of righteousness and stored up many good works in the inner chamber of his conscience; but afterward, if he grows negligent and after his labor inclines too readily toward pleasures and self-indulgence, all those seeds of good things and the fruits of holy work will be corrupted under the dominion of lust.
Commentary on Galatians

For he who sows in his own flesh, from the flesh shall also reap corruption. But he who sows in the spirit, from the spirit shall reap life everlasting.

Everything that we speak, do and think is sown in two fields, the flesh and the spirit. If the things brought forth from hand, mouth and heart are good, sown in the spirit, they will overflow with the fruits of eternal life. If they are evil, received by the field of the flesh, they will sprout for us a harvest of corruption. Another way: he who understands the law carnally also expects carnal promises, and things that are corrupted in the present age. But he who is a spiritual hearer sows in the spirit, and from the spirit shall reap life everlasting. At the same time let us note the sequence of the discourse and link it with what went before: the one who sows in the spirit is called a man, and when he has begun to reap life everlasting, he perhaps ceases to be a man. Cassianus, who, bringing in a putative (merely apparent) flesh of Christ, judges every union of male with female unclean, the most vehement heresiarch of the Encratites, used against us, on the occasion of the present testimony, an argument of this sort: If anyone sows in the flesh, from the flesh he shall reap corruption; but he who is joined to a woman sows in the flesh; therefore he too who has intercourse with a wife, and sows in her flesh, from the flesh shall reap corruption. He will be answered, first, that Paul did not say, "he who sows in the flesh," but, in his own flesh. Yet no one lies with himself and sows in his own flesh. Next, even if we grant him, over and above, this observation which we have noted, in his own flesh, it must be added that, by his reckoning, those also who eat and drink and sleep and do anything for the refreshment of the body sow in the flesh, and from it reap corruption. But if he takes refuge in saying that those who, whether they drink or eat or sleep, nevertheless do everything with reason in the name of the Lord do not sow in the flesh but in the spirit, we too will answer him in like manner that those also who follow God's first sentence, acting with reason: "Increase and multiply, and fill the earth" (Gen. 1:22), sow not in the flesh but in the spirit. And so his syllogism, futile and tottering, deceives the hearer at first by a sophism; but, carefully inspected, it is easily resolved. For we cannot say that Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and the other holy men who were born of the promise, and even the Lord's forerunner himself, because he was born in the flesh, sprouted from a seed of corruption. This also must likewise be observed, that he who sows in the flesh is set down with the addition "of his own flesh," whereas he who sows in the spirit is not said to sow in his own spirit, but simply in the spirit. For he who sows good things sows not in anything of his own, but in the spirit of God, from which he is also to reap life eternal.
